paragraphs.text: “Do you know why Iʼm only talking about Ráŕh and not about any other part of Gondwanaland? Elsewhere it was extremely cold and full of snowstorms. There was no proper environment there for human beings to evolve. Ráŕh had the living touch of warmth, so humans came there first. They founded the worldʼs most ancient civilization and culture, which we can call the original Ráŕh culture. ( 3 )
summary: “Do you know why Iʼm only talking about Ráŕh and not about any other part of Gondwanaland?
There was no proper environment there for human beings to evolve.
They founded the worldʼs most ancient civilization and culture, which we can call the original Ráŕh culture.

paragraphs.text: “Nothing is static in this world – neither animate nor inanimate. It is not only that these rivers carried vital force for existence. They also led the irresistible advance of civilization and culture swiftly toward union with the sea. The civilization that is founded upstream in the river reaches its fullness downstream. No two rivers carry identical civilizations. Thus, after two rivers merge, their combined flow carries yet a third civilization.
summary: “Nothing is static in this world – neither animate nor inanimate.
The civilization that is founded upstream in the river reaches its fullness downstream.
Thus, after two rivers merge, their combined flow carries yet a third civilization.

paragraphs.text: “Take, for instance, a small example. In our Birbhum there are two very small rivers: the Kopai and the Bakreshwara. The flow of these two civilizations and cultures is nearly the same. The spoken language of the people who live on their banks is also almost the same. But notice, I say ‘almost’ rather than ‘the same’ because they are not identical. Afterwards, when they join each other in Melanpur near Indas Village (the famous Indrahása from the Jain era) and become the Kuye River, then its accompanying civilization and culture becomes a little altered. The people who live on the banks of the Kuye River enjoy the blessings of both the Kopai and Bakreshwara Rivers.
summary: “Take, for instance, a small example.
The spoken language of the people who live on their banks is also almost the same.
The people who live on the banks of the Kuye River enjoy the blessings of both the Kopai and Bakreshwara Rivers.

paragraphs.text: “Dumka, Suri, Sainthia, and Kandi – these four towns are in the Mayurakshi Valley. Their customs, behaviour, mode of living and spoken language are the same, but the Mandar hill, which is very near Dumka, is situated on the Chandan River, and thus the customs, comportment and language there is different from Dumkaʼs. Kandi is quite far from Dumka, but they are alike in all ways. Kandi is very close to Jangipur, but Jangipurʼs culture is different; its spoken language is Shershahabadiiya Bengali. You will find this kind of history with all rivers. The rivers of Ráŕh did not simply carry sand and alluvium to the sea, thereby creating the Bengal plains; they also brought the verdant riches of civilization and culture to Bengal.

Kandi is very close to Jangipur, but Jangipurʼs culture is different; its spoken language is Shershahabadiiya Bengali.
The rivers of Ráŕh did not simply carry sand and alluvium to the sea, thereby creating the Bengal plains; they also brought the verdant riches of civilization and culture to Bengal.

paragraphs.text: “After the rise of the Himalayas from the ocean, the Ganges and the Brahmaputra brought the flow of civilization and culture with the current of their waters. The Ganges brought the Indo-Aryan culture, but near Sahebganj, where the Ganges turns south, the Gaoŕiya [a portion of Bengalee] influence over the cultural life increased. Similarly, as the Brahmaputra reached the Assam Valley near Sadiya there was a mixture of the Kiḿpuruśavarśiiya [Tibetan] and Suvarńa Dviipiiya [Burmese] civilizations. The triple mixture of these two with the Indo-Aryan gave rise to the Kamarup civilization which a little downriver became transformed into the Bengalee culture.

Similarly, as the Brahmaputra reached the Assam Valley near Sadiya there was a mixture of the Kiḿpuruśavarśiiya [Tibetan] and Suvarńa Dviipiiya [Burmese] civilizations.

paragraphs.text: “The verdancy and artistry of the Bengalee civilization and culture of today has been enriched by the civilization and culture carried by the many small rivers and tributaries of Ráŕh, and with the admixture of the Ganges and Brahmaputra civilizations the Bengalee civilization has achieved its incomparable sweetness.”

paragraphs.text: “Of course, I have a strong attraction for the terrain of Gondwanaland,” continued Manjula. “But I feel more attraction for the different plants and wild animals of this area, in a word, the flora and fauna. In the laterite soil of this land you find mostly, palásh [Butea monosperma], kuśum [Schleichera oleosa], piyál (piyáshál) [Mimosa odoratassima], sal [Shorea robusta], and kendu [Disopros ambriyotres] trees. You also come across wild jackfruit, wild mango and custard-apple trees. Was the tree-life and different birds and beasts of this area the same during the end of the [[Miocene or beginning of the Pliocene]] ages when ape-men first appeared?”

The tree was ten times taller than the palásh trees of today. The flowers were bright red but very big in size, and the fruits were quite small but sweet and juicy.”

paragraphs.text: “Your thinking is correct,” I said, “because there are more palásh trees in the eastern portion of Gondwanaland. Where rivers have more or less level land on both sides you get this red soil that the palásh tree favours. The interesting thing is that in all the river basins of that area, especially the Damodar, Ajaya, Ushri, Konar, Barakar, and the Mahanadiʼs central river basin, you get ample amounts of coal – high quality coal. The primary source of material for this coal is decomposed palásh trees. Those palásh trees were not like the palásh trees of today but were the forefathers of todayʼs palásh trees.

The interesting thing is that in all the river basins of that area, especially the Damodar, Ajaya, Ushri, Konar, Barakar, and the Mahanadiʼs central river basin, you get ample amounts of coal – high quality coal.

paragraphs.text: “The part of Gondwanaland in which we are now is more or less divided into east and west by the Koyel River. The difference between east and west is not only evidenced in the terrain, but also in the flora and fauna. I would guess that the western mountains which we now call the Vindhya and Satpura Mountains were once much higher. They had peaks even higher than the Himalayas. Flora and fauna could not evolve there in the ancient past due to excessive snowfall, but the eastern mountains, although very high and snow-capped, were not as high as the western mountains. It is likely that the first appearance in the world of both flora and fauna was here, in this area, where we find our ancient Ráŕh and Jharkhand. In the west, the melted ice ran into the Arabian Sea. Although there was water, the soil was unfertile, so there was little flora and naturally little fauna as well. However, in the east, where the water from the melted snows became rivers, the cold was not so severe. So the first expression of developed life was in the land of Ráŕh – this we can be certain of.
summary: “The part of Gondwanaland in which we are now is more or less divided into east and west by the Koyel River.
It is likely that the first appearance in the world of both flora and fauna was here, in this area, where we find our ancient Ráŕh and Jharkhand.
So the first expression of developed life was in the land of Ráŕh – this we can be certain of.

paragraphs.text: “Thus we find an abundance of prehistoric fossils in the eastern portion of the Ramgarh Hills, the Dalma Hills, the Meghasini belt, and the southeast portion of the Rajmahal Hills (Pakur and Rajmahal Subdivisions). The small hills of Bankura District, especially the Shushuniya Hills, are also an extension of this Ramgarh range. Fossils of various types of ancient animal have been found near and around these hills. Still, the greatest amount of fossils are lying in the areas closest to the Suvarnarehka, Kangsavatii, and Damodar.
summary: “Thus we find an abundance of prehistoric fossils in the eastern portion of the Ramgarh Hills, the Dalma Hills, the Meghasini belt, and the southeast portion of the Rajmahal Hills (Pakur and Rajmahal Subdivisions).
Fossils of various types of ancient animal have been found near and around these hills.
Still, the greatest amount of fossils are lying in the areas closest to the Suvarnarehka, Kangsavatii, and Damodar.

paragraphs.text: “It is quite clear that the brontosaurus and other dinosaurs lived in this region. Rhinoceroses also used to roam the extremely high grasses of this area. Just two hundred years ago rhinoceroses were living in Birbhum and Kandi Subdivision. Only 125 years ago rhinoceroses were spotted in Rajmahal and Pakur.There were also huge birds of the phiuṋe variety with loose, hanging tails. I would guess that the size of a single bird was about five or six feet. Their tails used to trail on the ground and the sabre-toothed tigers of those days used to catch them easily by stepping on their tails with their paws. But when the sabre-toothed tiger disappeared from Ráŕh about 700,000 years ago, these large-bodied birds also became extinct. The descendants of these huge birds, the phiuṋe and doyel birds of today, are much smaller in size. The hyena (govághá, huŕál, hud́ár, or huńd́ár in rural Bengali – in Madhya Pradesh vighavá) of today is the descendant of this sabre-toothed tiger. Ape-men or man-apes first took birth in this part of the earth.
summary: “It is quite clear that the brontosaurus and other dinosaurs lived in this region.
I would guess that the size of a single bird was about five or six feet.
Ape-men or man-apes first took birth in this part of the earth.

paragraphs.text: “There were some differences between the humans that evolved first on either side of the Koyel River in terms of intelligence and other qualities. Such differences still exist today among their descendants. On the eastern side was the dwelling place of the Muńd́á clan ( 4 ) of that primitive age, and on the western side lived the Oráṋo clan. The former belongs to the Austric group – also their language. Many Austric-family words are still used in modern Bengali – kuŕi [twenty], dulál (from dulár [darling child]) and ghád́a [neck], among others.
summary: “There were some differences between the humans that evolved first on either side of the Koyel River in terms of intelligence and other qualities.
On the eastern side was the dwelling place of the Muńd́á clan ( 4 ) of that primitive age, and on the western side lived the Oráṋo clan.
Many Austric-family words are still used in modern Bengali – kuŕi [twenty], dulál (from dulár [darling child]) and ghád́a [neck], among others.

paragraphs.text: “The language of the Oráṋo group is kuruka ( 5 ). This family of words [Dravidian] includes pallii [hamlet], miin [fish], and teṋtul [tamarind] (tintiri → teṋturi → teṋtur → teṋtul), among others.

This family of words [Dravidian] includes pallii [hamlet], miin [fish], and teṋtul [tamarind] (tintiri → teṋturi → teṋtur → teṋtul), among others.

paragraphs.text: “The Birhorh ( 6 ) community also arose in this area in very ancient times. They are also part of the Austric family. The original home of the Malpaharhiis is in the northeast part of this area. Later they were subdued by others and forced to take shelter in the forest at the far edge of the Rajmahal Hills.
summary: “The Birhorh ( 6 ) community also arose in this area in very ancient times.
The original home of the Malpaharhiis is in the northeast part of this area.
Later they were subdued by others and forced to take shelter in the forest at the far edge of the Rajmahal Hills.

paragraphs.text: “In those ancient days there was a great deal of fighting between the ape-men and man-apes. The apes did not know the use of fire so they could not use it to burn their enemies. When humans learned the use of fire, they started to burn to death their main enemies, the apes, and eat them. During the British era also, the Birhorhs used to burn apes to death and eat them. But they also had some attraction towards the human beings; however, there is no proof that they ever ate human beings. One can deduce from this that they used to kill the apes for the purpose of eating their enemies.
summary: “In those ancient days there was a great deal of fighting between the ape-men and man-apes.
During the British era also, the Birhorhs used to burn apes to death and eat them.
One can deduce from this that they used to kill the apes for the purpose of eating their enemies.

paragraphs.text: “There is still another clan from this Koyel River Basin – the Asuras. They originated here and developed their own separate culture. Later they left and headed northwest in the direction of Europe. A few words from their language can still be found among the Gypsies of Central Asia and in the Romansch language of Europe.
summary: “There is still another clan from this Koyel River Basin – the Asuras.
Later they left and headed northwest in the direction of Europe.
A few words from their language can still be found among the Gypsies of Central Asia and in the Romansch language of Europe.

paragraphs.text: “I can see that you really like your subject, so I also like it. How is it you know so much at such a young age?”
summary: “I can see that you really like your subject, so I also like it.
How is it you know so much at such a young age?

paragraphs.text: “A few minutes ago I hardly knew anything about this subject,” she replied. “Whatever you were thinking just came out of my mouth. And whatever you were saying was reflected in the mirror of my mind.”
summary: “A few minutes ago I hardly knew anything about this subject,” she replied.
“Whatever you were thinking just came out of my mouth.
And whatever you were saying was reflected in the mirror of my mind.

paragraphs.text: I continued. “Near the high mountains of this Gondwanaland there were many huge pits. With the passage of time the mountains eroded and became large hills, then smaller hills, knolls and mounds. Today also, Ráŕh and Jharkhand are full of these hills, hillocks and knolls. Thus the land is undulating. What is today the lowest portion of this undulating land was at one time deep pits. And the upper portions were very tall mountains. Although many large pits have filled up, not all of them have. In Ráŕhii Bengali they are called káṋdar (from kandara in Sanskrit). Still there are a few very large pits. You will also find large pits nearby wherever you find a colliery with an open pit.”
summary: “Near the high mountains of this Gondwanaland there were many huge pits.
And the upper portions were very tall mountains.
You will also find large pits nearby wherever you find a colliery with an open pit.

paragraphs.text: “When I hear the word ʼpitʼ I tremble and my throat goes dry,” said Manjula.
summary: “When I hear the word ʼpitʼ I tremble and my throat goes dry,” said Manjula.

paragraphs.text: “Why?” I asked.

“It was in a pit that we had our accident,” she replied. “It was a long time ago, during British rule. I was travelling by car from Hazaribag to Gaya with my friend Vasavi and my little brother Nilanjan to do some research about Magadh. As we were approaching Gobhi our car had to swerve to avoid getting hit by a truck and it fell into a huge gorge. Oh! If I think about it even today I lose consciousness. The last thing I heard was Nilanjan crying ʼDidiʼ. I can still hear him. He was driving the car. We all fell into the gorge and were severely hurt but no one died. We remained unconscious for a long time.”
summary: “It was in a pit that we had our accident,” she replied.
The last thing I heard was Nilanjan crying ʼDidiʼ.
We remained unconscious for a long time.

paragraphs.text: Listening to Manjula, I gradually fell asleep. Two or three times I said to myself: “Even today the three of us become afraid if we hear the word ʼgorgeʼ.”
summary: Listening to Manjula, I gradually fell asleep.
Two or three times I said to myself: “Even today the three of us become afraid if we hear the word ʼgorgeʼ.

paragraphs.text: I donʼt know when Manjula left. When I woke up again I saw a girl about Manjulaʼs age sitting in the room. I took a good look at her. It was the same Vasavi Basu that I had seen a few years before in Magadhʼs Pahariya Village. What a passion she had for archaeological research!
summary: I donʼt know when Manjula left.
I took a good look at her.
What a passion she had for archaeological research!

paragraphs.text: Then Vasavi started talking. “I canʼt tell you how long Iʼve wanted an opportunity to talk to you, but I never got the chance. But first, before we start talking, I have to take care of one thing. I want my locket to stay in your museum along with Nilanjanʼs pen and Manjulaʼs wristwatch. I wonʼt take ʼnoʼ for an answer. And just to be sure that you wonʼt get a chance to object, Iʼve put them in your suitcase in the car.”
summary: Then Vasavi started talking.
I want my locket to stay in your museum along with Nilanjanʼs pen and Manjulaʼs wristwatch.
And just to be sure that you wonʼt get a chance to object, Iʼve put them in your suitcase in the car.

paragraphs.text: “What are you saying?” I replied. “The key to the suitcase is in my pocket. How did you open the suitcase? You live here so I can see how you might have a duplicate key for the room, but thereʼs no question of having a duplicate key for my suitcase.”
summary: “What are you saying?
How did you open the suitcase?
You live here so I can see how you might have a duplicate key for the room, but thereʼs no question of having a duplicate key for my suitcase.

paragraphs.text: She replied, a little embarrassed. “Oh yes, youʼre right. How did I open it?… how did I open it?”
summary: She replied, a little embarrassed.
“Oh yes, youʼre right.

paragraphs.text: To save her from an embarrassing situation I asked, “Do you remember your research into eastern Magadh and your investigation of the idols and images?”
summary: To save her from an embarrassing situation I asked, “Do you remember your research into eastern Magadh and your investigation of the idols and images?

paragraphs.text: “Ye-e-s indeed. Most of all, your words left a strong impression on me. You really helped me so much! Do you expect that the results of cultural research throughout Magadh will be the same?”
summary: Most of all, your words left a strong impression on me.
You really helped me so much!
Do you expect that the results of cultural research throughout Magadh will be the same?

paragraphs.text: “Magadh culture can be divided into four branches,” I replied, “according to river valleys: 1) Shon-Punpun, 2) Naeranjana-Mohaniya-Phalgu, 3) Kiul Valley and 4) Kśuri Valley.
summary: “Magadh culture can be divided into four branches,” I replied, “according to river valleys: 1) Shon-Punpun, 2) Naeranjana-Mohaniya-Phalgu, 3) Kiul Valley and 4) Kśuri Valley.

paragraphs.text: “While it is certainly true that the Ganges flows through Magadh and that the civilization the Ganges brought with it from North India took on a new form when it came to Magadh, Magadh was in no way founded on the Ganges civilization. The heart of these four branches of culture was in Girivraja or Rajagir. ( 7 )
summary: “While it is certainly true that the Ganges flows through Magadh and that the civilization the Ganges brought with it from North India took on a new form when it came to Magadh, Magadh was in no way founded on the Ganges civilization.
The heart of these four branches of culture was in Girivraja or Rajagir.

paragraphs.text: “Today the rivers of Magadh have all but dried up, but it was not always so. At one time the source of its rivers was in the deep forest. There was a great deal of rainfall in those days and the rivers used to flow twelve months a year. Today, as a result of senseless destruction of the forest, Magadh is gradually being turned into a desert. The village where we met was a little outside the Kiul valley. It falls within the jurisdiction of the Kśuri Valley. Today the Kśuri River ( 8 ) has dried up, but at one time it was a very big river. This can be ascertained by measuring the width of its source.
summary: “Today the rivers of Magadh have all but dried up, but it was not always so.
The village where we met was a little outside the Kiul valley.
This can be ascertained by measuring the width of its source.

paragraphs.text: “It is true that, at that time, the Maháyánii Buddhist god Máriici was popular among the people. Some people used to do Maŕiici Pújá [worship] and others used to throw sand in the idolʼs face to make the god leave the village. Háriiti was also popular in Magadh, but one would not usually see both Máŕiici and Háriiti in the same place. At one spot in the Kśuri Valley we found idols of both Máŕiici and Háriiti. But these things Iʼve already told you. You took notes also.”
summary: “It is true that, at that time, the Maháyánii Buddhist god Máriici was popular among the people.
Háriiti was also popular in Magadh, but one would not usually see both Máŕiici and Háriiti in the same place.
But these things Iʼve already told you.

paragraphs.text: “I did take notes, but I lost them at the time of the car accident.”
summary: “I did take notes, but I lost them at the time of the car accident.

paragraphs.text: “How did it happen?”

“The gods live inside people,” Vasavi continued, “and the demons also build their homes inside people. Manjula certainly must have told you how we fell into a gorge and were gravely injured. We were stunned; our life-force was paralysed. Nobody lived in that area and no one came to rescue us. But one or two hours after the accident some dacoits arrived and robbed us of all our possessions. They took my notebook and whatever money and other property we had with us, but they didnʼt bother to call a doctor or try to save us by taking us to a hospital. The only things the thieves overlooked were Nilanjanʼs pen, Manjulaʼs wristwatch, and my locket, so weʼve given them to you. What good will it do if they remain in this dark underworld? Let them stay in the open air and light of your museum.
summary: “The gods live inside people,” Vasavi continued, “and the demons also build their homes inside people.
But one or two hours after the accident some dacoits arrived and robbed us of all our possessions.
Let them stay in the open air and light of your museum.

paragraphs.text: “A little while later, an English gentleman was passing by on the same road and noticed our situation. He took our three bodies in his car to a nearby health centre. Fortunately, we were still alive though our life-force was paralysed.
summary: “A little while later, an English gentleman was passing by on the same road and noticed our situation.
He took our three bodies in his car to a nearby health centre.
Fortunately, we were still alive though our life-force was paralysed.

paragraphs.text: I kept listening to what Vasavi was saying.
summary: I kept listening to what Vasavi was saying.

paragraphs.text: “But how long shall I go on talking about us?” she said. “You were talking about Háriiti?”
summary: “But how long shall I go on talking about us?
“You were talking about Háriiti?

paragraphs.text: “Háriiti was also a Maháyána Buddhist goddess,” I continued. “The difference between Máriici and Háriiti was that Háriiti was worshipped by both the Maháyána Buddhists and the Shvetámbara Jains. We found both Háriiti and Máriici in the Kśuri River basin. One can deduce therefrom that in this part of Magadh, both Buddhism and Jainism existed side by side. Whether as enemies or friends, they lived together.
summary: “Háriiti was also a Maháyána Buddhist goddess,” I continued.
We found both Háriiti and Máriici in the Kśuri River basin.
Whether as enemies or friends, they lived together.

paragraphs.text: “It may also be, moreover, that this river basin was the original centre of Maháyána Buddhism. It should not be forgotten that Rajagir-Nalanda, Barhgaon, Mahavihar (Biharsharif), Paharhiya (the village of Maharshi Saiṋjaya, the philosophy teacher of Lord Buddha), and Pavapurii (the place where Vardhaman Mahavir died) are all in the Kśuri River Valley. At one time, the river had a very sharp, ( 9 ) strong current. Thus in Sanskrit its name became kśuriká. Later that became kśuri in Bengali. Here it should also be remembered that the current dialects of the Magahi language have been spread through the river basins.
summary: “It may also be, moreover, that this river basin was the original centre of Maháyána Buddhism.
Thus in Sanskrit its name became kśuriká.
Here it should also be remembered that the current dialects of the Magahi language have been spread through the river basins.

paragraphs.text: “Magadh also has very clear, fixed natural boundaries: The Ganges in the north, the Shon River in the west, the Ramgarh Hills in the south, and in the east Sametashikhara or Pareshanath Mountain, ( 10 ) Cákái Hill (Cakravartii Mountain, that is, Cakravartii → Cakkavatii → Cakkavai → Cákái/Cakái), Grdhrakút́a Hill (Grdhrakút́a Gidhdhkúd́a → Gidhdhaud́a → Gidhaoŕa) and Kiul River Valley. In the direction opposite Grdhrakút́a Hill is Angadesh and opposite Cakravartii Mountain is Ráŕh.”

In the direction opposite Grdhrakút́a Hill is Angadesh and opposite Cakravartii Mountain is Ráŕh.

paragraphs.text: “How very interesting,” said Vasavi. “About a month after we met that time, I went back there to do some more extensive research into the Máriici and Háriiti idols, but this time I was unable to find any. Brokers who dealt in idols had stolen them and smuggled them out of the country.”
summary: “How very interesting,” said Vasavi.
“About a month after we met that time, I went back there to do some more extensive research into the Máriici and Háriiti idols, but this time I was unable to find any.
Brokers who dealt in idols had stolen them and smuggled them out of the country.

paragraphs.text: “This kind of sad occurrence is a daily event in Magadh,” I replied. “So much archaeological wealth has been and is being smuggled out of Magadh that in the near future Magadh will become destitute and empty. There is no dearth of educated people in Magadh nowadays, but it seems that they are not paying proper attention to this. What the universities are doing about it I canʼt say, but I will say that both the educated people of Magadh and the universities should come forward without delay in this matter. It is unthinkable that that part of the world which is richest in archaeological wealth should be deprived of everything it has.”

paragraphs.text: Again I started falling asleep.
summary: Again I started falling asleep.

paragraphs.text: The sound of the caretaker approaching woke me up. When I looked up, I saw Vasavi getting ready to leave. “The caretaker is coming so I have to go now,” she said and then left rather hastily. At first she went like the wind, then even faster . . . she went near that white object in the distance and disappeared somewhere. The next moment the caretaker entered my room.

At first she went like the wind, then even faster .
The next moment the caretaker entered my room.

paragraphs.text: When the caretaker entered my room he said: “Sir, you moved into the room last night! If you had told me that you were going to move into the room in the middle of the night, I would have made all the necessary arrangements. Ah, I see youʼve laid out your bedding yourself. The bedding has also been cleaned up. And I see that the deyálgii ( 11 ) [wall-lamp] has been lit. That was being kept in the storeroom. Why did you take the risk of going into the storeroom in the dead of night like that for the wall-lamp? What if you had had an accident?”

And I see that the deyálgii ( 11 ) [wall-lamp] has been lit.
What if you had had an accident?

paragraphs.text: I kept silent. If I had said anything at all it would mean having to say something about those three people. I pointed in the direction of the door and drew his attention to that white object in the distance. Then I said: “Last night, when I asked you what that white object in the distance was, you told me that you couldnʼt see properly in the darkness. Now itʼs time for me to leave. Please tell me.”

Then I said: “Last night, when I asked you what that white object in the distance was, you told me that you couldnʼt see properly in the darkness.
Now itʼs time for me to leave.

paragraphs.text: The caretaker answered as if he hadnʼt heard my question. “Oh sir, you have to leave now? Before you go, let me tell you a story of mine.
summary: The caretaker answered as if he hadnʼt heard my question.
“Oh sir, you have to leave now?
Before you go, let me tell you a story of mine.

paragraphs.text: “It took place quite some time back, during British rule. Three people were travelling by car from the direction of Chauparan. For what reason, I donʼt know, they had an accident. Their car ran into a deep gorge. The three of them didnʼt appear too badly injured but they were all knocked unconscious. Whether they were killed or not is difficult for anyone to say in my opinion. One of them was a gentleman and the other two were mishibábá ( 12 ) [ladies].
summary: “It took place quite some time back, during British rule.
Their car ran into a deep gorge.
One of them was a gentleman and the other two were mishibábá ( 12 ) [ladies].

paragraphs.text: “A little while after the accident, it seems, some rogues robbed them of all their valuables, but they made no attempt to save them or bring them to a health centre. Just see what kind of brutes they were! Sometime after, an English gentleman was travelling on the same road from Gaya to Catra (Hazaribag District). He noticed the damaged vehicle, stopped his car and went down into the ditch. When he examined the three bodies, he couldnʼt tell whether or not they were dead or had had their life-force paralysed.
summary: “A little while after the accident, it seems, some rogues robbed them of all their valuables, but they made no attempt to save them or bring them to a health centre.
Sometime after, an English gentleman was travelling on the same road from Gaya to Catra (Hazaribag District).
When he examined the three bodies, he couldnʼt tell whether or not they were dead or had had their life-force paralysed.

paragraphs.text: “One by one, he carried the three bodies to his car and drove them to a nearby health centre. At that time the clinicʼs doctor had been absent for about a month. His wifeʼs aunt was suffering from cough and cold, it seems. The English gentleman told the compounder: ʼPlease examine them and see if they are alive or not. If there is any chance at all of saving their lives, you must arrange it. Whatever the expense is, Iʼll cover it.ʼ

The English gentleman told the compounder: ʼPlease examine them and see if they are alive or not.
Whatever the expense is, Iʼll cover it.

paragraphs.text: “How much could a compounder know about medical science? To relieve himself of any responsibility, the compounder moved and shook the bodies a little, then pronounced them dead. The English gentleman brought the bodies straightaway to this rest-house and kept them in this room. Within a short time he arranged for their last rites and cremation.”

The English gentleman brought the bodies straightaway to this rest-house and kept them in this room.

paragraphs.text: “Were you able to find out who the people were?” I asked.
summary: “Were you able to find out who the people were?

paragraphs.text: “After a lot of effort,” he answered, “we were able to learn their names, but we werenʼt able to find out anything else about them.”
summary: “After a lot of effort,” he answered, “we were able to learn their names, but we werenʼt able to find out anything else about them.

paragraphs.text: “Can you tell me their names?”
summary: “Can you tell me their names?

paragraphs.text: “For that Iʼll have to look in the old register.”
summary: “For that Iʼll have to look in the old register.

paragraphs.text: “Donʼt go to too much trouble on my behalf,” I said; then he left the room to bring the old records.

paragraphs.text: As soon as the caretaker left the room, Nilanjan quickly stepped in. Needless to say, this time also he had not made a sound. “How come you are in such a hurry and looking so tired?” I asked.

Needless to say, this time also he had not made a sound.
“How come you are in such a hurry and looking so tired?

paragraphs.text: “Just now Iʼve come from Chauparan,” he replied. “The road is all right now. In one place a banyan tree had fallen. As you know, there are quite a lot of banyan trees in Magadh. Not only nowadays, during the Buddhist era also there used to be banyan trees ( 13 ) outside many villages. One of these very old banyan trees had fallen in the road. What was I to do? I couldnʼt move it myself. You know, my body is now very light. I influenced the minds of a few elephants in the nearby jungle and brought them to where the tree was lying, and with their help I moved the banyan tree just enough so that the road was clear for a car to pass. Now your vehicle can pass freely through there. But you should still drive carefully. I will also accompany you.”
summary: “Just now Iʼve come from Chauparan,” he replied.
I couldnʼt move it myself.
I will also accompany you.

paragraphs.text: “Do you have a motorcycle?” I asked.
summary: “Do you have a motorcycle?

paragraphs.text: “No,” he replied. “I donʼt have a motorcycle. How I will go still isnʼt fixed. When we get to Chauparan Iʼll tell you how I will go. The ladies also insist on coming.”
summary: “I donʼt have a motorcycle.
When we get to Chauparan Iʼll tell you how I will go.
The ladies also insist on coming.

paragraphs.text: “If they go with you and also come back with you,” I said, “then what objection can there be?”

paragraphs.text: “Iʼll let them know that youʼve given permission then. I also informed those who have taken responsibility to look after you after you leave Chauparan. Their bodies burn in the hot daytime sun so even if they want to come they wonʼt be able to do so. But theyʼll come with you secretly. They gave me their word that they wonʼt allow any harm to come to you before you get to Ranchi.”

Their bodies burn in the hot daytime sun so even if they want to come they wonʼt be able to do so.
They gave me their word that they wonʼt allow any harm to come to you before you get to Ranchi.

paragraphs.text: Then the sound of the caretaker coming could be heard and Nilanjan slipped out of the room. The caretaker handed me an old register from the time of British rule. While I was turning the pages I asked him: “Can you tell me when these disembodied forms first started appearing in this place?”

While I was turning the pages I asked him: “Can you tell me when these disembodied forms first started appearing in this place?

paragraphs.text: “Yes,” he replied. “It was just after the bodies were given last rites and cremated.”

paragraphs.text: “Do they move throughout the building?”
summary: “Do they move throughout the building?

paragraphs.text: “Yes, they go everywhere, but it was in this room that the bodies were kept, and probably for that reason they seem to frequent it a little more.”
summary: “Yes, they go everywhere, but it was in this room that the bodies were kept, and probably for that reason they seem to frequent it a little more.

paragraphs.text: “Have you seen them yourself?”
summary: “Have you seen them yourself?

footnotes.text: Some people use the word sámánya when they mean alpa [a little, some – translated above as "some"]. It is better not to do this. Sámánya does not mean “a little”. It means “common” or “general”. For example, if we say that Bengali is the sámánya language of this country we mean, that is the language of the common people. This word comes from samána [equal]. By what logic, then, can it mean “a little”?

Until the beginning of British rule, there used to be a pull-fan system in the houses of zamindars and foreigners and the person employed to pull the rope used to be called the páuṋkhábardár. This páuṋkhábardár used to sit in the little room at the end of the veranda, next to the bedroom in dak-bungalows, and pull the rope; inside the room the aristocrats would enjoy the breeze from the fan. paragraphs.text: Civilization is a collection of usages, manners, etiquette, formalities, ideologies and love. The culture of the entire humanity is the same, but civilization varies from society to society.

paragraphs.text: Human civilization is created in, and moves along, river valleys. Like a river, human civilization also has three stages – hill stage, plain stage and delta stage. From the hill stage, it moves to the plain stage and from the plain stage to the delta stage. A civilization starts in the hill stage, develops in the plain stage, and matures in the delta stage.
summary: Human civilization is created in, and moves along, river valleys.
From the hill stage, it moves to the plain stage and from the plain stage to the delta stage.

paragraphs.text: Why are civilizations created in, and why do they move along, river valleys? In ancient times, up until the Stone Age, humans could not dig wells and depended upon natural sources of water. As such, human habitation started from springs, fountains, waterfalls, rivers, etc. Animals also select such places for habitation; only birds do not follow this rule. Thus, human habitation started near valleys, fountains, waterfalls, springs, and particularly near rivers. Due to the assemblage of humans in the river valleys, the first stage of civilization started there.
summary: Why are civilizations created in, and why do they move along, river valleys?
Animals also select such places for habitation; only birds do not follow this rule.
Due to the assemblage of humans in the river valleys, the first stage of civilization started there.

paragraphs.text: The relation between man and man, man and woman, individual and collective requirements, individual and collective responsibilities – how to move singularly and collectively – the collection of all these is civilization. It has already been said that civilization starts in the hill stage, develops in the plain stage, and attains maturity in the delta stage. Naturally, the delta stage is the finality of a civilization.

It has already been said that civilization starts in the hill stage, develops in the plain stage, and attains maturity in the delta stage.

paragraphs.text: The hill stage of the Gauṋgá (Ganges) River Valley civilization in India started from the Garwal and Kumaun ranges of Uttar Pradesh (UP). The rest of UP and Bihar is in the plain stage, and the delta stage starts from Maldah in West Bengal. The hill stage of the Brahmaputra Valley civilization starts from Tibet and Arunachal. Its plain stage lies in Assam and its delta stage starts from the districts of Goalpara, Mymensingh, and Rangpur (now in Bangladesh).

The hill stage of the Brahmaputra Valley civilization starts from Tibet and Arunachal.

paragraphs.text: The delta is that stage where the river starts to merge into the sea by the shortest route. In the delta stage, tributaries have no prominent role. In the hill stage, tributaries play the dominant role, and there are hardly any branch rivers. In the plain stage also, tributaries have the dominant role in the growth and manifestation of civilizations, but branches also have some importance. However, in the deltaic stage, branch rivers have a more important role than the tributaries.

In the hill stage, tributaries play the dominant role, and there are hardly any branch rivers.

paragraphs.text: Original civilizations (maolik sabhyatá) and blended civilizations (vimishra sabhyatá) are the two basic characteristics of civilization. A particular civilization changes in a particular way as a river moves and merges with other rivers, thus giving rise to sub-civilizations.
summary: Original civilizations (maolik sabhyatá) and blended civilizations (vimishra sabhyatá) are the two basic characteristics of civilization.

paragraphs.text: The Mandakini and Alakananda river civilizations emerged in the plain stage. We find the blending of these two civilizations. At the hill stage, after passing through so many mountains, hills, fountains, etc., these two rivers, Mandakini and Alakananda, come in contact with each other at the hill stage. They merge near Hardwar, and there the two simple river civilizations, Garwali and Kumauni respectively, combine to produce a blended Gauṋgá civilization, which comes up to Prayaga.

paragraphs.text: Now, another river valley civilization, the Yamuna civilization along the river Yamuna, is also a collection of several sub-civilizations comprising many customs, costumes, manners, etc. It also comes up to Prayaga. The blended Gauṋgá civilization and the blended Yamuna civilization merge at Prayaga, and a blended Gauṋgá-Yamuna civilization occurs after the river confluence at Prayaga and moves towards Varanasi. Prayaga is the second blending of manners, customs, etc., of the Gauṋgá and Yamuna civilizations.

paragraphs.text: After Prayaga we find another blending of civilizations. Therefore, there are variations in the manners, customs, languages, intonations, physical structures and economic conditions of eastern UP and western UP. A further blending occurs in the blended civilizations of the Gauṋgá and Yamuna when the Gomati, Rapti, Sone and Saraju rivers bring new trends from the northern portion of the Himalaya and Chambal-Ghaghdra River from the Vindhya ranges. Thus civilizations vary and sub-civilizations, branch civilizations, emerge at different stages of the movement of a river and its blending with other river-civilizations.

The blended civilization of the Gauṋgá attains maturity in Bengal. Daha means the circular movement of water in a river; so it is called “Máldaha” (Maldah). At Maldah, the Gauṋgá turns to the right. The blended Gauṋgá civilization is in its highest form in the deltaic stage in Bengal.

paragraphs.text: The Brahmaputra civilization is a combination of the proto-Chinese and Indo-Tibetan civilizations. After this, the Brahmaputra turns to the left and enters Bengal, which is in its delta stage. The delta stage of the Brahmaputra civilization is its final stage. paragraphs.text: In Bengal there is another civilization as well, the civilization of Ráŕh. The hill stage, plain stage and delta stage of the Ráŕh civilization is in Bengal. So many rivers merge in the area of lower Bengal, which results in further blending. Thus in Bengal, there is a blending of three delta civilizations – the Gauṋgá, Brahmaputra and Ráŕh civilizations. This is the highest blended civilization of the world. Nature helps the people of Bengal in their intellectual progress, because no two great rivers like the Gauṋgá and the Brahmaputra merge together anywhere else in the world.

paragraphs.text: In original civilizations (maolik sabhyatá), people are physically strong. In blended civilizations, people are strong in the psychic stratum and the civilization is complicated as well as forceful. In the simple Gauṋgá civilization people are simple and physically strong; in the delta stage people are complicated, less physically strong and strong psychically.

paragraphs.text: The people of Bengal are intellectually developed because first, Bengal civilization is a blending of three deltaic civilizations and secondly, it is not a simple civilization but a great, complicated civilization – the blend and finality of three deltaic civilizations. Naturally, therefore, it is a powerful civilization, advanced in the intellectual and other spheres.

paragraphs.text: Though Sutanuka and her family were living in Burdwan they originally belonged to the Mitra family of Konnagar. Towards the end of Pathan rule, an intellectual society grew up in Hooghly District on the west bank of the river Bhagirathi. Konnagar was one of the intellectual centres. In those days the Ray-Mitras of Konnagar were the landlords. Konnagar was considered to be one of the most cultured and well-educated villages of Hooghly District of Ráŕh. Moreover it was one of the most famous places in the whole of Bengal. Its original name was Karnanagar. The name would be on the lips of every educated person of the locality. The people said that in Bengal if there was only one nagar or town it would be Karnanagar. If someone was asked, “Which town do you want to go?” They would reply, “There is only one town. Why should you ask ‘Which town’ [Kon nagar in Bengali]? – There is only one town: Konnagar.” And that is how the place became known as Konnagar.

paragraphs.text: I said to Sutanuka, “The name of the city weʼre about to leave is now known as Allahabad city, but its ancient name was Prayaga. Itʼs a fact that Prayaga is older than Konnagar. It was built towards the end of the Yajurvedic period [six thousand years ago]. But Burdwan is even more ancient than Prayaga. During Pathan rule Prayaga was renamed Álláha-ábád (Abode of Allah). Since then its popularity has been increasing. The Shia Moslems named the city Illahabad, but during the Mughal period, the fame and growth of the city came to a standstill. Thereafter, the city again began to flourish towards the end of the British rule when it became the capital of the United Provinces of then Agra and Oudh (UP for short).

paragraphs.text: We were travelling from west to east – from ancient Brahmávartta, or Brahmarśidesh, to the ancient Kashi kingdom. That part of the Gangetic Valley is considered as the middle part of the Ganges river civilization. The Prayaga area is considered to be the upper part of the Ganges river civilization. The area stretching from Prayaga to the confluence of the rivers Shon and Ganges is the middle part of the Ganges river civilization. And the area from the Shon-Ganges confluence to Sahebganj is regarded as the pre-Gaoŕá part of the Ganges river civilization. The area from Sahebganj, where the Ganges starts flowing southward, to Gangasagar is known as the final part of the Ganges valley civilization, or Gaoŕiiya [Bengalee] civilization. The Gaoŕiiya civilization reaches the peak of its individuality where the rivers of Ráŕh, carrying with them the local cultural specialities of Ráŕh civilization, and the Brahmaputra River, coming from the northeast [and] carrying with it the flow of Mongolian civilization, merge into the Ganges. If judged properly, the part of the Gauṋgá valley civilization which was the homeland of the pre-Gaoŕiiya and Gaoŕiiya civilization cannot be called the Aryan civilization. Actually, it is the East India civilization or extended Gauṋgá delta civilization.

A little further downstream, another river, the Charmanvati or Chambal, carrying the distinctive features of the western Indian civilization of Málava [Malwa] and Bundelkhanda, merges into the Yamuna. In this area a new mixed civilization came into existence, which can be called the Baghelii civilization. paragraphs.text: I replied, “Look, as far as I understand the matter from the linguistic point of view, the land of Ráŕh is the land where Sanskrit originated. But the ancient language which we describe as the Vedic language came to India from the northwest along with the Aryans. The Aryans first migrated to the Sindhu-Saoviira, and the land of Sapta-Sindhu, the Seven Rivers (Sutlej or Shatadru, Bias or Vipasha, Ravi or Iravati, Chenub or Candrabhaga, Jhelum or Vitasta, Kabul and Sind). These seven rivers together are known as the Sapta-Sindhu. Later on the land became known as the Punjab (paiṋj + áb), that is, the land of five waters [rivers]. The names of the Sindhu and the Kabul have been dropped, so there remain only five.

paragraphs.text: “This is the first phase of Vedic influence in India. In the second phase the Aryans moved further southeast: their influence extended to the northern part of the Yamuna Valley. paragraphs.text: “Then, in the next phase, the Aryans reached Prayaga around the Gauṋgá-Yamuna Valley. This we can describe as the third phase of Vedic influence. Then they moved further east, and their influence extended to the Gandakii River on the north and the Shon River on the south. This can be called the fourth phase of Vedic influence. In this area was situated the ancient Káshiirájya or Kingdom of Kashi. We are now journeying through the Káshiirájya. One thing to be noted here is that in the first phase, the Vedic language left two daughters behind: Páshcáttya and Paeshácii Prákrta. In the languages born out of Páshcáttya and Paeshácii Prakrta (for example, Pashto, Punjabi, etc.) there is a multitude of derived words from the Vedic language. In the second phase, that is, in the Hariyanavi language, the percentage of Vedic-derived words is somewhat less. In the third stage, the percentage of Vedic-derived words is still less, for instance in languages like Máŕoyári, Haŕaoti, Bundeli, Bagheli, Avadhi, Brajabháśa, etc. And in the languages of the fourth stage, like Bhojpuri, the percentage of Vedic-derived words is still less. But no one should misunderstand that in the fourth stage the Vedic influence was nil. No doubt the direct Vedic influence in the fourth stage was nil, but the indirect influence remained inextricably linked with pre-Gaoŕiiya and Gaoŕiiya civilizations, and that influence persists even today.”

paragraphs.text: “Take for example the case of the Thames: it is not a big river, either in length or in breadth. The part of the Thames where the ships sail is not really a river; it is only an estuary of the sea, just like the Matla near Canning. Many people think that the Matla is perhaps a wide and large river. They may think that in olden days that Vidyadharii, the southern branch of the Yamuna, emerging from the Ganges at Trivenii, moved southwards, and then it and the southeastern tributary Piyali of the Ganges both flowed separately for a certain distance and then joined together to form the Matla. Though this is a fact, yet the collective waters of these two combined rivers are quite small. In fact, the Matla is nothing but the backwater or kháŕi of the sea entering into the land. The proper English word for kháŕi is ‘estuary’.

paragraphs.text: “The deltaic portion of the Thames is somewhat similar. The more one proceeds down the river from the source of the Thames, the greater is the Anglo-Saxon and Norman influence. If one moves from the northern side of the river towards the port of Grimsby on the delta at the coast, there is a greater Anglo-Saxon influence than Norman influence. If one moves towards the coast, the Norman influence becomes negligible. Where there is Norman influence, there are large numbers of Latin derivations in the spoken language.
