But what you said was correct: I was expected to arrive at Burdwan at ten on Wednesday morning.” He paused for a while and then continued. “They shouldnʼt catch any train which will get them there late at night or at dawn – I apprehend some danger.”
summary: “No, I didnʼt see them,” said Arupratan.
But what you said was correct: I was expected to arrive at Burdwan at ten on Wednesday morning.
“They shouldnʼt catch any train which will get them there late at night or at dawn – I apprehend some danger.

paragraphs.text: “If you sense some impending danger, under no circumstances should they catch any Burdwan train at that particular time. You should get off the train at the next station and find some way to go to Kashi.” And I advised him, “Youʼd better go to Kashi and look for them in all the probable places. They have to be prevented from taking any of those Burdwan trains.” He said, “Thatʼs a good idea. Thatʼs a good idea.”
summary: “If you sense some impending danger, under no circumstances should they catch any Burdwan train at that particular time.
” And I advised him, “Youʼd better go to Kashi and look for them in all the probable places.
” He said, “Thatʼs a good idea.

paragraphs.text: The train slowed down. We were approaching a station, no doubt. Arupratan jumped to his feet, rushed to the door, and, looking like a crow ruffled by a raging tempest, leapt onto the platform without waiting for the train to stop. He had reason enough to be worried.
summary: The train slowed down.
Arupratan jumped to his feet, rushed to the door, and, looking like a crow ruffled by a raging tempest, leapt onto the platform without waiting for the train to stop.
He had reason enough to be worried.

paragraphs.text: As soon as the train stopped, my private secretary hurriedly entered my compartment. I guessed he had just finished his dinner of lit́t́i [a type of fried, unleavened bread] with his in-law. Perhaps his in-law had also served him kaŕiibaŕii [a type of dumpling made of chick-pea flour and served in yoghurt water] and mákhána kśiir [a type of sweet] for dessert. My private secretary sat beside me and asked me if I had been inconvenienced in any way. I said I hadnʼt. Our train was moving from west to east across the border of the ancient Kashi state.
summary: As soon as the train stopped, my private secretary hurriedly entered my compartment.
Perhaps his in-law had also served him kaŕiibaŕii [a type of dumpling made of chick-pea flour and served in yoghurt water] and mákhána kśiir [a type of sweet] for dessert.
Our train was moving from west to east across the border of the ancient Kashi state.

paragraphs.text: I had told Himavan, that this was the last area to come under Aryan influence. In the fourth phase of the Aryan invasion of India, Kashi can be regarded as a border state of northern India [Áryávartta]. In those days the Sarayu was considered to be the eastern border of Áryávartta. The Sarayu not only carried the Aryan influence along its banks but also Mongol and to some extent Austric influence as well. That is why its eastern bank was considered to be non-Aryan land. Later on this boundary was further extended to the Gandakii (Náráyańii Gańd́ak) which was accepted as the eastern end of the land. The Kanyakubja Brahmans of those days did not like to cross the Sarayu. As the land on the other bank was non-Aryan, it was regarded as unholy. They were afraid they would lose their Aryan purity. Those Kanyakubja Brahmans who dared to cross the river, being lured by the fertile land of the trans-Sarayu area, were declared outcastes. They lost their identity as Kanyakubja Brahmans and became known as Sarayupari Brahmans.
summary: I had told Himavan, that this was the last area to come under Aryan influence.
Later on this boundary was further extended to the Gandakii (Náráyańii Gańd́ak) which was accepted as the eastern end of the land.
They lost their identity as Kanyakubja Brahmans and became known as Sarayupari Brahmans.

paragraphs.text: During Pathan rule, the last boundary of Áryávartta was the present Ghazipur District. In those days North India consisted of three subas [administrative divisions]: Suba Bangal on the east, Suba Punjab on the northwest and Suba Hindustan between the two. Even today, the people of Bengal and the Punjab call the inhabitants of the middle part of northern India “Hindostani”. Some people are of the opinion that as Hindustan means the whole of India, why should the inhabitants of a small part of India be called Hindustani? However, this is wrong, because the term “Hindustani” is used for the people who were once the inhabitants of Suba Hindostan, and not in the sense of Hindustan as being the whole of India. During the Mughal period when Akbar divided his empire into fifteen subas, the northern part of Suba Hindostan and the southern part were named Oudh and Suba Agra respectively. Ghazipur District was the last boundary of Suba Agra. On the east of Ghazipur District lies Balia District (Bahliika). In those days Balia District was in existence. Previously it was only a subdivision of Ghazipur District. Similarly, there was no Deoria District in those days. It was only a subdivision of Gorakhpur District.
summary: During Pathan rule, the last boundary of Áryávartta was the present Ghazipur District.
Ghazipur District was the last boundary of Suba Agra.
It was only a subdivision of Gorakhpur District.

paragraphs.text: The British occupied both Agra and Oudh Subas and made one administrative unit out of them – the United Provinces of Agra and Oudh (UP for short) with its capital at Allahabad. In the last part of British rule, the capital was moved to Lucknow. In any case, there was a marked influence of Mongol and Austric cultures on the Aryan society inhabiting the Sarayu River Valley. Later on many Aryans crossed the Sarayu and declared the banks of the Gandakii as the boundary line of Áryávartta. The area lying on the west of the Gandakii Valley was called Shákyárańya and the area on the east was called Videha or Mithila. This latter area was not considered as an Aryan colony. I personally consider it as part of the area covered by the pre-Gaoŕiiya Gangetic Valley civilization.
summary: The British occupied both Agra and Oudh Subas and made one administrative unit out of them – the United Provinces of Agra and Oudh (UP for short) with its capital at Allahabad.
Later on many Aryans crossed the Sarayu and declared the banks of the Gandakii as the boundary line of Áryávartta.
I personally consider it as part of the area covered by the pre-Gaoŕiiya Gangetic Valley civilization.

paragraphs.text: King Mithi occupied Videha. To sanctify the land he held a Trihotriiya Yajiṋa (a big sacrificial rite presided over by three priests). It was then declared sacred. The land sanctified by the performance of a Trihotriiya Yajiṋa was named Trihut. The land of Shákyárańya, although not widely valued by the Aryans, was respected by the Buddhists. Lord Buddha visited it several times. Later, it became known as Shárańa (Shákyárańya → Shákyárańa → Shárańa). In later years it was wrongly spelt as Sharan.
summary: King Mithi occupied Videha.
The land of Shákyárańya, although not widely valued by the Aryans, was respected by the Buddhists.
In later years it was wrongly spelt as Sharan.

paragraphs.text: On the north of Shákyárańya was the ancient and famous place, Champakárańya. A reference is made to it in the Rámáyańa [one of the two great Sanskrit epics] (Campakárańya → Campárańya → Campárań). Shakyaranya and Campakaranya are situated on the western bank of the Náráyańii-Gańd́aka Valley. On the eastern bank is Videha or Mithila or Trihut, the land which was occupied by King Mithi. Mithi + lá [holder] + d́a [suffix] + á [feminine suffix] = Mithilá. In the Buddhist period one of the famous villages of Shákyárańya was Hatthiigrám (Hastiigráma in Sanskrit). Buddha visited this place a number of times. It is now known as Háthoyá. During British rule the Háthoyá estate was one of the biggest estates in India.
summary: On the north of Shákyárańya was the ancient and famous place, Champakárańya.
Mithi + lá [holder] + d́a [suffix] + á [feminine suffix] = Mithilá.
During British rule the Háthoyá estate was one of the biggest estates in India.

paragraphs.text: Then came the river Gandakii – Náráyańii Gańd́aka. The biggest cattle fair in India, known as the Hariharkśetra fair, is held once a year on the banks of this river. Nearby is the Shonpur railway station.
summary: Then came the river Gandakii – Náráyańii Gańd́aka.
The biggest cattle fair in India, known as the Hariharkśetra fair, is held once a year on the banks of this river.
Nearby is the Shonpur railway station.

paragraphs.text: Immediately after crossing the Gandakii River bridge at Shońpur we reached Mithila. During the Mughal period and the early part of British rule, the Mithila division of Bengal Presidency consisted of three districts: Trihut, Champaran and Sharan. The district headquarters of Champaran was Motihari, that of Sharan was Chapra, and that of Trihut was Muzaffarpur. This latter district was named after Muzaffar Shah. It covered a wide area, and until the early part of the British period its fertile soils were thickly forested. The forests contained an abundance of numerous species of flora and fauna, notably tigers, antelopes, crocodiles, pythons and deer. The large lake (called ma-a-na in local dialect) on the ancient river course of the Lakhandei in the eastern part of Muzzaffarpur town covered a larger area in those days and was surrounded by extensive forests full of abundant flora and fauna. A major part of the forest was part of the king of Darbhangaʼs estate. Some of it was within the Shúraśańd́a kingdom, and some part belonged to the estate of the Bettiah king. People today, out of necessity, but also out of immense greed have destroyed most of the forest, particularly in Trihut District.
summary: Immediately after crossing the Gandakii River bridge at Shońpur we reached Mithila.
The forests contained an abundance of numerous species of flora and fauna, notably tigers, antelopes, crocodiles, pythons and deer.
People today, out of necessity, but also out of immense greed have destroyed most of the forest, particularly in Trihut District.

paragraphs.text: At Vaeshali ( 2 ) in Trihut District Vardhaman Mahavir was born into a Vaeshya family. His fatherʼs name was Siddhartha and his mother was called Trishala. Trihut District as well as Mithila were located partly in the Náráyańii-Gańd́aka Valley and partly in the Burigandaka and Lakhandei Valleys. There was more Gaoŕiiya influence here than that of Áryávartta. The Bengali script was used here. It is to be noted that both Buddha and Mahaviira were born in a place where there was relatively less Aryan influence.
summary: At Vaeshali ( 2 ) in Trihut District Vardhaman Mahavir was born into a Vaeshya family.
There was more Gaoŕiiya influence here than that of Áryávartta.
It is to be noted that both Buddha and Mahaviira were born in a place where there was relatively less Aryan influence.

paragraphs.text: Trihut District was quite large in area. The British divided it into two parts: Muzaffarpur District in the west with its headquarters at Muzaffarpur, and Darbhanga District in the east with its headquarters at Laheriasarai village (which has since become a large city; it almost touches the city of Darbhanga). The old Muzaffarpur District is now divided into three districts: Sitamarhi, Muzaffarpur and Vaeshali (Hajipur). This is the same Muzaffarpur which was regarded as one of the most cultured places in the whole of the then Suba Bangal. The old Darbhanga District has since also been divided into three districts: Madhubani (a place where there is an abundance of forest honey); Darbhanga (named after the famous Dáŕibhangá Shah; in Maethili the town is called “Daiŕbhanga” but spelt “Daŕibhangá”); and Samastipur (named after Samasti Narayan Ray).
summary: Trihut District was quite large in area.
The old Muzaffarpur District is now divided into three districts: Sitamarhi, Muzaffarpur and Vaeshali (Hajipur).

The old Darbhanga District has since also been divided into three districts: Madhubani (a place where there is an abundance of forest honey); Darbhanga (named after the famous Dáŕibhangá Shah; in Maethili the town is called “Daiŕbhanga” but spelt “Daŕibhangá”); and Samastipur (named after Samasti Narayan Ray).

paragraphs.text: The Maethili branch of the pre-Gaoŕiiya Valley civilization was enriched by the Mongol-Tantric civilization that flourished in the Náráyańii-Gańd́aka, Buri-Gandaka, Lakhandei, Bagmati, Kamalabalan and Koshii Valleys. King Prithvi Narayan Shah established the Gorkha empire in Nepal at this time. The Gorkhas occupied Tirhut District and advanced up to Hajipur. Thereafter they were defeated by the British (the British commander-in-chief was General Octorloney, in whose name the Englishmen living in Kolkata built a war memorial – in recent times, the leaders, ignorant of history, have changed the name of the Octorloney Memorial to Shahid Minar [Martyrsʼ Column]) and were forced to sign the Treaty of Sugaoli (Champaran District). According to the terms of the treaty, the British got possession of Garhwal and Kumayun regions from Nepal, which was included in the United Provinces of Agra and Oudh, and they also reclaimed a major portion of Champaran and Trihut Districts. Part of the northern portion of Trihut was left in Nepal and is still part of Nepalese territory. The former capital of Mithila, Janakpur, is situated in that area. Many people of Bengal know the famous Janakpur catechu.”
summary: The Maethili branch of the pre-Gaoŕiiya Valley civilization was enriched by the Mongol-Tantric civilization that flourished in the Náráyańii-Gańd́aka, Buri-Gandaka, Lakhandei, Bagmati, Kamalabalan and Koshii Valleys.

According to the terms of the treaty, the British got possession of Garhwal and Kumayun regions from Nepal, which was included in the United Provinces of Agra and Oudh, and they also reclaimed a major portion of Champaran and Trihut Districts.
Many people of Bengal know the famous Janakpur catechu.

paragraphs.text: I got off the train at Muzzafarpur and spent two days of intense activity there. I arrived home about a week later, my mind full of pleasant memories. Waiting for me on the table was a letter from Himavan, sent from Burdwan, in which he wrote: “Dear Uncle, We had a shocking experience on our return to Burdwan. We left Kashi late Tuesday evening and were sure that we would reach home either late Tuesday night or Wednesday morning at dawn. Late into the night, mother and I were discussing river valley civilizations when we suddenly heard a huge crash and felt a severe jolt. I donʼt remember ever having heard such a loud noise in all my life. In a fraction of a second the train seemed to be smashing into pieces. There was commotion all around – people were screaming – chaos reigned everywhere. The train smashed into smithereens. Mother and I were violently thrown out of the derailed compartment. Pieces of train and the passengersʼ baggage were scattered here and there. We realized we were the victims of a tragic accident and death was inevitable – who knows how many were lying dead. Both of us were violently thrown towards a huge part of the derailed train. We screamed in fear. Then an amazing thing happened. Suddenly both of us perceived my father, Shri Aruprathan Mitra, rushing towards us. Grabbing each of us by the hand and pulling us out of the wreckage, he flung us to some distance. Thus we were saved from the jaws of inevitable death. What happened next we cannot say, for we both became unconscious.
summary: I got off the train at Muzzafarpur and spent two days of intense activity there.
Mother and I were violently thrown out of the derailed compartment.
What happened next we cannot say, for we both became unconscious.

paragraphs.text: “When the rays of the rising sun fell onto our faces we regained consciousness and, looking around, discovered that we were lying on a hay-stack on the edge of a paddy field beside the railway line. As we had fallen onto hay, our injuries were not severe – just some pain in our bones. A crowd of villagers had gathered around us. We saw the wreckage of the train in the distance and heard the pitiful screams and lamentations of the seriously wounded.
summary: “When the rays of the rising sun fell onto our faces we regained consciousness and, looking around, discovered that we were lying on a hay-stack on the edge of a paddy field beside the railway line.
A crowd of villagers had gathered around us.
We saw the wreckage of the train in the distance and heard the pitiful screams and lamentations of the seriously wounded.

paragraphs.text: “The local people were very kind, as the people of Burdwan usually are. On seeing the slightest hardship of others, tears come into their eyes. Those people standing around us desperately wanted to help and kept asking what they could do to make us feel more comfortable. They were prepared to do anything to help. We asked them, ‘Please look for my father and to bring him to where we are lying.’
summary: “The local people were very kind, as the people of Burdwan usually are.
Those people standing around us desperately wanted to help and kept asking what they could do to make us feel more comfortable.
We asked them, ‘Please look for my father and to bring him to where we are lying.

paragraphs.text: They searched everywhere for him, but without success. ‘Thereʼs no one called Arupratan Mitra here,ʼ they said. They helped us get to our feet – which we could only do with great difficulty – so that we could also look for him. But our search was also unsuccessful. My father was not to be seen anywhere. By that time the railway auxiliary van had arrived from Burdwan. We approached the authorities and with their help returned to Burdwan. The site of the accident was near Burdwan so we didnʼt have much difficulty getting home.
summary: They searched everywhere for him, but without success.
My father was not to be seen anywhere.
The site of the accident was near Burdwan so we didnʼt have much difficulty getting home.

paragraphs.text: “Well, uncle, how were we saved? Is it called ‘fate’ or is it perhaps the work of destiny?”
summary: “Well, uncle, how were we saved?
Is it called ‘fate’ or is it perhaps the work of destiny?

paragraphs.text: I was utterly shocked by what I read. Himavan wrote further: “Father has not yet arrived in Burdwan. We went to the airport to make some enquiries about him and learnt that the plane he was supposed to take still hadnʼt reached Dumdum Airport. The ground staff informed us that they had received no news as to the planeʼs whereabouts, nor was it possible for them to find out for reasons of military security. The plane was carrying a military cargo and the passengers were military personnel. As a result, the military department was trying to black out all news about the non-arrival of the plane.”
summary: I was utterly shocked by what I read.
The ground staff informed us that they had received no news as to the planeʼs whereabouts, nor was it possible for them to find out for reasons of military security.
As a result, the military department was trying to black out all news about the non-arrival of the plane.

paragraphs.text: No sooner had I finished reading the letter than I heard an announcement on the radio news. The news bulletin disclosed that there was a serious plane crash somewhere along the Mediterranean coastline last Monday at 8.45 p.m. Due to certain military reasons, the exact details could not be disclosed earlier. All the passengers died in the crash. From the passenger list provided at the airport it appears there were twenty Indian passengers. Their names and addresses have been confirmed, but the dead bodies were so severely burned that identification is impossible. The names of the Indians are 1)… 2)… 3)… 4)… Among the passengers there was a man from Kolkata, a Shri Arupratan Mitra.
summary: No sooner had I finished reading the letter than I heard an announcement on the radio news.
All the passengers died in the crash.
The names of the Indians are 1)… 2)… 3)… 4)… Among the passengers there was a man from Kolkata, a Shri Arupratan Mitra.

paragraphs.text: I was speechless. I pieced all the events together and concluded that it was indeed at 9 p.m. on Monday that Shri Arupratan, gasping for breath, rushed into my compartment at Benares railway station. He told me that he had been feeling considerable mental unease for the past fifteen minutes, since 8.45. His mind was terribly restless. He had come to me in quest of peace. He had travelled a long distance and that is why he was gasping for breath.
summary: I pieced all the events together and concluded that it was indeed at 9 p.
His mind was terribly restless.
He had travelled a long distance and that is why he was gasping for breath.

paragraphs.text: After hearing the news I was so bewildered that I was unable to decide what to do. How should I reply to Himavanʼs letter, I thought.
summary: After hearing the news I was so bewildered that I was unable to decide what to do.
How should I reply to Himavanʼs letter, I thought.

paragraphs.text: January 1986, Kolkata
summary: January 1986, Kolkata

footnotes.text: A subá was an administrative division. –Trans.
Vaeshali was the land of the Licchavis; it was the oldest republic in the world. –Trans.

chapters.title: “This Is the Same Gaoŕa Where We Were Born and Are Destined to Die”

paragraphs.text: Perhaps many of you are aware that Gaoŕa Desh is the old, traditional name of our Bengal. It was named Gaoŕa Desh because it earned worldwide recognition in the production of guŕ [raw sugar]. Not only raw sugar made from sugarcane, but she also produced, and still does, a range of raw sugar made out of date palms, palmyra, coconut trees (prepared from the sap), juice of gol trees [Nipa fruticans], etc. Raw sugar was also extracted in ancient Bengal from a class of potatoes known as sháṋkhálu [yam bean, Pachyrrhizus erosus], as also from the mahul (madhuka → madhula → mahuyá → mahul) flower [Madhuca indica] of Ráŕh. The mahul flower is boiled before raw sugar is produced from its decoction. Besides raw sugar itself, several varieties and several types of sugar were also produced from raw sugars with the help of pát́áshyáolá [a type of reagent]. This sugar was sold at premium rates to the Egyptian, European and Chinese markets. There was a large demand for cakes (pát́áli or navát) of raw sugar also. Nor did the sweetmeat guŕsandarbha, made by mixing sunned rice powder with raw sugar, enjoy any lesser acclaim.
summary: Perhaps many of you are aware that Gaoŕa Desh is the old, traditional name of our Bengal.
The mahul flower is boiled before raw sugar is produced from its decoction.
Nor did the sweetmeat guŕsandarbha, made by mixing sunned rice powder with raw sugar, enjoy any lesser acclaim.

paragraphs.text: This land of ours had the distinguished name Paiṋca Gaoŕa because it was primarily divided into five parts. The first was Ráŕh, which was also the largest. The word ʼRáŕhʼ is a derivative of the Austric word ‘Ráŕho’, which signifies a land of undulating slopes with a red soil. This territory of ours called Ráŕh comprises the contemporary districts of Midnapur, Howrah, Hooghly, Burdwan, Birbhum, Bankura, West Murshidabad or Ráŕh-Murshidabad, Dumka, Sahibganj, Deoghar, Gadda, Dhanbad, Purulia, Singbhum, Bhanjabhum, the eastern part of Ranchi, and southeast Giridih. This land of Ráŕh – the cradle of human civilisation, the fountainhead of Bengalee civilisation – is over three hundred million years old.
summary: This land of ours had the distinguished name Paiṋca Gaoŕa because it was primarily divided into five parts.
The word ʼRáŕhʼ is a derivative of the Austric word ‘Ráŕho’, which signifies a land of undulating slopes with a red soil.
This land of Ráŕh – the cradle of human civilisation, the fountainhead of Bengalee civilisation – is over three hundred million years old.

paragraphs.text: Samatat, the second part of Gaoŕa Desh, is the area covered by the Gauṋgá-Brahmaputra delta. The commonly used Bengali term for Samatat is Bagri, which consists of contemporary East Murshidabad (Bagri Murshidabad), Nadia, North 24-Parganas, South 24-Parganas, Kolkata, Khulna, Jessore, Kushthia, Goalanda, Gopalaganj and Patuakhali Districts and parts thereof. Nor is the civilisation of Samatat a modern-day one; it is decidedly pre-Vedic. It is true that the men of Ráŕh, clearing the jungle, set up habitation in Samatat when it raised itself out of the depths of the seas, with the help of their axes and shovels. So, the predecessors of the present inhabitants of Samatat came from Ráŕh. That was a long time back. Till this day, the Brahmans of Samatat are Ráŕhii Brahmins, the Kayasthas and Vaidyas [castes] are Ráŕhii Kayasthas and Ráŕhii Vaidyas. King Sagara, who finds mention in the Rámáyańa, was a king of the same Samatat. The word ságara [“sea”] is obtained by the conjunction of sagara [“all”] with the suffix ań. Samatatʼs fame in the art of warfare has endured since prehistoric ages.
summary: Samatat, the second part of Gaoŕa Desh, is the area covered by the Gauṋgá-Brahmaputra delta.
That was a long time back.
Samatatʼs fame in the art of warfare has endured since prehistoric ages.

paragraphs.text: Ámáder sená yuddha kareche sajjita caturauṋge,
summary: Ámáder sená yuddha kareche sajjita caturauṋge,

paragraphs.text: Dashánanjayii Rámacandrer prapitámahera sauṋge.
summary: Dashánanjayii Rámacandrer prapitámahera sauṋge.

paragraphs.text: [Our army has fought battles in quadripartite formations against the great grandfather of Rámachandra, who vanquished Dashánana, Ravana.]
summary: [Our army has fought battles in quadripartite formations against the great grandfather of Rámachandra, who vanquished Dashánana, Ravana.

paragraphs.text: Even in modern ages, many a son of Samatat has displayed particular talent in the art of warfare. King Bhagirath of this same Samatat excavated a hundred canals (Bhagirathii, Jalangi, etc.) from the river Padma and connected them to the sea. This is why the Ganges is also known as “Shatamukhii” [“river with a hundred mouths”]. These branches of the Ganges have rendered the soil of Samatat even more green and fertile.
summary: Even in modern ages, many a son of Samatat has displayed particular talent in the art of warfare.
) from the river Padma and connected them to the sea.
These branches of the Ganges have rendered the soil of Samatat even more green and fertile.

paragraphs.text: The third part of Gaoŕa Desh – Barendra (Bariind) – was to the north of Samatat, that is, on the northern shores of the Ganges or Padma and the eastern shores of the river Koshii. Samatat has been named thus because it is a plain (samatal) region – the same applies to Bagri. In just the same manner, the northern part of Padma is named Barendra, as it is composed of a mixture of different types of soils. The word bar means “the best”; so does the word indra. The etymological meaning of barendra is, therefore, “the best among the best”. The land of Barendra is somewhat older than Samatat. Besides, there were a number of large islands in the ocean adjoining this region in those days. Subsequently, the areas surrounding these islands filled up and became one and the same with the main land. The topography of these ancient Bariind plains can be seen in present-day Maldah-Dinajpur.
summary: The third part of Gaoŕa Desh – Barendra (Bariind) – was to the north of Samatat, that is, on the northern shores of the Ganges or Padma and the eastern shores of the river Koshii.
The etymological meaning of barendra is, therefore, “the best among the best”.
The topography of these ancient Bariind plains can be seen in present-day Maldah-Dinajpur.

paragraphs.text: The part of Gaoŕa Desh that lies to the north of the banks of the Padma or the Ganges, however, to the west of River Koshii, is known as Videha or Mithilá (mithi + lá + d́a + t́á, meaning “the land that was conquered by King Mithi”) or Tirhuta. The land that was sanctified by King Mithi through Trihotriiya Yajiṋa [a ritual which is performed by three chief priests or hotá] is Tirhuta or Tirabhúmi.
summary: The part of Gaoŕa Desh that lies to the north of the banks of the Padma or the Ganges, however, to the west of River Koshii, is known as Videha or Mithilá (mithi + lá + d́a + t́á, meaning “the land that was conquered by King Mithi”) or Tirhuta.
The land that was sanctified by King Mithi through Trihotriiya Yajiṋa [a ritual which is performed by three chief priests or hotá] is Tirhuta or Tirabhúmi.

paragraphs.text: The portion of Gaoŕa to the east of Barendra and Samatat, which was watered by many rivers, had the name Vauṋga (D́abáka). Vauṋga was an extremely fertile land. Although young by geological considerations, the civilization of Vauṋga evolved much before the emergence of the Vedic civilization. If not in well-defined documentation, Vauṋga does find mention in the Shatapatha Bráhmańa. The word bauṋga means “a fine or thin metal”. As the superior craftsmen and goldsmiths of Bauṋga were capable of producing delicate ornaments, the land was named “Bauṋga” (whose original meaning is “tin” or “ráuṋ”) as a mark of appreciation for these artisans. In later years, many people started writing “Vauṋga” instead of “Bauṋga”. Therefore, both “Vauṋga” and “Bauṋga” are acceptable spellings in Sanskrit. The Dhaka region of the present day represents this ancient Vauṋga. There was a time when the craftsmanship, wisdom, and acute desire to fulfil the ultimate aims of humanity that distinguished Vauṋga won the praise of the whole world.
summary: The portion of Gaoŕa to the east of Barendra and Samatat, which was watered by many rivers, had the name Vauṋga (D́abáka).

In the [Sanskrit story] Vetálapaiṋcaviḿshati, the Vetala [ghoul] is said to tell Emperor Vikramaditya, “Emperor, in the city of Burdwan of Gaoŕa Desh…” In the Caryácaryavinishcaya we find [the sentence] “Bhu-su-ku, today you have become a Bengalee” (Bhu-su-ku áj tu Bauṋgálii bhaelii). Some people think that the name “Bauṋgál” came into being after the Pathan rule. However, this is not quite true. Over the past five thousand years, this Gaoŕa Desh of ours has been referred to as “Baiṋjalá” in the Chinese language. In Latin, the land is called “Banjal” (a product of Bengal is banjalitis in Latin). In the Turkish language, it is “Báuṋgálá” and in Arabic it is “Báuṋgálá”. (In ancient Arabic, there was no distinction between ga and ja – as an example, both gawahar and jawahar were in use. This usage had its influence on other Middle Eastern languages as well.) It is “Bauṋgál” in Farsi, Urdu and Hindi, “Bengal” in English, “Gaoŕa Desh” in Sanskrit, and “Báuṋgládesh” [Bangladesh] in Bengali.

paragraphs.text: Ka means “water”, ke means “in water”. Ke + vrtt (vartt) = kevartta. Kevartta + ań = kaevartta. The words kevartta and kaevartta can be used in the same sense. The etymological meaning of the word kaevartta is “one who lives in water”, that is, “one who makes a living based on water”. In common usage kaevartta means 1) “one who makes a living based on fish”, one who is called in Bengali, Jálik Kaevartta... Jele Kaevartta (kaevartta → kaevat́t́a → kevat́t́a → keot́a). ( 1 ) 2) The second meaning of the word kaevartta is “boatman” – meaning either the helmsman or the oars man. The word májhi refers to the person who does the steering of the boat (karńa in Sanskrit), and dáṋŕi refers to the person who plies the oar or who makes the boat move on with the help of the oar. The steering is called karńa. That is why a boatman is called karńadhár in formal Bengali. We hear in an ancient Bengali song:

paragraphs.text: In North India even now a boatman is called keot́. Theoretically and also as a matter of fact all the people of Bengal were Kaevarttas at one time. The entire Bengalee race earned its livelihood based on water. That is why people took pride in those days to introduce themselves as Kaevarttas or Keot́. Then came from the western part of the world [from the Aryans] the nightmare of the ruinous system of the division of castes. ( 2 ) Those who were intelligent enough started forming small castes and sub-castes in imitation of western India. Even then in the beginning the bond of caste was not very strong in Bengal. Social relations and marriages between different castes still prevailed. The notion of untouchability was not so pronounced as it was in North India. Notwithstanding the facts that newer and newer castes were formed, Bengalees remained, by and large, Kaevarttas. It was a matter of common sense that the mushroom growth of these new castes cannot outnumber the Ját Báuṋálii [original Bengalee] Kaevarttas. The saddest thing is that Bengalees who were primarily and originally Kaevarttas formed small castes and sub-castes based on different groups and sub-groups, and began to consider the original kaevarttas as lower caste. A great misfortune came down in the social life of Bengal… there came down the curse of fatal fragmentation.
summary: In North India even now a boatman is called keot́.
Even then in the beginning the bond of caste was not very strong in Bengal.
A great misfortune came down in the social life of Bengal… there came down the curse of fatal fragmentation.

paragraphs.text: In the Buddhist period fishing began to be considered as a mean job. If fishing is a mean job, then how is eating fish not also a mean job! Catching fish and slaughtering fish is certainly not good, but why do the fishermen catch fish at all? Is it not because there are people who eat fish? Theoretically speaking, if catching fish is a mean job then eating fish is not only an equally mean job, it is, in fact, a meaner job. But in the Buddhist period while catching fish was considered a mean job, eating fish was not considered so. During the time of Chaitanya Mahaprabhu catching fish was considered a mean job, but Mahaprabhu did not oppose the act of eating fish. He never opposed the eating of fish in Bengal and in the entire area stretching between Bengal and Kashi [Varanasi]. He opposed fish-eating in the lands to the west of Kashi. So, in those days many people used to ridicule the Vaeśńavas by saying:

paragraphs.text: During the reign of the second Devapal, in the last phase of the Buddhist period, a great Kaevartta rebellion took place in North Bengal. The Kaevarttas declared that the vitality of the Bengalee race does not lie in a few artificially- constructed new castes and sub-castes… It lies in the Kaevarttas who are original Bengalees. It is unfortunate that soon afterwards the Kaevarttas became divided under the pressure of a few so-called high-caste people. Those who gave up fishing as a livelihood became known as Hálik Kaevarttas [“Kaevarttas using the plough”] or Cáśii Kaevarttas [“Kaevarttas who are farmers”] or Máhiśyas [“those who tend buffaloes”]. They were recognized as high- caste people. And those (the fishermen) who continued to make a living based on fish became known as Jálik or Jele Kaevarttas [“Kaevarttas using the fishing net”]. However, anthropologically it is difficult to find any difference between a Brahman or a Kayastha of Bengal and a Jele Kaevartta. The same sweet, graceful facial structure, the same well-built physique with tender appearance, the same emotional disposition, the same lively humanitarian qualities and temperament, manifested in joys and sorrows of life.

paragraphs.text: Kuc + ghaiṋ = koc [Koch]. The meaning of the root kuc is “to attract”, “to give shelter”, “to attract so as to give shelter”. This story comes from a long time back, though long after the creation of Ráŕh, when the rest of Bengal came into existence – several lakh [hundreds of thousands of] years ago – perhaps some time after the appearance of man – but certainly not too much later. It must be in between the Oligocene and the Mesozoic age. Eastern Ráŕh first emerged from the sand and silt, carried by the rivers of western Ráŕh. Then, just as the rivers of western and eastern Ráŕh in a similar process created the Samatat in the south, in the same way the formation of the land of Barendra began out of alluvium and sand, carried by the rivers Gauṋgá and Brahmaputra. paragraphs.text: When Aryan civilization reached Samatat and Vauṋga (as far as their cultural uniqueness and their blood, Bengalees are not Aryans), eventually Bengalees were impacted by Aryan culture. Not only Bengalees, the same applies to the rest of India east of Kashi. It was the people of Ráŕh who, crossing the Ganges, went to Barendra. Thus, when Ráŕh accepted the Brahmanic religion, this cult spread primarily from Ráŕh to Samatat and Vauṋga. After a few preliminary inquiries, you will come to know that Samatat has no shárasvat samáj (intellectual society) of its own. It was simply the transplanted culture of Ráŕh. The original Kayasthas and Vaidyas of Bengal are the people who migrated there from Haripal in Hooghly District and Shriikhanda in Burdwan District. The Brahmans of Vauṋga migrated from so many places in Ráŕh that no specific names can be mentioned. That is why in East Bengal there is no so-called Brahman born in Vauṋga. Even today, those who have been living there for generations introduce themselves as Brahmans of Ráŕh. In sociological language this is called cultural transplantation. Even with regard to Barendra, largely similar events transpired.
summary: When Aryan civilization reached Samatat and Vauṋga (as far as their cultural uniqueness and their blood, Bengalees are not Aryans), eventually Bengalees were impacted by Aryan culture.
The original Kayasthas and Vaidyas of Bengal are the people who migrated there from Haripal in Hooghly District and Shriikhanda in Burdwan District.
Even with regard to Barendra, largely similar events transpired.

paragraphs.text: When, after crossing the Ganges and Padma Rivers, the people of Ráŕh migrated northward instead of eastward, with spades and axes in their hands, accompanied by cows of the zebu subspecies, and with ploughs and yokes on their shoulders, there came from the north a substream of Mongolian culture. Through a sweet blending of these Ráŕhii and Mongolian cultures evolved the Bengalee society of Barendra. While a little paler in complexion than the Bengalees of Ráŕh, with somewhat flatter noses, they were very cultured, gracious and simple human beings. At that very point in time, we obtained the original Bengalee Kaevarttas of Barendrabhumi as vital resources for the Bengalee race. I have mentioned elsewhere that originally every Bengalee was a Kaevartta. Just as the Kaevarttas moved from Ráŕh to Samatat, they also migrated northwards from Ráŕh to Barendra. The Namashudras, who are the essence of the Bengalees of central Bengal, were merely an ornament of the Kaevarttas. The people of Barendra have likewise descended from the Kaevarttas. The subterranean flow of Kaevartta culture mingled together with the Máhiśya culture of South Bengal or Midnapore, meaning that their bloodstream reverberates with the tender and adamantine traits of the original Bengalees. In the last phase of the Buddhist era, the Kaevarttas of Barendra became vocal against the tyranny of King Devapal II. In the history of the world, such a well-organized peopleʼs resistance movement is rare – it may be that there has not been any comparable movement in history. The Kaevartta Rebellion [11th century] ushered in a unique renaissance of the Bengalee race – it infused in them an intense consciousness to discover new horizons of ideas.
summary: When, after crossing the Ganges and Padma Rivers, the people of Ráŕh migrated northward instead of eastward, with spades and axes in their hands, accompanied by cows of the zebu subspecies, and with ploughs and yokes on their shoulders, there came from the north a substream of Mongolian culture.
The Namashudras, who are the essence of the Bengalees of central Bengal, were merely an ornament of the Kaevarttas.
The Kaevartta Rebellion [11th century] ushered in a unique renaissance of the Bengalee race – it infused in them an intense consciousness to discover new horizons of ideas.

paragraphs.text: These very Kaevarttas moved to the north, northwest [and northeast]. Those who moved northwest settled down in Mithila and initiated a new way of life. Even today, thousands of original Bengalee Kaevarttas live in the Purnea – Saharsa region. Those who went northeast advanced throughout the entirety of the region of Bengal. In Kaevartta society, men slightly outnumbered women. Those who went towards the northeast corner were compelled to marry Mongolian women in order to preserve their society, thus creating a new branch of Bengalee ethnicity. These very people, moving gradually northwards, advanced near the peaks of the Himalayas. They settled down on both sides of the River Sankoch, which originated from Bhutan. This new generation of Bengalees came to be named Koch after the river Sankoch. In their days of woe, when Bengalee life was battered by the impact of the descent and explosion of gigantic meteors [socially], the Kaevarttas were the greatest refuge and asset of Bengal. That is why they were named Koch ( 1 ), not only after the River Sankoch, but also due to their characteristic of providing shelter to the shelterless.
summary: These very Kaevarttas moved to the north, northwest [and northeast].
Those who went towards the northeast corner were compelled to marry Mongolian women in order to preserve their society, thus creating a new branch of Bengalee ethnicity.
That is why they were named Koch ( 1 ), not only after the River Sankoch, but also due to their characteristic of providing shelter to the shelterless.

paragraphs.text: When an idealistic youth of the Koch race saw that the social life of Bengal was heading towards disaster, and had degenerated in its cultural life, he came forward as the living symbol of Bengalʼs resurrection. This Bengalee youth of the Mech dynasty established Kámtápur [Kamtapur] State in the Sankoch Valley with the help of only two hundred dedicated young men. (According to another opinion, the Mech people had not yet been recognized as a branch of the Koch society; they were treated as an undifferentiated part of the Koch race.) The name of that youth was Haridas Mondal (There is, of course, some difference of opinion on this question.)
summary: When an idealistic youth of the Koch race saw that the social life of Bengal was heading towards disaster, and had degenerated in its cultural life, he came forward as the living symbol of Bengalʼs resurrection.
(According to another opinion, the Mech people had not yet been recognized as a branch of the Koch society; they were treated as an undifferentiated part of the Koch race.
) The name of that youth was Haridas Mondal (There is, of course, some difference of opinion on this question.

paragraphs.text: Since the pre-Buddhist era, Bengal had remained divided into five parts for reasons of geographical diversity and administrative convenience: 1) Ráŕh, to the west of the Bhagirathi River, 2) the central region, comprising the Bhagirathi and Madhumati Rivers (Bagri), 3) Barendra, to the north of the Padma River, 4) Vauṋga, on the eastern side of the river Madhumati, and 5) Mithila, to the north of the Padma and west of the River Koshii (Kaoshikii). Compared to other regions, Ráŕh and Barendra were slightly larger in area. The other parts each had a bhukti [administrative district]; that is, Bagri Bhukti consisted of the entire Samatat. The entire Vauṋga area constituted Vauṋga Bhukti, and the entire Mithila constituted Tirhut Bhukti. Yet Ráŕh and Barendra, being larger in size, each had two bhuktis. The northern part of Ráŕh (north of where the Damodar River used to flow but no longer does today), meaning the present Dhanbad, Burdwan, Birbhum, Deoghar, Dumka, Gadda, Sahebganj, and Ráŕh-Murshidabad, comprised Burdwan Bhukti. (In those days Hooghly and Howrah were included in Burdwan.) Midnapore, Bankura, Manbhum, East Ranchi, Singbhum and Bhanjabhum comprised Dańd́a Bhukti (Midnapore). Similarly, in the southern part of Barendrabhumi was Paondrabardhan Bhukti, and its northern part formed Kamtapur Bhukti. The Bengalee Kaevarttas of those days, infused with vitality, selected Haridas Mondal as their leader and at the same time made him the king of Kamtapur. From the time of Haridas Mondal, the Kaevarttas of this region came to be called Koch. In the course of time the Koch people came to be divided into four characteristic branches: 1) Mech, 2) Rajbangshi, 3) Rajgun, and 4) Kolia (Kolliká – Koliá). Needless to say, all four branches were the original Bengalees, and they accepted as the quintessence of their existence the task of upholding, conveying and nourishing the original Bengalee culture, and continued to provide evidence of their worthiness as “the shelter or koch of Bengalee culture”.
summary: Since the pre-Buddhist era, Bengal had remained divided into five parts for reasons of geographical diversity and administrative convenience: 1) Ráŕh, to the west of the Bhagirathi River, 2) the central region, comprising the Bhagirathi and Madhumati Rivers (Bagri), 3) Barendra, to the north of the Padma River, 4) Vauṋga, on the eastern side of the river Madhumati, and 5) Mithila, to the north of the Padma and west of the River Koshii (Kaoshikii).
(In those days Hooghly and Howrah were included in Burdwan.

Needless to say, all four branches were the original Bengalees, and they accepted as the quintessence of their existence the task of upholding, conveying and nourishing the original Bengalee culture, and continued to provide evidence of their worthiness as “the shelter or koch of Bengalee culture”.

paragraphs.text: Later, Kamtapur split into two fragments – its eastern part was called Bijni and the western part was named Coochbehar. The Koch people had been Shaivites since ancient times. Though Jainism and Buddhism had some influence upon them, it was not extensive. However, in the southern part of Barendrabhumi, that is, in Paondrabardhan Bhukti, the impact of Buddhism was widespread. Later, the people of Paondrabardhan Bhukti, who had been influenced by Buddhism, accepted Islam as their religion. The same thing happened in Kamtapur Bhukti; but compared to Kamtapur Bhukti, the number of Muslims was far greater in the Paondrabardhan Bhukti. The names of Baneshwar, Bangarh, Jateshwar and Jalpeshwar remind us of the Shaivite influence in these areas even today.
summary: Later, Kamtapur split into two fragments – its eastern part was called Bijni and the western part was named Coochbehar.
However, in the southern part of Barendrabhumi, that is, in Paondrabardhan Bhukti, the impact of Buddhism was widespread.
The names of Baneshwar, Bangarh, Jateshwar and Jalpeshwar remind us of the Shaivite influence in these areas even today.

paragraphs.text: The Ahoms who came from Burma occupied the upper part of the Brahmaputra Valley, but they were not able to set their foot in the lower part, that is, Barendrabhumi. So though the impact of the Ahoms on Assamese culture was vast and pervasive, there was not one iota of influence by them on Kamtapur or Barendra. In the pronunciation of vowels and consonants in the Assamese language, the influence of the Ahoms is universally acknowledged. However, there is not the slightest Ahom influence on Barendra. A look at the spoken language of Kamrup and Goalpara makes this as clear as daylight.
summary: The Ahoms who came from Burma occupied the upper part of the Brahmaputra Valley, but they were not able to set their foot in the lower part, that is, Barendrabhumi.
In the pronunciation of vowels and consonants in the Assamese language, the influence of the Ahoms is universally acknowledged.
A look at the spoken language of Kamrup and Goalpara makes this as clear as daylight.

paragraphs.text: The British fully occupied the entire eastern part of Kamtapur; that is, Bijni, and transformed it into their estate under the Permanent Settlement Act. They also brought the western part, that is, a large part of Coochbehar, under their control and allowed only eight police precincts (thánás) as autonomous areas to be under the king. The large state of Kamtapur was finally reduced to those eight police precincts with the name of Coochbehar. These eight police precincts are Coochbehar, Tufangung, Dinhata, Mathabhanga, Mekhligang; Sitai, Sitalkuchi and Haldibari ( 2 ). The British brought the greater part of [what had been] Coochbehar under their control. They added its northwestern part, that is, the D́alimkot́ area, to the Himalayan mountainous region of Sikkim, to constitute Darjeeling District. The previous centre of activities for the D́alimkot́ region was Phansidewa. Later it was shifted to Siliguri.
summary: The British fully occupied the entire eastern part of Kamtapur; that is, Bijni, and transformed it into their estate under the Permanent Settlement Act.
The British brought the greater part of [what had been] Coochbehar under their control.
Later it was shifted to Siliguri.

paragraphs.text: At that time the inhabitants of the plains in Darjeeling District were still in Darjeeling; even now, Bengalees of the Koch group continue to live there. The dwellers of the hill regions, that is, Darjeeling, Kalimpong and Kharśáń (which is incorrectly called Kurseong), are Lepchas and Bhutias. (They are Buddhists of the Lama sect). After it was conquered by the British, many Nepalese migrated there from Nepal to earn their livelihood. These Nepalese speak diverse languages and are of different religious faiths. (They are primarily Hindus and Buddhists.) Most of them speak the Rai language. Also among them are people who speak the Gurung, Magar, Newari, Limba, Limpo, Tharu, Kirat and Sherpa languages. The present state language of Nepal is Gorkhali. Though the Gorkhas were not in the majority in Nepal, they were the rulers. Hence their language is now the state language. (Even today, people incorrectly describe Gorkháli as the “Nepali” language.)
summary: At that time the inhabitants of the plains in Darjeeling District were still in Darjeeling; even now, Bengalees of the Koch group continue to live there.
) Most of them speak the Rai language.
(Even today, people incorrectly describe Gorkháli as the “Nepali” language.

paragraphs.text: Before the advent of the Gorkhas, the king of Nepal was a Newari. At that time, the Maethili language, written in Maethil (Bengali) letters, was the state language of Nepal. In any case, a few people in the hill regions of Darjeeling speak Gorkháli (which, again, is incorrectly called the “Nepali” language).
summary: Before the advent of the Gorkhas, the king of Nepal was a Newari.
At that time, the Maethili language, written in Maethil (Bengali) letters, was the state language of Nepal.
In any case, a few people in the hill regions of Darjeeling speak Gorkháli (which, again, is incorrectly called the “Nepali” language).

paragraphs.text: Just a short while earlier, I mentioned that D́alimkot́ is now known as Siliguri. Excluding Dalimkot́, most of Coochbehar was occupied by the British, who named it Rangpur District. Rangpur became its headquarters (karvat́). Since the district was quite large in size, the British split it later on into three parts. The southern part continued to be called Rangpur, with its headquarters remaining at Rangpur. The northern part was named Jalpaiguri – Jalpaiguri town became its headquarters. The northeastern part was called Northeast Rangpur, and its headquarters was set up at Dhubri.
summary: Just a short while earlier, I mentioned that D́alimkot́ is now known as Siliguri.
Since the district was quite large in size, the British split it later on into three parts.
The northeastern part was called Northeast Rangpur, and its headquarters was set up at Dhubri.

paragraphs.text: In 1912, when the state of Assam was created, its poor economic condition was revealed. The annual financial returns of this newly created state of Assam were found to be less than the annual returns of the Kolkata Corporation. To enable the economic condition to become vibrant, Bengali districts such as Sylhet, Cachar and Northeastern Rangpur were included in this newly formed state. Rangpur remained in Bengal, and Northeastern Rangpur became part of Assam. This was an awkward situation. That is why the British changed the name of Northeastern Rangpur and gave it the new name Goalpara. However, its headquarters remained at Dhubri. Recently, the district of Goalpara has been divided into three parts: 1) Dhubri, 2) Kokrajhar and 3) Goalpara.
summary: In 1912, when the state of Assam was created, its poor economic condition was revealed.
This was an awkward situation.
Recently, the district of Goalpara has been divided into three parts: 1) Dhubri, 2) Kokrajhar and 3) Goalpara.

paragraphs.text: The western part of the present Kamrup District was once in Kamtapur state. Kamakhya Hill of Kamrup District was under the control of Kamtapur state for a long time. The Kamakhya Devii temple was also built by the kings of Kamtapur State, and they also repaired it several times. In this connection, the name of King Shukladhvaja of Kamtapur is worth remembering. Those who know the story of the Shákta-Maoyásáriá [religious] struggle of Assam must certainly be aware of it.
summary: The western part of the present Kamrup District was once in Kamtapur state.
The Kamakhya Devii temple was also built by the kings of Kamtapur State, and they also repaired it several times.
Those who know the story of the Shákta-Maoyásáriá [religious] struggle of Assam must certainly be aware of it.

paragraphs.text: Later, Kamrup came under the control of the Ahom kings. According to natural law, the long-standing rule of the Ahom kings brought the influence of the Ahoms on the spoken language and pronunciation of Kamrup (bhát́iá upabháśá of Assamese). However, for obvious reasons, there was no Ahom influence on the spoken language of Goalpara. Therefore, the cultural life of Goalpara is verily the reverberation of Barendra culture; in the wet soil of Goalpara there is only the fragrance of the Barendra way of life. Even today, Goalpara exudes the exquisitely sweet aroma of the warm-heartedness of the Koch people – the story of the rise and fall of their life.
summary: Later, Kamrup came under the control of the Ahom kings.
However, for obvious reasons, there was no Ahom influence on the spoken language of Goalpara.
Even today, Goalpara exudes the exquisitely sweet aroma of the warm-heartedness of the Koch people – the story of the rise and fall of their life.

paragraphs.text: In any case, you have come to know a brief history of the Koch people. I presume that you now feel very proud of them.
summary: In any case, you have come to know a brief history of the Koch people.
I presume that you now feel very proud of them.

chapters.title: The Original Bengalee Community of Earlier Times – 3 / The Original Inhabitants of Bengal

paragraphs.text: The original inhabitants of Bangalistan include the Rajbangshis from North Bengal; the Mahatos from Ráŕh; the Chakmas from Chattagram and Tripura; the Mahiśyas from Midnapur and 24 Paraganas; the Sadgopes from Birbhum; the Namashudras from Jessore and Khulna; and the Ugra Kśatriyas from Burdwan. These original Bengalees may be called the “Játa Báuṋálii”.
summary: The original inhabitants of Bangalistan include the Rajbangshis from North Bengal; the Mahatos from Ráŕh; the Chakmas from Chattagram and Tripura; the Mahiśyas from Midnapur and 24 Paraganas; the Sadgopes from Birbhum; the Namashudras from Jessore and Khulna; and the Ugra Kśatriyas from Burdwan.
These original Bengalees may be called the “Játa Báuṋálii”.

paragraphs.text: The proof that these communities are the original Bengalees is that they are clustered together in numerous adjacent villages throughout the regions they inhabit. Village after village of these original inhabitants are located together. They do not populate one or two isolated villages, nor are there merely several people from these communities scattered in a few villages throughout the region. This proves that the above-mentioned people were concentrated in particular areas. In contrast, the Brahmins and the Kayasthas are found in only a few villages and are few in number, thus we cannot be sure that they are the original inhabitants of Bengal. They may have come from other parts of Bengal to do some special kind of work, as priests for example, or they may have come from outside Bengal.
summary: The proof that these communities are the original Bengalees is that they are clustered together in numerous adjacent villages throughout the regions they inhabit.
This proves that the above-mentioned people were concentrated in particular areas.
They may have come from other parts of Bengal to do some special kind of work, as priests for example, or they may have come from outside Bengal.

paragraphs.text: Whenever you plan any developmental programme for Bengal, you should keep the interests of the Játa Báuṋálii uppermost, as they are the original inhabitants and taken together comprise the majority community. If they are benefited, the whole of Bangalistan will be benefited.
summary: Whenever you plan any developmental programme for Bengal, you should keep the interests of the Játa Báuṋálii uppermost, as they are the original inhabitants and taken together comprise the majority community.
If they are benefited, the whole of Bangalistan will be benefited.

paragraphs.text: The original name of the Bengalee community was “Kaevartta”, meaning “a community of fishermen”. They were divided into five groups – the Namashudras in the east; the Rajabangshis in the north; the Mahiśyas in the south; the Sadgopes in the northern part; and the Mahatos in the west. “Mahato” came from mahátmá. These original five communities were not tribals.
summary: The original name of the Bengalee community was “Kaevartta”, meaning “a community of fishermen”.
“Mahato” came from mahátmá.
These original five communities were not tribals.

paragraphs.text: In Bengal there are many small groups of people speaking non-Sanskritic languages – Indo-Tibetan and several other languages. These groups are known as “tribals” – those speaking non-Sanskritic languages. The Játa Báuṋálii are the indigenous population of Bengal and speak a pure Sanskritic language.
summary: In Bengal there are many small groups of people speaking non-Sanskritic languages – Indo-Tibetan and several other languages.
These groups are known as “tribals” – those speaking non-Sanskritic languages.
The Játa Báuṋálii are the indigenous population of Bengal and speak a pure Sanskritic language.

paragraphs.text: Human society is one and indivisible, so Bangalistan must not go against the interests or spirit of universal humanity. This is a must. You have to see the interests of the place where you remain, but you should not go against the spirit of universal humanity. Do not waste your time in dialects and sub-dialects as this is the approach of analysis. All dialects should merge in the main language. This is the approach of synthesis.
summary: Human society is one and indivisible, so Bangalistan must not go against the interests or spirit of universal humanity.
Do not waste your time in dialects and sub-dialects as this is the approach of analysis.
This is the approach of synthesis.

paragraphs.text: Varśa means “that which is being showered.” It is a masculine term. Its feminine form is varśá (when the feminine suffix á is added). The second meaning is “a large island”. In the Vedic age the world was divided into several vast islands or continents – Jambudviipa, Ságardviipa, Kraoiṋcadviipa, etc. The name of ancient India was Jambudviipa. This island extended from Central Asia to the frontiers of Burma. One of the regions of Jambudviipa was Bhárata Varśa. Another name of Burma was Suvarńadviipa. All the areas of the vast Jambudviipa were not equally fertile, nor equally rich in mineral resources. The particular portion of Jambudviipa that was fit for human habitation, with an abundance of food and water, was called Bhárata Varśa. Ancient Tibet was called Kiḿpuruśa Varśa. Of course, in the nomenclature of Kiḿpuruśa Varśa there is some humour. Tibetan males have hardly any beard or moustache, and from a distance people may wrongly think they are women. From their appearance, at least for outsiders, it was difficult to distinguish between men and women. That is why outsiders used to joke, “Are they males or females?,” or “Kiḿ Puruśah?” in Sanskrit. Varśa means “land”. Thus, Tibet came to be known as Kiḿpuruśa Varśa.
summary: Varśa means “that which is being showered.
All the areas of the vast Jambudviipa were not equally fertile, nor equally rich in mineral resources.
Thus, Tibet came to be known as Kiḿpuruśa Varśa.

paragraphs.text: The Sanskrit verb bhr means “to feed” (bharańa). So the government food department is called “Janasambharańa Vibhág”. A husbandʼs duty is to provide his wife with food and drink. So a husband is called bhartá in Sanskrit. Bhr [verbal root] + trń + first-case ending in singular number results in the word bhartá. Bháráta means the land where there is an abundance of food and drink, and ample scope for all-round development. India was not named after King Bharata, who lived and ruled long afterwards. In the Indian constitution, “India” or “Bharata” is mentioned, but in actual fact the name of the land is not “Bharata” but “Bháratavarśa”. Bharata + suffix śńa = bhárata + varśa = “Bháratavarśa”, a compound word. So at the end of this compound word, the term varśa or desha should also be used; otherwise it will be grammatically incorrect.
summary: The Sanskrit verb bhr means “to feed” (bharańa).
Bháráta means the land where there is an abundance of food and drink, and ample scope for all-round development.
So at the end of this compound word, the term varśa or desha should also be used; otherwise it will be grammatically incorrect.

paragraphs.text: Instead of continuing to dwell upon the ancient history of all India, I would rather concentrate on the Bengalee New Yearʼs day. Here we will have to use the term varśa in a special sense. Bengal is situated on the eastern extremity of Jambudviipa or Bháratavarśa. The boundary between two countries is the line regarding which the people on one side say, “This is the limit of our land,” and the people on the other side also say, “This is the limit of our land.” For example, Srinagar District is in the north of India, but Baramulla District is the northernmost extremity of India because it borders on Pakistan. Bengal is the easternmost area between Jambudviipa and Suvarńadviipa.
summary: Instead of continuing to dwell upon the ancient history of all India, I would rather concentrate on the Bengalee New Yearʼs day.
The boundary between two countries is the line regarding which the people on one side say, “This is the limit of our land,” and the people on the other side also say, “This is the limit of our land.
Bengal is the easternmost area between Jambudviipa and Suvarńadviipa.

paragraphs.text: You might have already heard from me that civilization advances along river banks and river valleys. If one moves even five hundred miles along a river bank, one will encounter a similar type of civilization. But if one travels forty miles away from the river bank, the outward expression of the civilization will be quite different. For example, the Ganges has its source at Gauṋgottari. (Some people wrongly say “Gauṋgotrii”, but this is incorrect.) Gauṋgottari is the place where the Ganges originates. The Ganges ends at Gangasagar. On either side of the Gangetic Valley the same type of civilization can be easily discerned. The civilization at Varanasi is quite similar to the civilization found at Patna, because the entire area is situated within the Gangetic Valley. However, if one moves only forty miles southward from Varanasi, one will notice a different culture and civilization, since that area does not come within the Gangetic Valley civilization. If we study the various expressions of civilization along the river valleys, we find a certain blended civilization in Bengal.
summary: You might have already heard from me that civilization advances along river banks and river valleys.
) Gauṋgottari is the place where the Ganges originates.
If we study the various expressions of civilization along the river valleys, we find a certain blended civilization in Bengal.

paragraphs.text: Take the case of old Gondwanaland. In the distant past, some areas of what is now India did not exist: There was neither northern India nor the D́abák and Samatat areas of Bengal, but there was old Gondwanaland. That was about 300 million years ago. At that time, the major parts of Sind, the Punjab, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and Bengal did not exist. They were all submerged under the vast oceans. The Himalayas also did not exist. But the Vindhya mountain range and its sister ranges – Satpura, Sahyadri, Rajmahal and Ramgarh – did exist. These mountains were very high, and always snow-covered. Because of these snow-clad mountains, the rivers originating from them used to have melted-snow water year round. They never dried up. The Suvarnarekha, the Kangsavati, the Keleghai, the Haldi, the Rupaharayan, the Dwarakeshwar, the Shilavati, the Jayapanda, the Gandheshwari, the Damodar, the Ajay and the Mayuraksi – these are the rivers of Gondwanaland. The land of Ráŕh slopes from the west to the east, so the rivers also flow from the west to the east.
summary: Take the case of old Gondwanaland.
The Himalayas also did not exist.
The land of Ráŕh slopes from the west to the east, so the rivers also flow from the west to the east.

paragraphs.text: This was the original homeland of the Bengalee civilization. The soil of Ráŕh is 300 million years old. Later on, the Himalayan mountain range was formed as a result of a tremendous earthquake caused by a volcanic eruption. Many rivers started to flow down the Himalayas – the Ganges, the Yamuna, the Gharghara, the Taptii, the Koshii, etc. With the sand and alluvium carried by these rivers, the vast plains of northern India came into being. With the same alluvium, Bengal was also formed. To this was added the old soil which came down the mountains of Gondowanaland due to erosion. According to history, the eastern part of Ráŕh, that is Tamkul Subdivision of Midnapore District, Howrah District, Hooghly District, the eastern part of Burdwan and the western part of Murshidabad District – these areas were formed out of the alluvium carried by the rivers of Ráŕh. These areas do not have the same soil as the original areas of the 300 million-year-old Ráŕh. The oldest soil is in Manbhum, ( 1 ) Bankura, the major part of Midnapur District, the western part of Burdwan District, and Birbhum. The soil of this part of Bengal is the most ancient.
summary: This was the original homeland of the Bengalee civilization.
With the same alluvium, Bengal was also formed.
The soil of this part of Bengal is the most ancient.

paragraphs.text: The oldest manuscripts of Bengali literature can be found in this western part – in fact, they are now being found. The script which was discovered written on a rock on Shushunia Hill of Bankura District is the oldest Bengali script. At Beletor village or Barjora Police Station of Bankura District, the oldest manuscript of the Bengali language was discovered. Shrii Krśńa Kiirttana, written by Baru Chandidas, was composed in Ráŕh. The village Jayda of Chandil Police Station of the former Manbhum District is now in Bihar, even though it is a Bengali-speaking area. In this village, the oldest Bengali script, Abhijiṋánapatra, has been discovered. All these things should be carefully preserved.
summary: The oldest manuscripts of Bengali literature can be found in this western part – in fact, they are now being found.
Shrii Krśńa Kiirttana, written by Baru Chandidas, was composed in Ráŕh.
All these things should be carefully preserved.

paragraphs.text: However, let us come to the original topic.
summary: However, let us come to the original topic.

paragraphs.text: Bengal is situated on the boundary line between Jambudviipa and Suvarńadviipa [ancient names of India and Burma]. The civilization that grew along the banks of the Mayurakshi, Ajay and Damodar later blended with the civilization which developed in the areas of Páond́ravardhana Bhukti, Samatat, and D́abák. A new civilization was born in Bengal – a blending between the Ráŕh civilization of Gondwana ( 2 ) and the Gangetic civilization. That is why the people of Bengal are not exactly the same as those of northern India. The modes of worship and the priesthood system are different from those of northern India. Bengali script and intonation are also different, as indeed is the physical appearance of the Bengalees. From their facial lineaments, one can conclude that these people are of Bengalee stock. This has been possible due to blending of civilizations.
summary: Bengal is situated on the boundary line between Jambudviipa and Suvarńadviipa [ancient names of India and Burma].
The modes of worship and the priesthood system are different from those of northern India.
This has been possible due to blending of civilizations.

paragraphs.text: Not only that. Even the type of thought varies between the different communities. The blending of the dark-complexioned people of Ráŕh with the fair-complexioned Aryans led to the formation of the Bengalee race. But this is not the end of the story. In fact, the Brahmaputra flowed into India from the interior of Tibet, where its name was Sang Fo, meaning “Son of a God”. In other words, it came from within a Mongolian ( 3 ) country. The people of Tibet are Mongolian of the Indo-Tibetan group. The Mongolians are divided into a few branches, one of them being the Indo-Tibetan group. The Brahmaputra, or the Sang Fo, carries that Mongolian civilization and not the Gangetic civilization.
summary: Even the type of thought varies between the different communities.
In other words, it came from within a Mongolian ( 3 ) country.
The Brahmaputra, or the Sang Fo, carries that Mongolian civilization and not the Gangetic civilization.

paragraphs.text: That Mongolian civilization was criticized by the Aryans in the Kúrma Puráńa:
summary: That Mongolian civilization was criticized by the Aryans in the Kúrma Puráńa:

paragraphs.text: Sarve máḿsaratáh múŕháh mleccháh gobrahmaghátakáh;
summary: Sarve máḿsaratáh múŕháh mleccháh gobrahmaghátakáh;

paragraphs.text: Kuvacakáh pare múrháh ete kút́ayonayoh;
