Now the question may arise, why was the spring festival in Bengal not observed in a grand way? Because the winter in Bengal is not very severe, so spring also is not very conspicuous. In Bengal there are three seasons: summer, rainy season, and autumn. Autumn is very conspicuous, but spring is not. In autumn, the kash and shiulii (lower) blossom, the rains are over, and the land is all green. In this season the planetary position is as follows. If the full moon comes during the presence of the stars Púrva Phalgunii or Uttar Phalgunii in the northern hemisphere (north of the equator), the lunar month is called Phálguna, and the name of the solar month is also Phalguna. On the night before the full moon, people burn the effigy of an old woman which represents winter. This is the astrological as well as the astronomical interpretation of the spring festival.
summary: Jád́yápahá means that which kills or removes dullness.
Autumn is very conspicuous, but spring is not.
This is the astrological as well as the astronomical interpretation of the spring festival.

paragraphs.text: In Indo-Aryan mythology there is mention of a king named Hirańyakashipu. His sister, Holika, was a woman of violent nature. She was a cannibal. (You should note that she was a cannibal, not homivorous. A human eating another human is called a cannibal, whereas an animal eating human flesh is called homivorous. Holika was a cannibal, whereas a tiger is homivorous). The people out of anger burnt Holika alive the night before the full moon, and to celebrate this occasion, they arranged a festival of joy which was called Holikadahana (the burning of Holika). That is why even today in northern India particularly in the Punjab and Uttar Pradesh, this Holi festival is celebrated. And since the moon enters the zodiac sign of the Uttar Phálgunii star, the festival is popularly called Pháguyá in Bihar and in the eastern regions of Uttar Pradesh. But as neither winter nor spring is conspicuous in Bengal, so neither festival, Holi nor Pháguyá, is celebrated. The festival that is celebrated on that day in Bengal is the Dolyátrá of Shriikrśńa, and thus that day is also observed as a holiday in Bengal.
summary: In Indo-Aryan mythology there is mention of a king named Hirańyakashipu.
The people out of anger burnt Holika alive the night before the full moon, and to celebrate this occasion, they arranged a festival of joy which was called Holikadahana (the burning of Holika).
The festival that is celebrated on that day in Bengal is the Dolyátrá of Shriikrśńa, and thus that day is also observed as a holiday in Bengal.

paragraphs.text: The history behind the festival is this. About 500 years ago Mahaprabhu Shrii Caetanya once went to visit Brindaban, where he observed the Holi festival. Brindaban is situated in the western part of India, where the Holi festival is celebrated, not the Pháguá, which is popular as far as Allahabad. To the west of Allahabad, i.e.in the non-Bhojpurii-speaking areas, there Holi is celebrated.
summary: The history behind the festival is this.
Brindaban is situated in the western part of India, where the Holi festival is celebrated, not the Pháguá, which is popular as far as Allahabad.
in the non-Bhojpurii-speaking areas, there Holi is celebrated.

paragraphs.text: After his return to Bengal, Mahaprabhu pondered deeply and decided to introduce the festival but, of course, in a different form. He said to his followers, “Go to the Krśńa temple on that day, and apply red powder and red colour to Krśńa. Then you should play with the red powder and colour amongst yourselves,” And those who gave red powder and colour to others would also feed them with malpoa [delectable sweet]. In Bihar there are both poa and malpoa sweets. The difference between the two is that if flour is mixed with sugar and spices, and dipped in sugar-water, it is called poa. And if flour without sugar is first fried in ghee and then dipped in sugar-water, it is called malpoa. What is known as poa in Bihar and Uttar Pradesh is known as malpoa in Bengal. And what is known as malpoa is known as dhákái malpoa. Mahaprabhu was very fond of malpoa. In his biography it has been written, Malpoa sarbhájá ár, luchi purii, ananda bhojan karen nadiiya biharii. (“Malpoa, sarbhaja, luchi and puri are relished by Mahaprabhu”). In my boyhood days when I first heard these lines, I said, “Well, it's all right that Mahaprabhu relished malpoa, sarbhaja, luci, puri, etc. – but is there anyone who does not relish these delicacies? Personally as far as I know, all people like them!”
summary: After his return to Bengal, Mahaprabhu pondered deeply and decided to introduce the festival but, of course, in a different form.
And what is known as malpoa is known as dhákái malpoa.
Personally as far as I know, all people like them!

paragraphs.text: As I said, Mahaprabhu saw the festival in Brindavan and then introduced it in Bengal. It has never become a social festival in Bengal, as Pháguyá has become a social festival in Bihar and in the eastern part of Uttar Pradesh. Rather, it has become a kind of religious festival in Bengal. So it is neither Holi festival nor Pháguyá – it is the Dolyátrá of Shriikrśńa, and the government of West Bengal has declared that day as a holiday.
summary: As I said, Mahaprabhu saw the festival in Brindavan and then introduced it in Bengal.
Rather, it has become a kind of religious festival in Bengal.
So it is neither Holi festival nor Pháguyá – it is the Dolyátrá of Shriikrśńa, and the government of West Bengal has declared that day as a holiday.

paragraphs.text: Now, what is the significance of Dolyátrá? The winter is over, and the people are active again. Various colourful ideas and plans are appearing in their minds, and they plan to do so many things for the benefit of society. Similarly when they think of Lord Krśńa, their minds are filled with joy. The very thought of Krśńa produces ripples of joy in people's minds, and these vibrations of joy in the devotees' minds also produce a corresponding vibration in Krśńa's mind. They think, “Oh Krśńa, I love you – but you also love me, that I know.” In this way the ripples of joy in their own minds also create vibrations of joy in His mind. This is the inner significance of the Dolyátrá of Shrii Krśńa. In our Ananda Márga Caryácarya, this festival is celebrated as a spring festival.
summary: Now, what is the significance of Dolyátrá?
The very thought of Krśńa produces ripples of joy in people's minds, and these vibrations of joy in the devotees' minds also produce a corresponding vibration in Krśńa's mind.
In our Ananda Márga Caryácarya, this festival is celebrated as a spring festival.

paragraphs.text: In the days of Mahaprabhu, the prevailing rule was to seek the prior permission of the person to whom you were going to give the red powder. If that person gave permission, then only could you smear him or her with coloured powder, and then treat them to malpoa. These days all these customs have degenerated.
summary: In the days of Mahaprabhu, the prevailing rule was to seek the prior permission of the person to whom you were going to give the red powder.
If that person gave permission, then only could you smear him or her with coloured powder, and then treat them to malpoa.
These days all these customs have degenerated.

paragraphs.text: Let us discuss the science of colour. In Saḿskrta language there are two similar words: varńa and rága. Though the meanings are approximately the same, they are not completely synonymous. Varńa means colour (what is termed in Bengali as rauṋg). But this word varńa does not indicate the colour which will colour other objects as well; an object has its own colour but its colour may not necessarily dye other objects. But the word rága means that particular colour which can dye other objects also. So the inner spirit of the science of colour in Vaeshnavii Tantra is this – that each and every expression of this universe has its own rhythm, its own vibration, its own sound, and its own colour, and thus it has its own form as well. And as it has its own sound, it has a particular sweetness of its own. Suppose there is a person who is dumb but very good; and there is another person who is equally good, but speaks well also. Obviously you will prefer the second man, because he possesses the power of expression. Dumb people can give expression to their inner thoughts only with their gestures and postures, whereas those who can speak can express themselves with gesture, posture, and also language. A dumb person can only look at you and express through gesture to come to him, but a person who can speak can say, “Come little child, come to me.” This vocal expression of the second person conveys more sweetness.
summary: Let us discuss the science of colour.

So the inner spirit of the science of colour in Vaeshnavii Tantra is this – that each and every expression of this universe has its own rhythm, its own vibration, its own sound, and its own colour, and thus it has its own form as well.
” This vocal expression of the second person conveys more sweetness.

paragraphs.text: When Tantra was first invented, there was only one science of Tantra; but later various cults emerged according to their respective philosophical viewpoints. Each had a different name although their inner spirit was the same: for instance, Baoddha Tantra, Jaina Tantra, and in later times Shaeva Tantra, Shákta Tantra, Saora Tantra, Gáńapatya Tantra, Vaeśńviiya Tantra, etc. The inner idea of the Vaeśńaviiya Tantra is that there is form and colour (both rága and varńa) in the rhythmic expressions of Parama Puruśa, and those cosmic rhythms also have a sweet sonic vibration. This sonic vibration is instrumental in giving expression to various other forms in this universe as well. The resonance of the collective vibrations of the universe is called the flute sound of Krśńa, another name for oṋḿkára, the cosmic sound which reaches the ears of spiritual aspirants in various ways. When human beings attain spiritual progress step by step, they will also hear this sound with their own ears.
summary: When Tantra was first invented, there was only one science of Tantra; but later various cults emerged according to their respective philosophical viewpoints.
This sonic vibration is instrumental in giving expression to various other forms in this universe as well.
When human beings attain spiritual progress step by step, they will also hear this sound with their own ears.

paragraphs.text: In this expressed world full of various emanations there are so many varieties of colours – not only seven colours, but numerous colours made through permutations and combinations. And all these colours which people know, as well as all those which they do not know – all are included in that divine sound, that oṋḿkára. It the Upaniśads it is said,
summary: In this expressed world full of various emanations there are so many varieties of colours – not only seven colours, but numerous colours made through permutations and combinations.
And all these colours which people know, as well as all those which they do not know – all are included in that divine sound, that oṋḿkára.

paragraphs.text: Yá eko'varńo bahudháshaktihyogád Varńananekán nihitártho dadháti Vicaeti cánte vishvamádhao sa devah Sa no-buddhyá shubhayá saḿyunaktu.
summary: Yá eko'varńo bahudháshaktihyogád Varńananekán nihitártho dadháti Vicaeti cánte vishvamádhao sa devah Sa no-buddhyá shubhayá saḿyunaktu.

paragraphs.text: “That one Parama Puruśa has been creating this unique colourful world with His various powers. Why He is doing so is known to Him alone; no one else knows it.”
summary: “That one Parama Puruśa has been creating this unique colourful world with His various powers.
Why He is doing so is known to Him alone; no one else knows it.

paragraphs.text: The scriptures on devotion emphatically insist that only He knows the answer, no one else. It is a fact that human beings with their limited intellect can never understand the secrets of why and how Parama Puruśa has been creating this universe; their wisdom can never fathom this mystery. That is why the scriptures say, “Be a good person, but do not be foolish. Be intelligent and clever.” Now what is the clever approach? Just as on the one hand you are moving towards Parama Puruśa to attain Him by concentrating your mind through mudrá, práńáyáma and kiirtana, at the same time you should constantly remember why He is creating all these things, and what is your relation with Him. You should think, “My little intellect cannot fathom all this – rather let me do one thing, let me establish a relation of sweet love with Him. When this relation of love is established, He will be my own, and I will know His inner secret; I will certainly find the answers to all the questions 'why'.”
summary: The scriptures on devotion emphatically insist that only He knows the answer, no one else.
” Now what is the clever approach?
When this relation of love is established, He will be my own, and I will know His inner secret; I will certainly find the answers to all the questions 'why'.

paragraphs.text: To find the answer to those questions of “why”, just as the devotees run towards His sonic expression which the Vaeśńavas call His flute sound, they also run towards the expressions of His colour. They think, I will colour my mind with the same colour in which He manifests Himself before me, and move towards Him. If I can colour my mind in His colour, I will be very close to Him. This attempt to colour oneself with the colour of Parama Puruśa is called anurága (anu means “afterwards,” and rága means “colour”). Those who want all their actions to be crowned with success should love Parama Puruśa with all their hearts, and understand what He likes and what He dislikes, what He wants and what He does not want. They should not even go near those things which Parama Puruśa dislikes. And when they guide all their desires and ambitions according to His wishes, their success will be inevitable, because whatever He wants will surely be fulfilled.
summary: To find the answer to those questions of “why”, just as the devotees run towards His sonic expression which the Vaeśńavas call His flute sound, they also run towards the expressions of His colour.
This attempt to colour oneself with the colour of Parama Puruśa is called anurága (anu means “afterwards,” and rága means “colour”).
And when they guide all their desires and ambitions according to His wishes, their success will be inevitable, because whatever He wants will surely be fulfilled.

paragraphs.text: Kii habe iccháy, iccháte kii nay Krśńa icchá viná phal phalená.
summary: Kii habe iccháy, iccháte kii nay Krśńa icchá viná phal phalená.

paragraphs.text: [Even if one wishes, the wish may not be fulfilled; without the wish of Krśńa, no wish can bear fruit.]
summary: [Even if one wishes, the wish may not be fulfilled; without the wish of Krśńa, no wish can bear fruit.

paragraphs.text: So all must work according to the wishes of Parama Puruśa. [[To dye oneself in the colour of Parama Puruśa I call anurága. In the cult of devotion, it is said that the best sádhaná is the sádhaná of kevalá bhakti. “I do not ask anything – I do not ask anything from You. Do whatever You think proper]], and do not do what You think improper. I will not apply my little intellect to You, because Your intellect is infinitely superior to mine.”
summary: So all must work according to the wishes of Parama Puruśa.
“I do not ask anything – I do not ask anything from You.
I will not apply my little intellect to You, because Your intellect is infinitely superior to mine.

paragraphs.text: In the cult of devotion, a higher [[form of sádhaná is]] rágánuga bhakti. The word rágá is derived from the word rańj + ghaiṋ suffix. The verb rańj means “to colour”. Rágánuga bhakti means that type of devotion which gives expression to one's inner devotion. The psychology behind this type of bhakti is, “Because of my rágánuga bhakti, because I have dyed my mind with His colour, He will be pleased. And when He is pleased, I will also get pleasure.” Some people may think, “Parama Puruśa likes to eat malpoa, so let me prepare a few pieces of malpoa for Him. When He will eat malpoa He will feel pleasure, and when He feels pleasure, I will derive joy from His joy.”
summary: In the cult of devotion, a higher [[form of sádhaná is]] rágánuga bhakti.
The psychology behind this type of bhakti is, “Because of my rágánuga bhakti, because I have dyed my mind with His colour, He will be pleased.
When He will eat malpoa He will feel pleasure, and when He feels pleasure, I will derive joy from His joy.

paragraphs.text: But there is a still higher type of devotion than rágánuga, in which devotee thinks, “I will do exactly as He wants, I will colour my mind with His colour, and I will not think whether that will bring joy to me or not. Let Him be pleased… that is my only wish.” This is the highest stage of devotion.
summary: But there is a still higher type of devotion than rágánuga, in which devotee thinks, “I will do exactly as He wants, I will colour my mind with His colour, and I will not think whether that will bring joy to me or not.
Let Him be pleased… that is my only wish.
” This is the highest stage of devotion.

paragraphs.text: According to Vaeśńava Tantra, a person in a certain circumstance is coloured with a particular vibrational colour. Thus unit beings must offer that particular colour to Parama Puruśa saying, “Oh Parama Puruśa, please accept my colour, and colour my mind with your colour.” To offer the colour of one's mind to Parama Puruśa, is a kind of ragasádhaná.
summary: According to Vaeśńava Tantra, a person in a certain circumstance is coloured with a particular vibrational colour.
Thus unit beings must offer that particular colour to Parama Puruśa saying, “Oh Parama Puruśa, please accept my colour, and colour my mind with your colour.
” To offer the colour of one's mind to Parama Puruśa, is a kind of ragasádhaná.

paragraphs.text: When Mahaprabhu first introduced the Dolyátrá festival, the psychology behind this festival was to give one's mental colour to Parama Puruśa. The inner idea was, “Let my mind vibrate in the same way as Krśńa's mind is vibrating” This Dolyátrá has no relation to the Holi festival of north India or the Pháguá of central and east India, for it is something purely psychic. The word Dolyátrá is popular in the almanacs of Orissa, Bengal, Assam, Manipur, and Mithila. The inner significance of Dolyátrá is, in the swinging vibration in which the entire universe is vibrating, I will also be vibrated.
summary: When Mahaprabhu first introduced the Dolyátrá festival, the psychology behind this festival was to give one's mental colour to Parama Puruśa.
The word Dolyátrá is popular in the almanacs of Orissa, Bengal, Assam, Manipur, and Mithila.
The inner significance of Dolyátrá is, in the swinging vibration in which the entire universe is vibrating, I will also be vibrated.

paragraphs.text: During the Vedic age, the post-Vedic age, the Mahábhárata era, the Buddhist and post-Buddhist eras, during the reign of the kings of the Sen dynasty in Bengal, and in the southern part of East Bengal during the rule of the kings of the Chandra dynasty, the language of the legal courts was Sanskrit. However, [during the later of these periods] Bengali became prevalent for matters related to the general public. From the Pathan period onwards, the language of the court became Persian; but Bengali remained the peopleʼs language. During British rule, English became the language of the court, yet Bengali continued to be used as language for matters relating to the common people, and this is still the practice today. Since the proceedings of the court continued to be conducted for a long time in Sanskrit, many legal terms are still in Sanskrit. Neglecting those words and attempting to create new terminologies are simply a waste of time and energy.
summary: During the Vedic age, the post-Vedic age, the Mahábhárata era, the Buddhist and post-Buddhist eras, during the reign of the kings of the Sen dynasty in Bengal, and in the southern part of East Bengal during the rule of the kings of the Chandra dynasty, the language of the legal courts was Sanskrit.
During British rule, English became the language of the court, yet Bengali continued to be used as language for matters relating to the common people, and this is still the practice today.
Neglecting those words and attempting to create new terminologies are simply a waste of time and energy.

paragraphs.text: The use of Bengali in official work was first introduced by the maharajas [kings] of Tripura (who were designated by the people as “Maharaj Manikyabahadur”). The king of Ráŕh (according to some, he was a feudal king), Ichai Ghosh, was possibly the first in the pre-Pathan era to use Bengali in conducting royal affairs. Yet he also retained Sanskrit words in the language of the court. In matters relating to the common people, however, he began using Bengali instead of Sanskrit.
summary: The use of Bengali in official work was first introduced by the maharajas [kings] of Tripura (who were designated by the people as “Maharaj Manikyabahadur”).
Yet he also retained Sanskrit words in the language of the court.
In matters relating to the common people, however, he began using Bengali instead of Sanskrit.

paragraphs.text: The mention of Ichai Ghosh reminds me of several kingdoms of ancient Ráŕh. Ráŕh was the cradle of civilization. It was not only the cradle, it was also a hub whose influence spread everywhere.
summary: The mention of Ichai Ghosh reminds me of several kingdoms of ancient Ráŕh.
Ráŕh was the cradle of civilization.
It was not only the cradle, it was also a hub whose influence spread everywhere.

paragraphs.text: The northernmost is Birbhum (Kandi and Jangipur Subdivisions of the present Murshidabad District, Rampurhat Subdivision of the present Birbhum District, and Sahebganj of Bihar [Rajmahal Subdivision]). The farthest border of Birbhum extended up to Mirzachouki, the outermost boundary of Sahebganj. These kings of Birbhum were Kayasthas with “Singh” as their surname.
summary: The northernmost is Birbhum (Kandi and Jangipur Subdivisions of the present Murshidabad District, Rampurhat Subdivision of the present Birbhum District, and Sahebganj of Bihar [Rajmahal Subdivision]).
The farthest border of Birbhum extended up to Mirzachouki, the outermost boundary of Sahebganj.
These kings of Birbhum were Kayasthas with “Singh” as their surname.

paragraphs.text: To the south of Birbhum was Gopabhum. By Gopabhum is meant the Shiuri Subdivision of present Birbhum District, the newly-created Bolpur Subdivision, Pakur Subdivision of the present Sahebganj District of Jharkhand (in Sanskrit Parkat́ipur, from which has come the “Pákŕáshii” surname of present Bengalee society), Dumka Subdivision and Deoghar Subdivision. The kings there were Sadgopes with the surname Ghosh. Hence the state came to be called Gopabhum.
summary: To the south of Birbhum was Gopabhum.
The kings there were Sadgopes with the surname Ghosh.
Hence the state came to be called Gopabhum.

paragraphs.text: To the south of Gopabhum was Samantabhum, and to the west of Samantabhum was Shikharbhum. Samantabhum referred to Durgapur Subdivision in Burdwan District, Asansol Subdivision and Jamtura (the word “Jámtáŕá” ( 1 ) is the derived form of “Jámtuŕá”) Subdivision of Dumka District. The kingdom of Samantabhum was known during British rule as Raniganj Subdivision. When, in 1856, the district of Santal Pargana was constituted, Jamtura in Samantabhum was included in it. When Asansol became a bigger town than Raniganj, the headquarters of the Subdivision was shifted from Raniganj to Asansol (Cheridanga). Still later, in independent India, when Durgapur turned into a very big town, this subdivision split in two. Its eastern part formed a separate subdivision called Durgapur. The kings of Samantabhum were Ugrakśatriyas having the surname “Sámanta”.
summary: To the south of Gopabhum was Samantabhum, and to the west of Samantabhum was Shikharbhum.
When Asansol became a bigger town than Raniganj, the headquarters of the Subdivision was shifted from Raniganj to Asansol (Cheridanga).
The kings of Samantabhum were Ugrakśatriyas having the surname “Sámanta”.

paragraphs.text: Just west of Samantabhum was the kingdom of Shikharbhum, to the north of which lay part of Birbhum and Samantabhum, to the south of which lay Panchakot or Manbhum, and to the west of which lay Jharkhand or the Chut́iá-Nagpur kingdom. (The British pronounced the name “Chotanagpur” or “Chot́ánagpur”.) The Pareshnath Hills, situated in the Tundi Police Precinct in the present Dhanbad District and Pirtar of Giridih District, are on its western border. In ancient times, the hills were known as Sametshikhar. That is why the kingdom was named Shikharbhum. The present-day Dhanbad District used to be known as Shikharbhum.
summary: Just west of Samantabhum was the kingdom of Shikharbhum, to the north of which lay part of Birbhum and Samantabhum, to the south of which lay Panchakot or Manbhum, and to the west of which lay Jharkhand or the Chut́iá-Nagpur kingdom.
In ancient times, the hills were known as Sametshikhar.
The present-day Dhanbad District used to be known as Shikharbhum.

paragraphs.text: To the south of Samantabhum and Shikharbhum, three kingdoms existed side by side. One was Mallabhum. (The Vishnupur Subdivision of present Bankura District; the kings bore the surname “Malla”, which is why the kingdom was called “Mallabhum”.) Exactly to its west was Senbhum, consisting of Bankura Subdivisional headquarters and parts of Purulia and Midnapur Districts. The kings were Vaidyas with “Sen” as their surname. That is why the name of the kingdom was “Senbhum”. Its ancient capital was Senpahari. Later, King Banku Roy set up a new capital at the confluence of the Darakeshwar and Gandheshwari Rivers, and the new capital was called Bankura after the king, Banku Roy.
summary: To the south of Samantabhum and Shikharbhum, three kingdoms existed side by side.
The kings were Vaidyas with “Sen” as their surname.
Later, King Banku Roy set up a new capital at the confluence of the Darakeshwar and Gandheshwari Rivers, and the new capital was called Bankura after the king, Banku Roy.

paragraphs.text: To the west of Senbhum was Manbhum or Paiṋcakot́, [also known as] Páchet́i Kingdom or Páiṋcet Kingdom. Later, the kingdom was named Manbhum after King Mansinghadev, and its capital was Manbazar. To the north of the kingdom was the river Damodar, to the south Barahabhum, to the east the Sushunia Hills, and to the west Jharkhand or Chut́iá-Nagpur. The western boundary of Manbhum was near Angara where the hills ended and the plains of Ranchi began.
summary: To the west of Senbhum was Manbhum or Paiṋcakot́, [also known as] Páchet́i Kingdom or Páiṋcet Kingdom.
To the north of the kingdom was the river Damodar, to the south Barahabhum, to the east the Sushunia Hills, and to the west Jharkhand or Chut́iá-Nagpur.
The western boundary of Manbhum was near Angara where the hills ended and the plains of Ranchi began.

paragraphs.text: To the south of Mallabhum, Senbhum and Manbhum was Shabarbhum (Midnapur). Shabars, that is, Kheriá Muńd́á kings, ruled the kingdom. To the west of Shabarbhum was Dhabalbhum, which consisted of Jhargram Subdivision of the present Midnapur District, part of the present Bankura District, and Dhabalbhum Subdivision (Tatanagar) of the present Jharkhand State. The surname of the kings was “Dhabaldev”. For this reason, the kingdom was named “Dhabalbhum”.
summary: To the south of Mallabhum, Senbhum and Manbhum was Shabarbhum (Midnapur).

To the west of Shabarbhum was Dhabalbhum, which consisted of Jhargram Subdivision of the present Midnapur District, part of the present Bankura District, and Dhabalbhum Subdivision (Tatanagar) of the present Jharkhand State.
For this reason, the kingdom was named “Dhabalbhum”.

paragraphs.text: Adjacent to the north and northwestern extremities of Dhabalbhum was Barahabhum (Barabhum). Its capital was Barahabazar (Barabazar). Two Muńd́á brothers, Adibaraha and Keshbaraha, founded the kingdom. Barahabhum Kingdom consisted of the southern part of the present-day Purulia District, Chandil of Singbhum District and Patamda, and the Ichagar and Nimdih Police Stations of Singhbhum District. The kingdom is surrounded by the Dalma Hills range. Very ancient relics of the Bengali language and script have been found and are still being found, largely in Barahabhum. On the western side of Dhabalbhum was Singbhum. The kings of that kingdom belonged to the Kole sub-tribe. Singbhum was bifurcated some time before the Pathan era. The western part retained the name of Singbhum, and the eastern part was named Porahat. (The Keraikela kingdom, situated southeast of Ranchi District, was included.) Later, the Porahat kingdom split in two parts – the western part was called Kharsoan and the eastern part Seraikela. To the south of the Dhabalbhum and Porahat kingdoms was Bhanjabhum (the current name is Mayurbhanja). Since the kings of that kingdom used the surname Bhanjadeo, it was named “Bhanjabhúm”. They used the peacock symbol in their thrones and crowns and in the ornaments of their queens, so the kingdom later came to be called “Mayurbhanj”. ( 2 )
summary: Adjacent to the north and northwestern extremities of Dhabalbhum was Barahabhum (Barabhum).
The kings of that kingdom belonged to the Kole sub-tribe.
They used the peacock symbol in their thrones and crowns and in the ornaments of their queens, so the kingdom later came to be called “Mayurbhanj”.

paragraphs.text: The collection of these bhúms constituted the ancient Ráŕh Bhúmi or land of Ráŕh.
summary: The collection of these bhúms constituted the ancient Ráŕh Bhúmi or land of Ráŕh.

paragraphs.text: The eastern part of Howrah, Hooghly and Burdwan Districts and the northern portion of Ghatal Subdivision of Midnapur District in eastern Ráŕh were not included in any bhúm. This portion was once called the kingdom of Bhurisreśt́ha [Bhurishreshtha]. Today we colloquially call it Bhurshut. The capital, Gar Mandaran, was located where the Amodar River, which originates from Sumudrabandh [Lake], converges with the Damodar.
summary: The eastern part of Howrah, Hooghly and Burdwan Districts and the northern portion of Ghatal Subdivision of Midnapur District in eastern Ráŕh were not included in any bhúm.
Today we colloquially call it Bhurshut.
The capital, Gar Mandaran, was located where the Amodar River, which originates from Sumudrabandh [Lake], converges with the Damodar.

paragraphs.text: From very ancient days to the time of the Sen dynasty, the kings of Ráŕh were practically independent. Of course, they used to pay a nominal tribute (nazráńá) to the king of Gaoŕa (Bengal) or, if not paying so, would accept in writing the sovereignty of the king. I came across the ruins of an ancient Jain Shiva temple at Mardu village in the Silli Police Station on the banks of the Suvarnarekha River, in the ancient kingdom of Manbhum or Panchakot. I also found near the house of a Muńd́á villager, a stone statue of Dákśáyańii. Dákśáyańii was the state goddess of Bengal during the Sur dynasty, which means that Manbhum Kingdom acknowledged the sovereignty of the Sur kings of Gaoŕa. During the Pathan rule, most of the kingdoms of Ráŕh were independent principalities. Only under the Mughals did these principalities accept the suzerainty of the nawab of Bengal. They paid only a nominal tribute to him. In Bhurshut, the Mughal rulers had tremendous influence. Burdwan, in Bhurshut, was the capital of Bengal a number of times. [Some say] the word “Burdwan” came from [the Persian] bár-e-diiván. The British spelled it “Burdwan”. Previously the name of this administrative division was Sharifabad.
summary: From very ancient days to the time of the Sen dynasty, the kings of Ráŕh were practically independent.
Only under the Mughals did these principalities accept the suzerainty of the nawab of Bengal.
Previously the name of this administrative division was Sharifabad.

paragraphs.text: In those days, the bhúmyadhikáriis or bhaomiks (bhaomik → bhouaṋa → bhuṋiá) [landlords] of Bengal struggled hard to maintain their independence. King Pratapaditya of Jessore, King Kandarpanarayana of Chandradvip, King Lakshmanmanikya of Bhulua, and also Isha Khan, Kedar Roy and Sitaram Roy were amongst them. It is difficult to say what the outcome would have been had all these kings cooperated with each other. However, as each of them fought alone, they were defeated.
summary: In those days, the bhúmyadhikáriis or bhaomiks (bhaomik → bhouaṋa → bhuṋiá) [landlords] of Bengal struggled hard to maintain their independence.
It is difficult to say what the outcome would have been had all these kings cooperated with each other.
However, as each of them fought alone, they were defeated.

paragraphs.text: The king of Jaipur, Raja Man Singh, entered into an agreement with Akbar, the emperor in Delhi, and became commander-in-chief of the Mughal army. There were twelve [kings] who were particularly prominent. Raja Man Singh took upon himself the onerous responsibility of subduing these twelve. He defeated Pratapaditya of Jessore and carried off the statue of Yashoreshvarii, the guardian deity of Jessore. He installed her in the Ambar Fort of Jaipur, bringing the Bengalee priest of the temple along with her. It was Raja Man Singh who built the Ramnakali, or Dhakeshvari, temple in Dacca.
summary: The king of Jaipur, Raja Man Singh, entered into an agreement with Akbar, the emperor in Delhi, and became commander-in-chief of the Mughal army.
He defeated Pratapaditya of Jessore and carried off the statue of Yashoreshvarii, the guardian deity of Jessore.
It was Raja Man Singh who built the Ramnakali, or Dhakeshvari, temple in Dacca.

paragraphs.text: When King Jagatnarayan of Bhurshut saw other rulers of Bengal in rebellion against Mughal rule, he too became encouraged to revolt. The nawab of Bengal used to stay sometimes in Burdwan and sometimes in Dhaka. One commander [under the nawab] was posted in Dhaka, one in Gaoŕa [Samatat], one in Burdwan and another in Azimabad (the present Patna city). Emperor Akbar separated Suba Bihar from Suba Bengal, so Azimabad was no longer part of Bengal. A new nawab was posted in Azimabad. Many soldiers were transferred to this newly-established capital from the Burdwan Commissionary [in Bhurshut].
summary: When King Jagatnarayan of Bhurshut saw other rulers of Bengal in rebellion against Mughal rule, he too became encouraged to revolt.
Emperor Akbar separated Suba Bihar from Suba Bengal, so Azimabad was no longer part of Bengal.
Many soldiers were transferred to this newly-established capital from the Burdwan Commissionary [in Bhurshut].

paragraphs.text: King Jagatnarayan decided to declare independence, taking advantage of the circumstances. This decision was welcomed by his ministers, as well as his own queen, Bhavasundari. Everyone agreed that when Bhurishrestha was superior to many other principalities and had a glorious heritage of its own – in art and architecture, in wisdom, in literature and in all spheres of life – then surely it should declare its independence to uphold its dignity. Bhurishrestha was the best not only in name, it had then reached the pinnacle of glory in agriculture and industry, trade and commerce, education and knowledge, etc. Why should such a kingdom remain under the bondage of the far-off Delhi emperor? Why should it not launch a struggle to assert its own sovereignty and dignity?
summary: King Jagatnarayan decided to declare independence, taking advantage of the circumstances.
Bhurishrestha was the best not only in name, it had then reached the pinnacle of glory in agriculture and industry, trade and commerce, education and knowledge, etc.
Why should it not launch a struggle to assert its own sovereignty and dignity?

paragraphs.text: This royal declaration was loudly acclaimed by the strongly-built, hard-working Játbáuṋáliis ( 3 ) [sons of the soil of Bengal]. The Ugra Kśatriyas, Sadgopes, Máhiśyas and Bágdis of Bengal volunteered for the army. They shouted the slogan, “Outsiders stay out! Bhurishreshtha has never submitted and never will.”
summary: This royal declaration was loudly acclaimed by the strongly-built, hard-working Játbáuṋáliis ( 3 ) [sons of the soil of Bengal].
They shouted the slogan, “Outsiders stay out!
Bhurishreshtha has never submitted and never will.

paragraphs.text: Akbar sensed danger. Bhurshut was the most fertile and prosperous territory within his empire. Bhurshut produced the largest crops of sugar cane, the most raw sugar, the largest crops of cotton, the most cloth, the largest crops of rice paddy, the largest mining output and the most silk, all of which the merchants used to export abroad, making huge profits. Akbar would collect a huge fortune for the royal treasury by levying taxes on those merchants. As such, the important Bhurshut could not be allowed to secede from the empire.
summary: Bhurshut was the most fertile and prosperous territory within his empire.
Akbar would collect a huge fortune for the royal treasury by levying taxes on those merchants.
As such, the important Bhurshut could not be allowed to secede from the empire.

paragraphs.text: The emperor sent his commander-in-chief, Man Singh, to suppress the rebellion. Even at that time the journey to Burdwan from Delhi or Agra was not difficult. During the middle part of the Mughal era there had suddenly emerged a mighty Pathan emperor, Shershah Suri. He was an intelligent ruler and a prominent mass leader. He introduced radical agrarian reforms by popularizing the system of leasing land. He built a long, broad highway from Suvarna Gram in Dacca via Kalighat, Sutanuti and Govindapur, and from there through Howrah and Burdwan to Delhi and up to Attak, Punjab. In those days people used to call this royal highway variously such names as the Benares Road, the Kashi Road, or the Kingʼs Road. The British called it the Grand Trunk Road [in short G.T. Road]. Man Singh with his large army marched to Burdwan along this highway.
summary: The emperor sent his commander-in-chief, Man Singh, to suppress the rebellion.
He introduced radical agrarian reforms by popularizing the system of leasing land.
Man Singh with his large army marched to Burdwan along this highway.

paragraphs.text: It is Burdwan which emerged and developed in prehistoric times. The Rgveda does not mention it. Astiknagar, referred to in the Yajurveda, is the ancient name of this Burdwan. Astiknagar and Kanchannagar – both these names were prevalent side by side. Astiknagar and Kanchannagar now lie buried under the earth. One can still hear groans from the graves of this city. It is this very Burdwan where King Chandraketu ruled during the Mahábhárata era. Bithur (Briśt́ipur) or Prayag (Allahabad), the oldest town in North India, had not yet been built. Of course, Mathura existed, but it emerged in the post-Vedic era. It is the same Burdwan that was resplendent with pride and glory during the rule of Ashoka and Chandragupta. And it is in this very Burdwan, then the capital of Gaoŕa, where the great king Vikramaditya used to hear [stories] from the lips of Betal [a legendary figure].
summary: It is Burdwan which emerged and developed in prehistoric times.
One can still hear groans from the graves of this city.
And it is in this very Burdwan, then the capital of Gaoŕa, where the great king Vikramaditya used to hear [stories] from the lips of Betal [a legendary figure].

paragraphs.text: During the Buddhist era, when Sanskrit was transmuted into Mágadhii Prákrta, the name of Astiknagar became Atthinagar. When the Buddhist era began, Vardhaman Mahavir visited Astiknagar. He was the son of the famous tradesman, Siddhartha, of Vaishali town in the land of Videha. His motherʼs name was Trishala. For several years in Magadh, Vardhaman Mahavir preached his ideals, his religious doctrines, his precept that “non-violence is the supreme dharma,” and his doctrine of nirgrantha [nudism]. The people of Magadh could not accept his excessive non-violence or his doctrine of nirgrantha.
summary: During the Buddhist era, when Sanskrit was transmuted into Mágadhii Prákrta, the name of Astiknagar became Atthinagar.
His motherʼs name was Trishala.
The people of Magadh could not accept his excessive non-violence or his doctrine of nirgrantha.

paragraphs.text: In those days, the residents of Magadh used to follow the path of argument [and debate.] The reasons for which Magadh could not accept the Vedas were the same as for its rejection of Vardhaman Mahavirʼs nirgrantha doctrine (the Digambar doctrine) and its obsession with non-violence. Vardhaman Mahavir came to Atthinagar, and preached his religious ideas there for seven long years. For the same purpose, he went from Atthinagar to even as far as Swamisthan. Swamisthan later became a sacred religious place for the Jains. The present name of Swamisthan is Sáiṋthiyá (Sainthia). The well-to-do vaeshyas [merchants] of Atthinagar, who were extremely fascinated by him, changed the name of their town to Vardhaman (Burdwan). At that time, for a brief period Pandua was the capital of Ráŕh, and later on Mahanad [of Hooghly District].
summary: In those days, the residents of Magadh used to follow the path of argument [and debate.
Swamisthan later became a sacred religious place for the Jains.
At that time, for a brief period Pandua was the capital of Ráŕh, and later on Mahanad [of Hooghly District].

paragraphs.text: Since then, the name “Vardhaman” has remained. During Akbarʼs time, the name “Vardhaman” became “Bar-e-diwan” (from which has come the English name “Burdwan”), which is a slightly distorted form of “Vardhaman”.
summary: Since then, the name “Vardhaman” has remained.
During Akbarʼs time, the name “Vardhaman” became “Bar-e-diwan” (from which has come the English name “Burdwan”), which is a slightly distorted form of “Vardhaman”.

paragraphs.text: Man Singh pitched his tents at Shákt́igar ( 4 ) [Shaktigarh]. The news of the arrival of the Mughal army reached Mandaran. Mandaran is not very far from Shaktigarh. If one proceeds a little farther east along the bank of the Damodar, one soon reaches Mandaran. It was just at the confluence of the Damodar and the Amodar. King Jagatnarayanʼs courage was deflated when he heard the news of Raja Man Singhʼs arrival. His bravery waned; he stopped bragging and boasting about his military strength. He called his ministers and said, “I am just a small castor-oil plant. How can I dare to fight against the huge banyan tree? I want you to send a messenger with a white flag to Man Singh at Shaktigarh. I want to unconditionally surrender. The sun of Bhurishresthaʼs days of glory are over. It will never again see the glorious dawn.”
summary: Man Singh pitched his tents at Shákt́igar ( 4 ) [Shaktigarh].
His bravery waned; he stopped bragging and boasting about his military strength.
It will never again see the glorious dawn.

paragraphs.text: The ministersʼ faces fell. But the kingʼs subjects and soldiers had not yet heard of the kingʼs mental setback. It is easily imaginable what they would have done had they learned of it.
summary: The ministersʼ faces fell.
But the kingʼs subjects and soldiers had not yet heard of the kingʼs mental setback.
It is easily imaginable what they would have done had they learned of it.

paragraphs.text: Queen Bhavasundari received the news through the prime minister. She immediately rushed to Jagatnarayan. She said, “It is not a question of your personal honour, neither is it a question of the honour of the kingdom. It is a question of the dignity of the whole country of Bengal. Moreover, it is not merely a matter of prestige; it is for the survival of the entire Bengalee race. I beg you to summon all your courage and rise to the occasion. We are all with you. Whether you win or lose, the honour of Bengal will be enhanced.”
summary: Queen Bhavasundari received the news through the prime minister.
It is a question of the dignity of the whole country of Bengal.
Whether you win or lose, the honour of Bengal will be enhanced.

paragraphs.text: King Jagatnarayan took no heed of his queenʼs advice. Rather he remonstrated, saying, “You are just a woman who should keep to [your] inner apartments. How little you know and understand about warfare – donʼt meddle in these delicate issues. Itʼs better to go back to the royal apartments and attend to the petty household duties.” Bhavasundari turned away with a heavy heart. A violent storm was raging in her mind. She could not bear to sit silent, so she called the council of ministers to the royal apartments.
summary: King Jagatnarayan took no heed of his queenʼs advice.
Itʼs better to go back to the royal apartments and attend to the petty household duties.
She could not bear to sit silent, so she called the council of ministers to the royal apartments.

paragraphs.text: The queen told the ministers that the king had developed a mental derangement. “He wants to throw the prestige of Bengal on the ground. I am a daughter of and you are sons of Ráŕh. The honour and prestige of all Bengal depends on you and me. Under these circumstances, are you willing to go to Man Singh at Shákt́igaŕ carrying a white flag in hand?”
summary: The queen told the ministers that the king had developed a mental derangement.
I am a daughter of and you are sons of Ráŕh.
Under these circumstances, are you willing to go to Man Singh at Shákt́igaŕ carrying a white flag in hand?

paragraphs.text: The army generals cried out with one voice, “No! We will go to welcome Man Singh with naked swords.”
summary: The army generals cried out with one voice, “No!
We will go to welcome Man Singh with naked swords.

paragraphs.text: Bhavasundari said, “Will you support me in the struggle for the freedom of Bhurshut?”
summary: Bhavasundari said, “Will you support me in the struggle for the freedom of Bhurshut?

paragraphs.text: They responded, “Yes, Your Majesty, and without the least hesitation.” Bhavasundari took upon herself the entire administration of Bhurshut. She immediately arrested the king with the help of the security forces. At her command, they put the king in prison. She organized her combat forces within three days.
summary: They responded, “Yes, Your Majesty, and without the least hesitation.
She immediately arrested the king with the help of the security forces.
She organized her combat forces within three days.

paragraphs.text: The emperorʼs forces had already reached Shákt́igaŕ, a village just beside the Grand Trunk Road. I have said before that the Grand Trunk Road was a cobblestone road. There were no metalled roads in those days to be found either in India or anywhere else in the world. Some time after the death of Akbar, Emperor Jahangir surfaced the road with stones and gravel. That gravel was collected from the quarries of Birbhum. However, when the battle was fought with the forces of Mansingh, there was no imperial highway cobbled with gravel.
summary: The emperorʼs forces had already reached Shákt́igaŕ, a village just beside the Grand Trunk Road.
Some time after the death of Akbar, Emperor Jahangir surfaced the road with stones and gravel.
However, when the battle was fought with the forces of Mansingh, there was no imperial highway cobbled with gravel.

paragraphs.text: Speaking of Jahangir brings to mind a few more stories. Jahangir was a man of extremes, both in merits and demerits. He had many positive qualities, along with a cornucopia of defects. This son of Akbarʼs Rajput wife, as a prince, was known as Selim. An alcoholic with an impetuous nature, Selim cared little for any rules. Several times Emperor Akbar received complaints that Prince Selim was not offering prayers [namáz in Islamic parlance] and not observing rozá [holy fasting from sunrise to sundown during the month of Ramadan] and was an extreme alcoholic. Emperor Akbar usually did not interfere in anyoneʼs religious affairs. Thus Selimʼs waywardness was on the rise.
summary: Speaking of Jahangir brings to mind a few more stories.
An alcoholic with an impetuous nature, Selim cared little for any rules.
Thus Selimʼs waywardness was on the rise.

paragraphs.text: At that time Burdwan was the capital of Bengal, and Sher Afghan was the governor. His wife, Meher-Un-Nisa, was a Persian lady. This exquisitely beautiful woman fell into many hands before coming to India and was at last married to Sher Afghan. Although Sher Afghanʼs name included “Afghan”, the family had come from Persia. Hence though they spoke Bengali in public, they spoke Persian at home. Urdu had not yet become the state language of India; it became the state language starting from the time of Shahjahan.
summary: At that time Burdwan was the capital of Bengal, and Sher Afghan was the governor.
Although Sher Afghanʼs name included “Afghan”, the family had come from Persia.
Urdu had not yet become the state language of India; it became the state language starting from the time of Shahjahan.

paragraphs.text: Prince Selim had his eyes on Meher-Un-Nisa. He tried several times to snatch her by force from Sher Afghan. Emperor Akbar expressed his extreme displeasure and severely rebuked Selim for this. After Akbarʼs death, there was no one to keep Selim in check. He took the name of Emperor Jahangir and occupied the throne of Delhi. After becoming the emperor, his first act was to lead an army to Burdwan. With his army, he reached Burdwan by the royal highway. He asked Sher Afghan to hand over Meher-Un-Nisa. Sher Afghan refused and a fierce battle followed. It was fought in the northeastern part of the then Burdwan. From Baje Pratappur to Kanai Natshal – this extensive area turned into a battle field. Plenty of blood was shed in this fierce battle. Thousands of innocent soldiers, who had nothing whatsoever to do with either Selimʼs appetites or Sher Afghanʼs honour, died. In those days, Báṋká was a lively river. In addition, it was the rainy season. It is said that thousands of bodies of slaughtered soldiers, without being buried, were set afloat in the river Báṋká. Sher Afghan died where the present Burdwan railway station stands. Since thousands of people died at that spot, the residents of Burdwan deserted the place. No one would go anywhere near it after dark. The place came alive only after the railway station came into existence. After the construction of the Curzon gate, the town gradually extended towards the east. Prehistoric Burdwan and Burdwan of the Jain era receded into the west, and subsequently vanished into the abyss of time. The Burdwan of those days, built with thin, large-sized bricks, today lies deep under the earth. King Banbehari Kapur made some attempts to recover the memory of the [former] Burdwan from under the earth. I have not heard of any further serious efforts. The recently discovered Bardhamaneshvar Shiva is a very ancient Jain Shiva.
summary: Prince Selim had his eyes on Meher-Un-Nisa.
In those days, Báṋká was a lively river.
The recently discovered Bardhamaneshvar Shiva is a very ancient Jain Shiva.

paragraphs.text: Be that as it may, Prince Selim, alias Emperor Jahangir, returned to the capital with Meher-Un-Nisa. Sher Afghanʼs dead body was buried in Burdwan. His tomb remains there still. For a fickle-minded man like Jahangir, it was quite impossible to run the administrative machinery of a huge state like India. Therefore, as regards official matters and royal duties, he slipped into the grip of Meher-Un-Nisa. After their marriage, her new married name became Nur-Jahan (“the light of the world”). Nur-Jahan was a very sharp-witted woman – a lady of developed tastes, as well as highly fashionable and luxury-loving. She used to bathe in rose water, and after her bath, she would spray rose attar (iitr) on her body and clothes. She did not invent attar; it existed in India long before her time. Yet it was she who first produced rose attar. Though white roses were Indiaʼs indigenous flowers, roses of diverse colours came there from Persia. The word gul is essentially a Persian word. Nur-Jahan was also a poetess of high quality. She had compared the eyebrows of dear ones with the moon. The Bengali rendering of one of her famous poems is as follows:
summary: Be that as it may, Prince Selim, alias Emperor Jahangir, returned to the capital with Meher-Un-Nisa.
She used to bathe in rose water, and after her bath, she would spray rose attar (iitr) on her body and clothes.
She had compared the eyebrows of dear ones with the moon.

paragraphs.text: Gariiv gore keu dviip jvelo ná
summary: Gariiv gore keu dviip jvelo ná

paragraphs.text: Sájáio ná keu gule,
summary: Sájáio ná keu gule,

paragraphs.text: Shyámá pokár ná poŕe pákhá,
summary: Shyámá pokár ná poŕe pákhá,

paragraphs.text: Dágá ná páya bulbule.
summary: Dágá ná páya bulbule.

paragraphs.text: [Do not light lamps on the grave of a poor soul, Do not decorate it with roses, Let not the flies burn their wings here, Let not the bulbul ever feel sad.]
summary: [Do not light lamps on the grave of a poor soul, Do not decorate it with roses, Let not the flies burn their wings here, Let not the bulbul ever feel sad.

paragraphs.text: Poet Nur-Jahan says: “I am poor and my grave is poor and simple. Let no one light lamps on it, for if lamps are lit, the flies would get their wings burnt and die, which I will not be able to tolerate. Let no one place wreaths on my grave, for then roses would have to be brought from the rose garden and my bulbul will feel hurt, which I will not be able to bear.”
summary: Poet Nur-Jahan says: “I am poor and my grave is poor and simple.
Let no one light lamps on it, for if lamps are lit, the flies would get their wings burnt and die, which I will not be able to tolerate.
Let no one place wreaths on my grave, for then roses would have to be brought from the rose garden and my bulbul will feel hurt, which I will not be able to bear.

paragraphs.text: In any case, the events of Jahangir and Nur-Jahan took place much later than the era of Bhavasundari.
summary: In any case, the events of Jahangir and Nur-Jahan took place much later than the era of Bhavasundari.

paragraphs.text: As soon as news of the arrival of the Mughal army reached Mandaran, the people sounded the war drums. However small Bhavasundariʼs army might be, it was large in morale and conviction. Although her army chiefly consisted of recruits from the Tuntule Bágdis of Ráŕh, there was also a large number of young, brown-skinned soldiers from the Ugra Kśatriyas, Sadgopes and Máhiśyas, the original inhabitants of Ráŕh. Their eyes glowed with joy at the coming victory, with the valour and eagerness to uphold the dignity and prestige of Bhurishrestha and Bengal.
summary: As soon as news of the arrival of the Mughal army reached Mandaran, the people sounded the war drums.

Although her army chiefly consisted of recruits from the Tuntule Bágdis of Ráŕh, there was also a large number of young, brown-skinned soldiers from the Ugra Kśatriyas, Sadgopes and Máhiśyas, the original inhabitants of Ráŕh.
Their eyes glowed with joy at the coming victory, with the valour and eagerness to uphold the dignity and prestige of Bhurishrestha and Bengal.

paragraphs.text: King Jagatnarayan, restless within the prison walls, shouted repeated warnings to Bhavasundari to desist from the path of inevitable disaster. “Bhavi,” he said, “you are treading a dangerous path. I request you to give up this path. You are simply a noblewoman. It doesnʼt behoove you to take to the warpath.”
summary: King Jagatnarayan, restless within the prison walls, shouted repeated warnings to Bhavasundari to desist from the path of inevitable disaster.
I request you to give up this path.
It doesnʼt behoove you to take to the warpath.

paragraphs.text: Queen Bhavasundari went to meet the imprisoned king and spoke to him from outside the cell. She reprimanded him: “When the question of collective interest is involved, some people will have to sacrifice themselves, O king. You should understand that. I didnʼt have much formal education; I was schooled only a little. You may say that ”a little learning is a dangerous thing,“ but I cannot agree with that. I am convinced that there are times when one has to sacrifice self-interest to protect the interest of many others. The one who readily sacrifices his self-interest is the best among all. He is acclaimed and crowned king of the people. Yah rájate sah rájáh [”He who rules is king“]. You were the king. This was your first duty. According to the scriptures, the king should take care of his subjects. You failed in your duty, so I had to decide what my responsibility should be.”
summary: Queen Bhavasundari went to meet the imprisoned king and spoke to him from outside the cell.
The one who readily sacrifices his self-interest is the best among all.
You failed in your duty, so I had to decide what my responsibility should be.

paragraphs.text: “Bhavi,” the king pleaded, “I implore you, I entreat you, to shun this path of war. If Emperor Akbar is like the Himalayas, then our army is just the small Shushunia Hill of Bankura. Who and what is your source of strength in treading such a risky path?”
summary: “Bhavi,” the king pleaded, “I implore you, I entreat you, to shun this path of war.
If Emperor Akbar is like the Himalayas, then our army is just the small Shushunia Hill of Bankura.
Who and what is your source of strength in treading such a risky path?

paragraphs.text: “Ideology is my source of strength,” she replied; “the honour of Bengal is my pride. The blood of the fighters for Bengal, and my own, too, is the offering.”
summary: “Ideology is my source of strength,” she replied; “the honour of Bengal is my pride.
The blood of the fighters for Bengal, and my own, too, is the offering.

paragraphs.text: “You can continue to indulge in your dreams of doom, Iʼm off to the battlefield. I am not fighting merely for my prestige; I am waging war so that the future generations of my motherland can dream of a glorious future. I am going to war. This isnʼt the time to decorate my feet with red ochre and draw a veil over my head. ( 5 ) I leave those things to you.”
summary: “You can continue to indulge in your dreams of doom, Iʼm off to the battlefield.
This isnʼt the time to decorate my feet with red ochre and draw a veil over my head.
( 5 ) I leave those things to you.

paragraphs.text: The king, while trying desperately to dissuade her, wanted to say something. But she was adamant (Tel dáo siṋdur dáo Bhavii bholbár nay [“Give good-quality oil or vermilion. ( 6 ) But Bhavi is not going to be cajoled”]).
summary: The king, while trying desperately to dissuade her, wanted to say something.
But she was adamant (Tel dáo siṋdur dáo Bhavii bholbár nay [“Give good-quality oil or vermilion.
( 6 ) But Bhavi is not going to be cajoled”]).

paragraphs.text: Bhavasundari advanced towards Burdwan along the southern bank of the Damodar. She and her forces were challenged by the Mughal army on the way. The Mughals had arrayed themselves where Amirpur and Manikahati now stand on the left bank of the Damodar and Natugram stands on the right. It was an unequal battle. The fighting went on for two days. Amar Ghosh, the leader of the Sadgopes, led the troops along the right bank, and Nityananda Singh, the leader of the Bágdis, came down the left bank at a place near Shuṋŕe-Kalna. The Ráŕh fighters were routed. Amar Ghosh and Nityananda Singh died on the battlefield.
summary: Bhavasundari advanced towards Burdwan along the southern bank of the Damodar.
The fighting went on for two days.
Amar Ghosh and Nityananda Singh died on the battlefield.

paragraphs.text: Queen Bhavasundari found herself alone. There was no one either to her left flank or her right, in front or behind. Her sword was already unsheathed; she would not retreat to Mandaran. Akbar and Raja Man Singh had given orders that Bhavasundari should not be physically harmed, and she was taken captive untouched.
summary: Queen Bhavasundari found herself alone.
Her sword was already unsheathed; she would not retreat to Mandaran.
Akbar and Raja Man Singh had given orders that Bhavasundari should not be physically harmed, and she was taken captive untouched.

paragraphs.text: Man Singh said to her, “You were born and brought up in a noble family, you married royalty, so why did you take such grave risks in bloody battle?”
summary: Man Singh said to her, “You were born and brought up in a noble family, you married royalty, so why did you take such grave risks in bloody battle?

paragraphs.text: “Yes, I was born into nobility,” Bhavasundari replied, “and I married royalty. Because of that, I took to battle.”
summary: “Yes, I was born into nobility,” Bhavasundari replied, “and I married royalty.
Because of that, I took to battle.

paragraphs.text: “Now there is no one to help you,” Man Singh taunted. “What of that? I myself am here!” she said. Man Singh found himself in a very awkward position. He sent a detailed report to the emperor explaining the situation.
summary: “Now there is no one to help you,” Man Singh taunted.
Man Singh found himself in a very awkward position.
He sent a detailed report to the emperor explaining the situation.

paragraphs.text: Akbar wrote back. “I accept the independence of Bhurishrestha, but let Bhurishrestha accept the supremacy of the Delhi emperor. Bhurishrestha need not pay any tax or tribute to Delhi. It shall be independent as regards internal matters. I have never known any woman as great as Bhavasundari. She is not only the pride of Bengal, she is the pride of the whole of India. I order her release and confer [on her] the royal title ”Ráybághinii“. (The title ”Ráybághinii“ has three meanings. One meaning is ”a lady of the Ray family having the prowess of a bághinii [tigress]“, the second is ”the queen of tigers“, and the third is ”a queen who is as powerful as a tigress”.)
summary: “I accept the independence of Bhurishrestha, but let Bhurishrestha accept the supremacy of the Delhi emperor.
She is not only the pride of Bengal, she is the pride of the whole of India.
One meaning is ”a lady of the Ray family having the prowess of a bághinii [tigress]“, the second is ”the queen of tigers“, and the third is ”a queen who is as powerful as a tigress”.

paragraphs.text: For a long time afterwards, the story of Queen Bhavasundari and her title “Ráybághinii” continued to be popular among the people. The word ráybághinii came to denote a high-spirited lady. It gained a permanent place in the popular rhymes of Ráŕh.

The word ráybághinii came to denote a high-spirited lady.

paragraphs.text: After her release, she triumphantly returned to her capital Mandaran. The subjects gave her a tremendous welcome, with conches blowing and women ululating and throwing parched rice. Bhavasundari released her husband from prison and said to him, “Bhurishrestha is your kingdom; you should rule it as the king. But remember that women are not to take care of the kitchen twenty-four hours a day. They must come out whenever the needs of the nation call them. They must face the clashes of life with or without the men.”
summary: After her release, she triumphantly returned to her capital Mandaran.
But remember that women are not to take care of the kitchen twenty-four hours a day.
They must face the clashes of life with or without the men.

paragraphs.text: The king said, “You are right, Bhavi, I now realize my mistake.” King Jagatnarayan lived for seven more years. He consulted Queen Bhavasundari on every important matter, particularly in correspondence with the Delhi emperor or the nawab of Bengal. He would not make any decisions alone.
summary: The king said, “You are right, Bhavi, I now realize my mistake.
He consulted Queen Bhavasundari on every important matter, particularly in correspondence with the Delhi emperor or the nawab of Bengal.
He would not make any decisions alone.

paragraphs.text: It is related that before her death she said, “The tree which I planted for the future women of Bengal should not be allowed to wither or be cut down by anyone. ( 8 )
summary: It is related that before her death she said, “The tree which I planted for the future women of Bengal should not be allowed to wither or be cut down by anyone.

paragraphs.text: “As has been said in the scriptures, putrádicched parájayam or shiśyádicched parájayam [‘accepting being outdone by oneʼs son or disciplesʼ], I am also praying to God before death that women of Bengal in the future move ahead, leaving me far behind; let the speed of their movement take them closer and still closer to the sun.”
summary: “As has been said in the scriptures, putrádicched parájayam or shiśyádicched parájayam [‘accepting being outdone by oneʼs son or disciplesʼ], I am also praying to God before death that women of Bengal in the future move ahead, leaving me far behind; let the speed of their movement take them closer and still closer to the sun.

paragraphs.text: After Emperor Akbar, Emperor Jahangir had Bhurishrestha included in the Mughal Empire. There was no longer any Bhavasundari or Ráybághinii to resist this annexation. Bhurishrestha became lost somewhere in time.
summary: After Emperor Akbar, Emperor Jahangir had Bhurishrestha included in the Mughal Empire.
There was no longer any Bhavasundari or Ráybághinii to resist this annexation.
Bhurishrestha became lost somewhere in time.

paragraphs.text: Emperor Jahangir divided the land into several parganas [administrative divisions]. Among them, Sharifabad Pargana (Burdwan) and Arambag Pargana (Jahanabad) deserve special mention. Bhurishrestha or Bhurshut was now to be found written on the torn pages of history.

Among them, Sharifabad Pargana (Burdwan) and Arambag Pargana (Jahanabad) deserve special mention.
Bhurishrestha or Bhurshut was now to be found written on the torn pages of history.

paragraphs.text: Why should I say “written on the torn pages of history”? Even the ink with which its name was written was also very indistinct. Bhurishrestha, surging with vitality in those days, was lost in the whirlpool of darkness.

paragraphs.text: The Gorkhas came to the hilly areas of Bengal in 1787, that is, exactly 30 years after the British conquered Bengal in the battle of Plassey. Prior to that, the Lepchas and Bhutias lived in the hills of Darjeeling. When the Gorkhas came from Nepal, the Sherpas came from Tibet almost at the same time. During the reign of the Chou Dynasty in China, some Tibetans migrated from Tibet and settled in the hilly regions of Darjeeling. They still live there, but in a very poor minority.

The Santals had still not migrated to Bengal. Afflicted by the devastating famine of 1769, they came to Bengal from the eastern part of Madhya Pradesh. The Santals rose in rebellion 86 years later, that is, in the year 1875. Therefore, the Santals are not aborigines of Bengal. They were originally tribal people dwelling in Madhya Pradesh. It is true that, in the beginning, they grabbed lands belonging to Lodhas, Bede-Mahatos, Malpahariis and Kurmii-Mahatos at the point of bows and arrows. Later on, they associated themselves intimately with the soil of Bengal as peace-loving citizens, and they remain so even today.
