chapters.title: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

paragraphs.text: At that time I used to go for a walk nearly every day in the mountains east of Jamalpur. I used to sit on the second mountain. One after another, several small and large mountains run parallel to each other. The summit of the second mountain was the highest place among them. I used to arrive there in the middle of the afternoon and stay there until about eight at night. Then I would climb through the gáb (a large variety of kendu or mangosteen) forest that lay in the valley between two mountains. In this valley there was also a small lake. First I would cross the mountain, passing by the right side of the lake, and then I would take a shortcut back home.
summary: At that time I used to go for a walk nearly every day in the mountains east of Jamalpur.
I used to arrive there in the middle of the afternoon and stay there until about eight at night.
First I would cross the mountain, passing by the right side of the lake, and then I would take a shortcut back home.

paragraphs.text: One day I was sitting on the peak. It was the bright lunar fortnight and I knew the path through the forest well so there was no need of a torch. Behind me, that is, to the east, there was a high plateau that was completely covered with woods. Most of the trees were sal [Shorea robusta], piyál (piyáshál) [Mimosa odoratassima], and palásh [Butea monosperma]. In front of me, that is, to the west, on the slope of the mountain, was a dense gáb forest. After that, in the valley in front, was an old tamarind tree. Other than this, there was very little vegetation. The mountain in front was completely barren.
summary: One day I was sitting on the peak.
In front of me, that is, to the west, on the slope of the mountain, was a dense gáb forest.
The mountain in front was completely barren.

paragraphs.text: It was the lunar fortnight, beautiful moonlight. I was probably the only person for several miles, completely alone. To my right was a dried-up spring. The spring would have water for three or four months during the rainy season when the water would rush down quickly from above into the valley below. From that mass of water the lake was formed and the overflow from the lake would flow through many small streams into the little Dakra River which emptied into the Ganges west of Monghyr, below the Monghyr-Patna Road.
summary: It was the lunar fortnight, beautiful moonlight.
To my right was a dried-up spring.

From that mass of water the lake was formed and the overflow from the lake would flow through many small streams into the little Dakra River which emptied into the Ganges west of Monghyr, below the Monghyr-Patna Road.

paragraphs.text: Behind me, the jungle-covered plateau, though not plentiful with wildlife, still had some tigers, bears, hyenas, and the shambar and bársiuṋgá varieties of deer. That evening, however, I had not heard any sounds from them. Most likely they would not begin making sounds until after 10:00 or so at night. Beside the peak that I was seated on was a path that led down the mountain; they would take this path down to the lake to drink.
summary: Behind me, the jungle-covered plateau, though not plentiful with wildlife, still had some tigers, bears, hyenas, and the shambar and bársiuṋgá varieties of deer.
Most likely they would not begin making sounds until after 10:00 or so at night.
Beside the peak that I was seated on was a path that led down the mountain; they would take this path down to the lake to drink.

paragraphs.text: That day a strong, sweet breeze coming from the forest was caressing my back and blowing out towards the mountain in front. I started feeling a little drowsy, having worked more than normal that day.
summary: That day a strong, sweet breeze coming from the forest was caressing my back and blowing out towards the mountain in front.
I started feeling a little drowsy, having worked more than normal that day.

paragraphs.text: I was about to get up when I heard what sounded like someone approaching me from behind. I turned around to look and saw a fair-skinned person wearing western clothes. I was somewhat surprised, for three reasons. First of all, it was extremely unlikely that anyone would be in that area after the sun went down. Secondly, though there was a lot of forest, even thieves would not dare come to cut wood for fear of wild animals. Thirdly, in those days western clothes were completely out of place there.
summary: I was about to get up when I heard what sounded like someone approaching me from behind.
First of all, it was extremely unlikely that anyone would be in that area after the sun went down.
Thirdly, in those days western clothes were completely out of place there.

paragraphs.text: Though this was the time of British rule, everyone knew that Westerners never came anywhere near such places. I asked him in English: “Who are you?” Looking at him, I could see that he was a real gentleman but he approached me without replying. He started looking around in all directions until his eyes came to rest on the valley in front of us. This time I asked him in Angika who he was and what he was doing there so late at night in such a deserted place. In those days such places were not completely safe. Then he answered me in a very soft and sweet, but unnatural, Bengali. “As long as you are here Iʼm not at all afraid.”
summary: Though this was the time of British rule, everyone knew that Westerners never came anywhere near such places.
This time I asked him in Angika who he was and what he was doing there so late at night in such a deserted place.
“As long as you are here Iʼm not at all afraid.

paragraphs.text: I was speechless. At any rate, his face bore the stamp of a gentle, courteous soul. As best as I could see in the moonlight he looked to be about twenty-three or twenty-four years old and from a good family. I invited him to sit down on the rock next to me. He thanked me politely and sat down. As he sat, I felt a change in the environment around me, as if someone had fashioned a dream world out of the power of Máyá.
summary: At any rate, his face bore the stamp of a gentle, courteous soul.
I invited him to sit down on the rock next to me.
As he sat, I felt a change in the environment around me, as if someone had fashioned a dream world out of the power of Máyá.

paragraphs.text: “I am very near and dear to you,” he said. “You know me but perhaps nowadays youʼve forgotten me.” I gazed at him and noticed his unblinking eyes. It was as if all the wonder in the world, a fathomless, magical collyrium, was contained in those eyes. My ears pricked up to hear what he had to say and I looked at him carefully. His body did not seem to be of this world. Somehow it seemed to be made of light and shadow… as if I were watching a talking picture.
summary: “I am very near and dear to you,” he said.
It was as if all the wonder in the world, a fathomless, magical collyrium, was contained in those eyes.
Somehow it seemed to be made of light and shadow… as if I were watching a talking picture.

paragraphs.text: Seating my guest near me, I asked him in Angika: “Are you one of our Angadesh boys?”
summary: Seating my guest near me, I asked him in Angika: “Are you one of our Angadesh boys?

paragraphs.text: “No,” he replied, “but I have been here so long that I have become one with the soil. I love Angadesh with all my heart.”
summary: “No,” he replied, “but I have been here so long that I have become one with the soil.
I love Angadesh with all my heart.

paragraphs.text: “Why have you come to this solitary wilderness so late at night? By looking at you it seems to me that youʼve been here before.”
summary: “Why have you come to this solitary wilderness so late at night?
By looking at you it seems to me that youʼve been here before.

paragraphs.text: “You are quite right. I often come here; rather, you can say I come here daily.”
summary: “You are quite right.
I often come here; rather, you can say I come here daily.

paragraphs.text: “What do you mean?”
“If youʼll give me a few moments of your time,” he replied, “there are a few things Iʼd like to say. If I start bothering you, please let me know and Iʼll stop.”
summary: “If youʼll give me a few moments of your time,” he replied, “there are a few things Iʼd like to say.
If I start bothering you, please let me know and Iʼll stop.

paragraphs.text: Then my visitor continued speaking. “This happened a long time ago, at the end of the Mughal period when the kingdom was in disarray. At that time the capital of the Province of Bengal (Bengal, Bihar and Orissa) was Murshidabad, and there was a zamindar [landlord] in Singur (Hooghly District – at that time Burdwan District) by the name of Viirendravijaya Vasumálika. Although he was a small landlord, he was a man of strong and independent thought. While the other landlords were indulging in addictions and luxuries, he was not. He was directing all sorts of efforts to preserve the freedom of Bengali culture, civilization, and way of life.
summary: Then my visitor continued speaking.
Although he was a small landlord, he was a man of strong and independent thought.
He was directing all sorts of efforts to preserve the freedom of Bengali culture, civilization, and way of life.

paragraphs.text: “He was quite dissatisfied with the character and conduct of weaker-minded men like Nawab Alivardi Khan. The nawab should have made the governmental machinery strong by making sure the commander-in-chief and the subedárs ( 1 ) performed their respective duties properly; on the one hand to develop Bengalʼs military prowess and on the other hand to solidify its economic structure, but he failed to do this. While it is true that he was a man having both merits and demerits and his character was somewhat unblemished, still, in matters of behaviour and comportment he was prone to weakness at every step – something which his wife, Lady Sharf-Un-Nisa, was unable to check or hold together despite much effort. He used to hide many things from his wife.
summary: “He was quite dissatisfied with the character and conduct of weaker-minded men like Nawab Alivardi Khan.

While it is true that he was a man having both merits and demerits and his character was somewhat unblemished, still, in matters of behaviour and comportment he was prone to weakness at every step – something which his wife, Lady Sharf-Un-Nisa, was unable to check or hold together despite much effort.
He used to hide many things from his wife.

paragraphs.text: “At that time the Marathas of the Bhonsale family used to attack quite often. Those attacks, which were under the leadership of Bhaskar Pandit, were extremely bloody. The nawab was unable to make any provisions to resist them. This conduct of his was completely unpardonable. Rather, in order to avoid war, he was somehow able to strike a truce with the Marathas by giving them one fourth of the collected state revenue. When the Marathas arrived in Katoya, throwing Ráŕh into complete disorder, Alivardi Khan became aware of the danger but the nawab was not able to mount any resistance from Poŕahát (Seraikela-Kharsoan) to any part of Katowa. This weak conduct of the nawab continued to afflict the mind of the Bengalee people.
summary: “At that time the Marathas of the Bhonsale family used to attack quite often.
This conduct of his was completely unpardonable.
This weak conduct of the nawab continued to afflict the mind of the Bengalee people.

paragraphs.text: “Many of those who were wealthy took shelter in Kolkata and in Angadesh out of fear of the attacks of the Marathas. While the Marathas were skilled in land battle they were not known for their naval skills. Thus, to save Calcutta from Maratha attack, a ditch was dug northeast of Calcutta – today it is known by the name "Maratha Ditch". Seeing that he was being routed by the Marathas, the nawab committed yet another blunder. He took four large districts, Burdwan (what is today Burdwan, Hooghly, Howrah, and Jamtara), Midnapore, Chittagong, and 24 Parganas, formed from the eastern portion of Nadia-Chakla, and delivered them into the hands of the East India Company with the condition that the East India Company would help the nawab turn back the Marathas. The people of Bengal did not like this behaviour of the nawab – the freedom-loving Viirendravijaya Vasumálika was completely against it.
summary: “Many of those who were wealthy took shelter in Kolkata and in Angadesh out of fear of the attacks of the Marathas.
Seeing that he was being routed by the Marathas, the nawab committed yet another blunder.
The people of Bengal did not like this behaviour of the nawab – the freedom-loving Viirendravijaya Vasumálika was completely against it.

paragraphs.text: “Seeing the bad condition that Bengal was in at that time, Shobha Singh, the king of Midnaporeʼs Cheriyaberia, came forward. Shobha Singh was as brave in character as he was firm. Most of the people of Bengal wanted him to be king of the entire Bengal. The British also secretly wanted this and thus supported him from behind the scenes. Shobha Singh saw that the British had come to his country to do business and realized that if they were afforded convenient business opportunities their friendship could be won, but two people were thorns in Shobha Singhʼs path. One was Maharaja Bahadur of Burdwan. He was not a man of strong character but he was Bengalʼs biggest zamindar. ( 2 ) In a secret corner of his mind he felt that he had the greatest right to be Bengalʼs king. The second thorn in Shobha Singhʼs principled, strong-charactered path was the king of Mallabhum (Bishnupur of Bankura District) – Raghunath the Second (there is some difference of opinion in this matter).
summary: “Seeing the bad condition that Bengal was in at that time, Shobha Singh, the king of Midnaporeʼs Cheriyaberia, came forward.

Shobha Singh saw that the British had come to his country to do business and realized that if they were afforded convenient business opportunities their friendship could be won, but two people were thorns in Shobha Singhʼs path.

The second thorn in Shobha Singhʼs principled, strong-charactered path was the king of Mallabhum (Bishnupur of Bankura District) – Raghunath the Second (there is some difference of opinion in this matter).

paragraphs.text: “Raghunath was a man of vacillating character, a symbol of poor conduct. Forgetting his familyʼs illustrious tradition, he became infatuated with a certain Persian dancer by the name of Lalbai ( 3 ) and made up his mind to marry her. This fueled a dispute with the queen and with his ministers. Finally he met his death at the hands of the queen (Shobha Singhʼs daughter). Lalbai was probably also killed at this time. Anyhow, as a result of his own conduct Shobha Singh came into conflict with Raghunath the Second.
summary: “Raghunath was a man of vacillating character, a symbol of poor conduct.
Finally he met his death at the hands of the queen (Shobha Singhʼs daughter).
Anyhow, as a result of his own conduct Shobha Singh came into conflict with Raghunath the Second.

paragraphs.text: “The king of Singur, Viirendravijaya, helped Shobha Singh in many ways. He was not afraid of incurring the nawabʼs displeasure for this but Shobha Singh was stabbed and killed unexpectedly by the Princess of Burdwan. ( 4 ) After the death of Shobha Singh, Viirendravijaya was wondering what path should be taken to save Bengal. After the death of Alivardii Khan, his immature grandson became the nawab of Bengal, taking the name Mirza Mohammed Siraj-Ud-Daola. ( 5 ) In addition to his young age, he had many kinds of defect in his character and conduct. Virendravijay did not like this at all.
summary: “The king of Singur, Viirendravijaya, helped Shobha Singh in many ways.
After the death of Alivardii Khan, his immature grandson became the nawab of Bengal, taking the name Mirza Mohammed Siraj-Ud-Daola.
Virendravijay did not like this at all.

paragraphs.text: “At the time the East India Company was encroaching like a cat extending its claws, trying to gain control of the throne of Bengal by any means possible. On the other side, the public was divided into three camps. One group was vocally against the conduct and character of Siraj. Directly and indirectly, they supplied help to the East India Company.
summary: “At the time the East India Company was encroaching like a cat extending its claws, trying to gain control of the throne of Bengal by any means possible.
One group was vocally against the conduct and character of Siraj.
Directly and indirectly, they supplied help to the East India Company.

paragraphs.text: A second group supported the nawab regardless of his faults, following the policy of Nun khái yár guń gái tár [“If you eat someoneʼs salt then you have to praise their virtues”]. Mir Jafar, Jagat Seth and Umichand ( 6 ) fell into this category. Among them were also a few men who recognized the faults of the nawab but who did not want to allow the administration of Bengal to pass into the hands of the East India Company. For this reason alone they supported the nawab.
summary: A second group supported the nawab regardless of his faults, following the policy of Nun khái yár guń gái tár [“If you eat someoneʼs salt then you have to praise their virtues”].
Among them were also a few men who recognized the faults of the nawab but who did not want to allow the administration of Bengal to pass into the hands of the East India Company.
For this reason alone they supported the nawab.

paragraphs.text: “The third group consisted of those who could not support the bad behaviour of the nawab but who also did not want to allow the East India Company to gain political control over Bengal. They supported neither side. Queen Bhavani was of this mind. Her relationship with the nawab was extremely bitter. Yet when she was asked to help the East India Company against the nawab, she said: ‘I do not want to dig a canal to bring the river crocodiles into my backyard pond.’ Because of this the East India Company was quite displeased with Queen Bhavani. Viirendravijaya was of the same opinion as the queen. Thus it was impossible for him to do anything either for or against the nawab.
summary: “The third group consisted of those who could not support the bad behaviour of the nawab but who also did not want to allow the East India Company to gain political control over Bengal.
Yet when she was asked to help the East India Company against the nawab, she said: ‘I do not want to dig a canal to bring the river crocodiles into my backyard pond.
Thus it was impossible for him to do anything either for or against the nawab.

paragraphs.text: “There was one more thing worth mentioning about these last days of Mughal political dominance. The Bengalee people were unable to consider the family of the nawab of Murshidabad as their own. No matter how much fuss and bother the writers and historians of today make over Siraj, the family of Murshidabadʼs nawab was very distant from the common people of Bengal. It was not only that they were Urdu-speaking immigrant Shias; ( 7 ) though they had settled in Bengal and were Bengalees in the eyes of the law, they did not think of themselves as Bengalees. They called the Bengalees ”rustics“ or ”Muslim rustics” (cáśá Musalmán). ( 8 ) Of course, they learned to speak Bengali, more or less, so that they could communicate with these Muslim rustics, but at home they spoke Urdu or a corrupted form of Urdu that was mixed with Bengali, and put on airs that they were not out-of-fashion Bengalees. This mental attitude kept them quite removed from the common people.
summary: “There was one more thing worth mentioning about these last days of Mughal political dominance.
It was not only that they were Urdu-speaking immigrant Shias; ( 7 ) though they had settled in Bengal and were Bengalees in the eyes of the law, they did not think of themselves as Bengalees.
This mental attitude kept them quite removed from the common people.

paragraphs.text: “If a person is great, if their mental arena is very large, then people lose sight of their worldly identity. Because Sirajʼs character was not very expanded there was no scope for people to forget his worldly defects. It is true that most people accepted that he was broad-hearted and generous, but this was not enough for him to gain a seat in the heart of the Bengalee people. And he was the nawab for how long!
summary: “If a person is great, if their mental arena is very large, then people lose sight of their worldly identity.
It is true that most people accepted that he was broad-hearted and generous, but this was not enough for him to gain a seat in the heart of the Bengalee people.
And he was the nawab for how long!

paragraphs.text: “Most of the people who supported the nawab were senior Hindu officers. The East India Company put forth their best efforts to try to please the Hindus so that they would withdraw their support from Siraj.
summary: “Most of the people who supported the nawab were senior Hindu officers.
The East India Company put forth their best efforts to try to please the Hindus so that they would withdraw their support from Siraj.

paragraphs.text: “Viirendravijaya died shortly after the battle of Plassey. At the time of his death he told his only son, Viireshavijaya, that he should dedicate himself wholeheartedly to the task of strengthening Bengalʼs culture, unity and economic situation, and asked him to use both his intellect and his courage properly in this matter. At the time Viireshavijaya was a boy of eighteen or nineteen. Viireshavijaya carried out the instructions of his father and became well-versed in the martial treatises.
summary: “Viirendravijaya died shortly after the battle of Plassey.
At the time Viireshavijaya was a boy of eighteen or nineteen.
Viireshavijaya carried out the instructions of his father and became well-versed in the martial treatises.

paragraphs.text: “Neither Viirendravijaya nor Viireshavijaya could support Mir Jafar. Mir Jafar was an undisciplined, power-hungry, spineless drunkard. His main preoccupation was to keep his nawabship intact by whatever means possible. For some time after his death the throne of Bengal was thrown into confusion. Thereafter Mir Qasim became the nawab. His conduct was spirited, his behaviour showed individuality, and he was a man of strong character. Viireshavijaya came into contact with him and Mir Qasim, touched by his sincerity, befriended him. ”In those days the throne was the nawabʼs in name only. The power was in the hands of the East India Company; the administration was in the hands of the nawab but the economic power was not. Moreover, if one was to repel the East India Company, it would not be possible to accumulate power by sitting in Murshidabad because Murshidabad was right next to the East India Companyʼs chief outpost. Viireshavijaya advised Mir Qasim to shift his capital from Murshidabad to Monghyr. He did not advise him to move his capital to Azimabad (Patna) because Azimabad was, to some extent, a centre for the East India Company.
summary: “Neither Viirendravijaya nor Viireshavijaya could support Mir Jafar.
Viireshavijaya came into contact with him and Mir Qasim, touched by his sincerity, befriended him.
He did not advise him to move his capital to Azimabad (Patna) because Azimabad was, to some extent, a centre for the East India Company.

paragraphs.text: “There were one or two other reasons for making Monghyr the capital of Bengal. During the time of the Mahábhárata, when Angadesh was first accepted as an independent kingdom, Duryodhana made Karna the king of Angadesh, and rather than consider him a vassal, he allowed him to wear the crown of a sovereign king. Since ancient times the Anga region was not considered part of northern India. Neither Anga, Vauṋga nor Kalinga were considered part of northern India. Starting from this time, Anga was declared an appendix, or auṋga, of northern India and hence its name became ”Auṋgadesha”. Vauṋga remained outside of northern India. Kalinga gained acceptance as a part of southern India. Thus even today, Oriya Brahmins are sometimes known as Dakśińátya Vedic Brahmins in Bengal. At the time of Karna the capital of Angadesh was Champakanagar. ( 9 ) Karna also founded an auxiliary capital in Mudgagiri (mudgagiri → muuṋgagiri → muuṋgir → muuṋger), on the western border of the kingdom of Anga. Hence Monghyr has a tradition as a capital. ( 10 )
summary: “There were one or two other reasons for making Monghyr the capital of Bengal.
Vauṋga remained outside of northern India.
Hence Monghyr has a tradition as a capital.

paragraphs.text: “When Gujaratʼs Rastrakuts [a royal dynasty] defeated eastern India, then Angadesh came under their jurisdiction. The Khirkhiriya Hills that we are sitting on were the eastern boundary of the Rastrakut kingdom. Thus they established a capital in their border city of Muṋgagiri. So we see that Monghyr became a capital more than once. At that time the road system of Bengal, as well as India, was not at all developed. The long highway Shershah built that extended from Suvarnagram in Dhaka District to the city of At́ak [Attak] in western Punjab via Teota (Manikganj Subdivision) and Howrah-Burdwan, and passing by Kolkata, did not afford much convenience to Murshidabad, Monghyr or Patna, but Monghyrʼs water-route transport system was good. The waterway worked well all the way from Dhaka to Benares-Allahabad passing via Narayanganj, Teota, Rampur, Boyaliya (Rajsahi), Lalagola Ghat, Godagarii Ghat, Chapaghati, Rajmahal (at one time Rajmahal was the capital of Bengal), Bhagalpur, Monghyr and Azimabad. Benares and Allahabad used to be aided by the Shershah-built Badshahii Road. Thus, since Monghyr was marked as an important centre of water transport, the capital could be established there without any communication problems as such.
summary: “When Gujaratʼs Rastrakuts [a royal dynasty] defeated eastern India, then Angadesh came under their jurisdiction.
At that time the road system of Bengal, as well as India, was not at all developed.
Thus, since Monghyr was marked as an important centre of water transport, the capital could be established there without any communication problems as such.

paragraphs.text: “Mir Qasim accepted Viireshavijayaʼs reasoning and moved the capital to Monghyr. On Viireshavijayaʼs advice, the nawab set about preparing the capital in Monghyr with great speed and began constructing his armoury. A great fortress was built in Monghyr as well as a munitions factory, heavy-weapons arsenal, huge parade grounds (Karheya Maidan or Kora Maidan), and a new cultural centre, Kasimbazar. The East India Company recognized the danger. Seizing on various small pretexts they declared war against Mir Qasim. They had economic power and were prepared for war – the nawab had nothing. He had just begun organizing. On the other side, the East India Company had concentrated their power at Fort William in Kolkata and in Alinagar (present-day Alipur, now a part of Kolkata).
summary: “Mir Qasim accepted Viireshavijayaʼs reasoning and moved the capital to Monghyr.
Seizing on various small pretexts they declared war against Mir Qasim.
On the other side, the East India Company had concentrated their power at Fort William in Kolkata and in Alinagar (present-day Alipur, now a part of Kolkata).

paragraphs.text: “The first battle was a trifling affair; it took place in Katwa and the nawab was defeated. The second battle took place in Gheriya and there also the nawab was defeated. The third took place in Udhuya or in the Udhuyanala. The East India Company advanced along the Ganges in the direction of Monghyr. A great battle took place in the Dakra Canal. With his finger, my visitor pointed out to me the Dakra Canal which originated on the western border of the Khirkhiriya Hills and joined the Ganges a little to the west of Monghyr. In reality, the Dakra was not a canal but a river. In the East India Company records it is mistakenly called a canal. At the time of the monsoon deluge, the water of the Ganges goes upstream through the Dakra River and floods a wide area in Monghyr District. At the time my visitor pointed out the Dakra Canal there was heavy flooding.
summary: “The first battle was a trifling affair; it took place in Katwa and the nawab was defeated.
With his finger, my visitor pointed out to me the Dakra Canal which originated on the western border of the Khirkhiriya Hills and joined the Ganges a little to the west of Monghyr.
At the time my visitor pointed out the Dakra Canal there was heavy flooding.

paragraphs.text: “When the nawab was defeated in the battle of Dakra Canal he started heading by water for Azimabad. The map and plans of the next battle site remained in the hands of Viireshavijaya. The planning of how the next battle in Buxar and on the banks of the nearby Karmanasha River could be fought was not in the hands of the nawab. All he knew was that there would be a battle fought in those places. Viireshavijaya became separated during the fighting and fell back a little to the south. He was not able to reach the banks of the Ganges and go upriver to Azimabad. But the warplans and maps were in his hands so he took shelter in the jungle of the Khirkhiriya Hills.
summary: “When the nawab was defeated in the battle of Dakra Canal he started heading by water for Azimabad.
All he knew was that there would be a battle fought in those places.
But the warplans and maps were in his hands so he took shelter in the jungle of the Khirkhiriya Hills.

paragraphs.text: “Another of the nawabʼs chief difficulties was his severe lack of economic resources. Viireshavijaya knew that King Karnaʼs huge treasury was secretly preserved in a cave in the Khirkhiriya Hills. He set about searching for that treasure, thinking that if it came into his hands he would much better be able to help the nawab.
summary: “Another of the nawabʼs chief difficulties was his severe lack of economic resources.
Viireshavijaya knew that King Karnaʼs huge treasury was secretly preserved in a cave in the Khirkhiriya Hills.
He set about searching for that treasure, thinking that if it came into his hands he would much better be able to help the nawab.

paragraphs.text: “At this point I should say something about the history of Angadeshʼs terrain. In Karnaʼs time the north of Angadesh bordered on the Himalayas. ( 11 ) The southern border was the source of the Chandan River, a little to the north of Deoghar. On the western border was Ramdiri and Shamhodira (Samidhá) near Beguserai, and the eastern border was the Rajmahal Hills near Sahebganj where they approach the Ganges. The Rajmahal Hill Range occupies a large area in eastern Angadesh. Their eastern branch stops abruptly near Sahebganj and the Ganges; its western branch ends near Monghyr by the side of the Ganges. The western branchʼs Sanskrit name is the Kśirakśiriká Hills. In Auṋgiká [Angika] they are called Khirkhiriya Hills and in English the Kharagpur Hills. The Kharagpur Hills are a branch of the Rajmahal Hills.
summary: “At this point I should say something about the history of Angadeshʼs terrain.
The Rajmahal Hill Range occupies a large area in eastern Angadesh.
The Kharagpur Hills are a branch of the Rajmahal Hills.

paragraphs.text: “Southern Angaʼs chief river is the Chandan which has two companions, the Baruya and the Chiir. In this Chandan-Baruya-Chiir River Basin ( 12 ) one finds the Kalhan Hills (near Kahalgaon, named after Maharshi Kalhan), Ajagavii Hills (near Sulatanganj), Mandar Hills ( 13 ) (a little north of the railway station), and the Khirkhiriya Hills on the western border where one can find, scattered here and there, innumerable examples of the culture of ancient Angadesh. Like the Angika culture, the language also belongs to this place.
summary: “Southern Angaʼs chief river is the Chandan which has two companions, the Baruya and the Chiir.

In this Chandan-Baruya-Chiir River Basin ( 12 ) one finds the Kalhan Hills (near Kahalgaon, named after Maharshi Kalhan), Ajagavii Hills (near Sulatanganj), Mandar Hills ( 13 ) (a little north of the railway station), and the Khirkhiriya Hills on the western border where one can find, scattered here and there, innumerable examples of the culture of ancient Angadesh.
Like the Angika culture, the language also belongs to this place.

paragraphs.text: “Those who think that the Khirkhiriya Hills are the western border of Angadesh, however, are mistaken. To the west of the Khirkhiriya Hills lies the Dakra River Basin. This Dakra River Basin is Angaʼs final western border. Beyond the Dakra River Basin lies the Kiul River Basin where one can find many examples of Magadh culture, that is, it belongs to the land of Magadh.
summary: “Those who think that the Khirkhiriya Hills are the western border of Angadesh, however, are mistaken.
This Dakra River Basin is Angaʼs final western border.
Beyond the Dakra River Basin lies the Kiul River Basin where one can find many examples of Magadh culture, that is, it belongs to the land of Magadh.

paragraphs.text: “The Angika language has three chief dialects: Dharamapuriyá, Champánagarii or Chekáchekii, and Muṋgeriá. The Dharamapuriya dialect is spoken on the north bank of the Ganges. The Chekáchekii dialect is spoken in the far eastern region where the Rajmahal Hills approach the Ganges near Sahebganj, and in the western border area where the Khirkhiriya Hills stop near the Ganges. Miirzachauki, near Sahebganj, was at the border of the provinces of Bengal and Bihar during the time of Akbar. Miirzachauki was a busy checkpost. It occupied a narrow strip of land between the Ganges and the mountains and thus was an ideal spot for a checkpost. The Muṋgeriyá dialect is prevalent west of the Khirkhiriya Hills in the Dakra River Basin.
summary: “The Angika language has three chief dialects: Dharamapuriyá, Champánagarii or Chekáchekii, and Muṋgeriá.
Miirzachauki, near Sahebganj, was at the border of the provinces of Bengal and Bihar during the time of Akbar.
The Muṋgeriyá dialect is prevalent west of the Khirkhiriya Hills in the Dakra River Basin.

paragraphs.text: “Besides these, there are also two mixed sub-dialects of Angika: The first is the Shriipuriyá sub-dialect, which is used in the region lying between Purnea and Kisanganj. Purneaʼs language is Angika, and Bengali is the language of Kisanganj. The Shriipuriyá language that is spoken in the interlying areas is a mixture of Angika and Rauṋapurii Bengali (Suryapurii). The second sub-dialect is the Northern Khot́t́á dialect, which is used in the region between Katihar and Maldah. The language of Katihar is Angika, and in Maldah, Bengali. In certain places between the two one can find this Northern Khot́t́á sub-dialect. It is a mixture of Angika and Shershahabad Bengali. In Muṋgeriyá Angika one can find some influence of Magahi. Similarly, in the Magahi of the Kiul River Basin there is some influence of Angika.”
summary: “Besides these, there are also two mixed sub-dialects of Angika: The first is the Shriipuriyá sub-dialect, which is used in the region lying between Purnea and Kisanganj.
The language of Katihar is Angika, and in Maldah, Bengali.
Similarly, in the Magahi of the Kiul River Basin there is some influence of Angika.

paragraphs.text: “As I was saying,” my visitor continued, “I hope I am not annoying you by talking for so long. Earlier I told you that I loved Angadesh with all my heart. So when the topic of Anga comes up, I start going on without any hesitation. Then afterwards, I think to myself that I hope I havenʼt annoyed whoever Iʼve been talking to.”
summary: “As I was saying,” my visitor continued, “I hope I am not annoying you by talking for so long.
So when the topic of Anga comes up, I start going on without any hesitation.
Then afterwards, I think to myself that I hope I havenʼt annoyed whoever Iʼve been talking to.

paragraphs.text: “Why should I be annoyed?” I replied. “Rather, Iʼm quite astonished; I wonder how you came to know so much at such an early age.”
summary: “Why should I be annoyed?
“Rather, Iʼm quite astonished; I wonder how you came to know so much at such an early age.

paragraphs.text: The light and shadow body of my visitor trembled as he spoke. “These are all your own thoughts. Earlier I said that I am in your mind. So your thoughts are coming out from my mouth.”
summary: The light and shadow body of my visitor trembled as he spoke.
Earlier I said that I am in your mind.
So your thoughts are coming out from my mouth.

paragraphs.text: “Yes,” he continued. “Viireshavijaya started searching the forest of the Khirkhiriya Hills for Karnaʼs ”treasury“ in order to save it from the hands of the East India Company. Do you know,” he added, “when I visit these hills I feel as if my entire being is overwhelmed by that Viireshavijaya. It feels as if I am also searching for someone in these hills and in this forest. Shall I say one more thing?… Please donʼt mind. Please say you wonʼt mind.”
summary: “Viireshavijaya started searching the forest of the Khirkhiriya Hills for Karnaʼs ”treasury“ in order to save it from the hands of the East India Company.
It feels as if I am also searching for someone in these hills and in this forest.
Please say you wonʼt mind.

paragraphs.text: “No, I wonʼt mind,” I replied. “Go ahead.”
summary: “No, I wonʼt mind,” I replied.

paragraphs.text: “Now,” he continued, “it seems to me as if I have come searching for you.”
summary: “Now,” he continued, “it seems to me as if I have come searching for you.

paragraphs.text: I stared at him, speechless. There was the whisper of a smile on his guileless face.
summary: I stared at him, speechless.
There was the whisper of a smile on his guileless face.

paragraphs.text: “After a few daysʼ search, Viireshavijaya came across one of his faithful followers. He entrusted him with the secret plans and maps as well as various urgent matters and sent him to the nawab in Buxar. It was impossible for him to go himself. It would not have been so bad if he himself were to be caught, but it was essential that the war documents not fall into the hands of the Company. But to the good fortune of the East India Company and the misfortune of Bengal, his follower was caught by the Company near Surajgara. He was killed and the Company learned of the movements of both Viireshavijaya and the nawab.
summary: “After a few daysʼ search, Viireshavijaya came across one of his faithful followers.
It would not have been so bad if he himself were to be caught, but it was essential that the war documents not fall into the hands of the Company.
He was killed and the Company learned of the movements of both Viireshavijaya and the nawab.

paragraphs.text: “The Company dispatched a large advance army to Buxar and the bank of the Karmanasha River where they laid in ambush waiting to draw up battle formation. Needless to say, Mir Qasim lost the battle of Buxar and was completely routed in the battle of the Karmanasha. He had neither manpower nor economic resources. Disheartened, he went first to Zamaniya, then later to Gazipur. At the time Gazipur was under the control of Agra Province. The East India Companyʼs direct rule had not yet been established there. In poor health and with a broken spirit, Mir Qasim breathed his last in Gazipur. The nawab of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, Mir Qasim, died like an ordinary man, or not even, since no one dared to give him a proper burial for fear of the East India Company. Simply a hole was dug and he was thrown in. Even this was washed away and vanished when the Ganges flooded.
summary: “The Company dispatched a large advance army to Buxar and the bank of the Karmanasha River where they laid in ambush waiting to draw up battle formation.
The East India Companyʼs direct rule had not yet been established there.
Even this was washed away and vanished when the Ganges flooded.

paragraphs.text: “When he received news of the nawabʼs death,” my visitor went on, “Viireshavijaya became very sad but he didnʼt lose heart. He decided to leave the Khirkhiriya Valley and head for Ráŕh. There he thought to build a new army with the help of the Bágdiis [a fighting community belonging to the ”lower” strata of society].
summary: “When he received news of the nawabʼs death,” my visitor went on, “Viireshavijaya became very sad but he didnʼt lose heart.
He decided to leave the Khirkhiriya Valley and head for Ráŕh.
There he thought to build a new army with the help of the Bágdiis [a fighting community belonging to the ”lower” strata of society].

paragraphs.text: “In fact,” he went on, “Viireshavijaya was sitting and thinking in the very spot where you are sitting now, thinking and thinking.
summary: “In fact,” he went on, “Viireshavijaya was sitting and thinking in the very spot where you are sitting now, thinking and thinking.

paragraphs.text: “I was telling you about Gazipur City. Lord Cornwallis introduced a permanent land settlement for the landed property of Bengal Presidency. Before introducing the land settlement in Bengal, he went first to Gazipur District to make the same arrangements for the province of Agra. ( 14 ) Gazipur was at that time a huge district. Later, the eastern portion of this district was separated and a new district was formed called Baliya (Bahlik). When Cornwallis arrived in Gazipur City he fell ill and died there. His tomb is still there today.
summary: “I was telling you about Gazipur City.
( 14 ) Gazipur was at that time a huge district.
His tomb is still there today.

paragraphs.text: “Yes, since Mughal times, the city of Gazipur has been famous for rosewater and attar. This fame still continues to some extent. Rabindranath Tagoreʼs elder brother, Satyendranath Tagore, was the district magistrate of Gazipur city. It was in his government residence that Rabindranath wrote his book Naokád́ubi [The Wreck].
summary: “Yes, since Mughal times, the city of Gazipur has been famous for rosewater and attar.
Rabindranath Tagoreʼs elder brother, Satyendranath Tagore, was the district magistrate of Gazipur city.
It was in his government residence that Rabindranath wrote his book Naokád́ubi [The Wreck].

paragraphs.text: “Talking about Gazipur reminds me again of Monghyr. Shahjahanʼs son, Suja, had the same kind of relationship with Monghyr that Mir Qasim had with Gazipur. He fled the country from Monghyr for fear of his life during the Aurangzebʼs invasion. People today still call the wharf that his barge left from Sujiighat (Sujá-i-ghát́). Of course, Suja stopped for one night while passing through the city of Bhagalpur in order to draw up his next plans. Thereafter he went to Akiyab, the capital of Arakan [Burma], to take shelter with its king. But he disappeared into oblivion there – whatever happened there is still a mystery today.
summary: “Talking about Gazipur reminds me again of Monghyr.
People today still call the wharf that his barge left from Sujiighat (Sujá-i-ghát́).
But he disappeared into oblivion there – whatever happened there is still a mystery today.

paragraphs.text: “After Viireshavijayaʼs messenger fell into the hands of the East India Company in Surajgarha, they knew that he was holed up in the Khirkhiriya Hills. The Khirkhiriya Hills were then part of the zamindary kingdom of Dwarabhanga. Badshah Akbar had given them to Mahesh Thakur as a feudal estate. During Mir Qasimʼs time the Khirkhiriya region was controlled by the king of Dwarabhanga from his residential offices in Kharagpur. ( 15 )
summary: “After Viireshavijayaʼs messenger fell into the hands of the East India Company in Surajgarha, they knew that he was holed up in the Khirkhiriya Hills.
Badshah Akbar had given them to Mahesh Thakur as a feudal estate.
During Mir Qasimʼs time the Khirkhiriya region was controlled by the king of Dwarabhanga from his residential offices in Kharagpur.

paragraphs.text: “At the time that Viireshavijaya was wandering in the Khirkhiriya Hills, the director of the Kharagpur Zamindary offices was his maternal uncle, Mohankrisna Mitra. The East India Company didnʼt know that Viireshavijaya was Mohan Mitraʼs nephew. Mohan Mitra was well-aware of the steely character and fiery behaviour of his sisterʼs son. He also understood that his nephew was carrying out the instructions of his father. So despite the fact that Viireshavijaya was the same age as his own son, he showed him the greatest respect and helped him in every way possible.
summary: “At the time that Viireshavijaya was wandering in the Khirkhiriya Hills, the director of the Kharagpur Zamindary offices was his maternal uncle, Mohankrisna Mitra.
Mohan Mitra was well-aware of the steely character and fiery behaviour of his sisterʼs son.
So despite the fact that Viireshavijaya was the same age as his own son, he showed him the greatest respect and helped him in every way possible.

paragraphs.text: “The East India Company surrounded the Khirkhiriya Hills with their troops in an effort to trap Viireshavijaya, who got word of this through his uncle. Through similar means, Viireshavijaya discovered the cave where King Karnaʼs treasure-store was hidden; however, the treasure was no longer there. Someone, it seemed, had emptied the cave of all its wealth after King Karna had left. Viireshavijaya was only able to get hold of three siinakas [gold coins].” Then my visitor pointed out the cave to me with his finger. It was very close to where I was sitting.
summary: “The East India Company surrounded the Khirkhiriya Hills with their troops in an effort to trap Viireshavijaya, who got word of this through his uncle.
Viireshavijaya was only able to get hold of three siinakas [gold coins].
It was very close to where I was sitting.

paragraphs.text: “It is a very small cave,” he continued. “A few miles to the southwest of this hill is a cave with paintings from the Buddhist era, and to the east is Risikunda. Nowadays people have forgotten its history, so they say that it is the áshram [hermitage] of the Risyashrnga Muni mentioned in the Rámáyańa. Actually there was a Buddhist monastery here during the Buddhist era. On the western edge of these mountains you will find the grave of Jamal Miya. Jamal Miya came here from Rajnagar in Birbhum and was the first to propagate Islam in this area. This place was named Jamalpur after him.
summary: “It is a very small cave,” he continued.
Actually there was a Buddhist monastery here during the Buddhist era.
This place was named Jamalpur after him.

paragraphs.text: “Yes, I was talking about Rajnagar. Rajnagar is now a very small city but at one time it was the district headquarters. During the Mughal era, certain districts in the Province of Bengal were extremely large (Monghyr, Sylhet, Birbhum, Mymensingh, Purnea, etc.). In many districts the district administrator was called the Zila Hakim but in Birbhum and Purnea he was called the Bara Hakim or governor. The governor of Birbhum used to live in Rajnagar. The last governor, Alinakhii Khan II, only ruled Birbhum for a short time, and Purneaʼs last governor, Shaokatjang, ( 16 ) after being defeated in the Katihar war by Siraj-Ud-Daola, was removed from the post of Purneaʼs Bara Hakim.
summary: “Yes, I was talking about Rajnagar.
In many districts the district administrator was called the Zila Hakim but in Birbhum and Purnea he was called the Bara Hakim or governor.

The last governor, Alinakhii Khan II, only ruled Birbhum for a short time, and Purneaʼs last governor, Shaokatjang, ( 16 ) after being defeated in the Katihar war by Siraj-Ud-Daola, was removed from the post of Purneaʼs Bara Hakim.

paragraphs.text: “Anyhow, Jamal Miya came from Rajnagar. Later the area of Birbhum District was reduced and the district headquarters was shifted from Rajnagar to Suri. Various cultural artifacts are scattered throughout our Angadesh, but who is there to point them out? Angadeshʼs condition is like that of an orphaned child. What to speak of Angadesh, a great part of India is in the same condition today. Where will the historical materials come from if we continue to neglect these cultural artifacts? Nearby, for example, near Kahalgaon (Áńt́icak) was the Vikramshila university from the Buddhist Age, but how much research has been done on it? Yet, nowadays thousands of universities are springing up like mushrooms.”
summary: “Anyhow, Jamal Miya came from Rajnagar.
What to speak of Angadesh, a great part of India is in the same condition today.
Yet, nowadays thousands of universities are springing up like mushrooms.

paragraphs.text: My visitor paused for a moment, then said softly: “I am talking a lot, quite a lot. But you donʼt seem to be annoyed at all. Of course, these are all your thoughts. They are only coming out of my mouth.”
summary: My visitor paused for a moment, then said softly: “I am talking a lot, quite a lot.
Of course, these are all your thoughts.
They are only coming out of my mouth.

paragraphs.text: Then he continued. “Viireshavijaya began to worry that the Company had picked up his trail and might capture him at any time and persecute him. There was also the danger that they would learn about the work he had just begun with the help of his followers among the Bágdiis in Ráŕh and make them suffer greatly for it. One cannot bear to think about it. What kind of a future would Bengal have? Would Mother Bengal pass her days crying? Would the time he had spent on earth go in vain? This is what Viireshavijaya was thinking that night, seated in this very spot around 8:30 in the evening. Perhaps the next morning the Company would catch up with him. Viireshavijaya slowly made his way down to the rain-swollen falls and plunged into its waters. Within moments his body was swept up in the current and carried down into a deep cavern, from there to a lake, then to the Dakra River and finally to the Ganges. There was no one to attend the funeral services for this twenty-three year old, ideologically-dedicated young man. No one even knew his history.
summary: “Viireshavijaya began to worry that the Company had picked up his trail and might capture him at any time and persecute him.
This is what Viireshavijaya was thinking that night, seated in this very spot around 8:30 in the evening.
No one even knew his history.

paragraphs.text: My visitor slowly made his way down to the falls and stood there. He looked once at the sky, once at the ground, once at the forest before him and once at me. One leg was very close to the falls. I called out to him: “Take your left foot away from the falls. If you step back you may fall in.” A soft smile appeared on his bright face and he brought his foot forward. I said: “You were telling me such a long story, but you see, I have committed a great mistake by not asking your name.”

paragraphs.text: “No, no. You havenʼt made any mistake. I am the one who has made a mistake. My offence is that I am a gentleman, from a good family, but still I havenʼt introduced myself. I should have given you my name as soon as we first met. Please forgive me.”

paragraphs.text: “I am that Viireshavijaya Vasumálika,” he replied. Saying this, he threw himself into the water. The rapids flung his body around violently and carried him off towards a deep cavern. After that his body sank and disappeared from sight. A sudden strong gust of wind blew at my back from the direction of the forest. Then the gust of wind started blowing towards the mountain in front of me. All around me I could hear the sound soṋ, soṋ, soṋ [sound of the wind]. If someone else had been there they would not have heard anything else, but in the middle of this soṋ-soṋ sound I could hear Viireshavijayaʼs last words “má-má-má go” [mother, mother, oh my dear mother]. With steadfast eyes I looked at the rapids. Unknowingly, my eyes lit upon a few drops of water. In all directions one could hear the hills reverberating with the sound – má-má-má go.
summary: “I am that Viireshavijaya Vasumálika,” he replied.
Then the gust of wind started blowing towards the mountain in front of me.
In all directions one could hear the hills reverberating with the sound – má-má-má go.

The majority of Bengalee Muslims belong to the Sunni sect – the Shias are nearly all immigrants; in conduct, behaviour, character, language and physical makeup they are distinct from the Bengalee people. Practically speaking, there is no intermarriage. They live in small numbers in the urban areas of Murshidabad District. The Muslim rustics are Bengali people.

Generally these “Muslim rustics” live in those areas where the Shersháhábadiiyá dialect is prevalent, that is, they stay chiefly in Murshidabad District, Maldah District, the Bholahat, Gomastapur, Nacol, Shivaganj and Navabganj areas of Rajshahi District, the Nalhati and Murarai areas of Birbhum District, Pakur-Rajmahal Subdivision and certain parts of Sahebganj and Katihar. They also make their home in the river basins adjacent to Sahebganj. Everywhere they speak Shersháhábádiiyá Bengali. They are original Bengalees, extremely straightforward, hardworking, and they keep away from all kinds of falsehood or crookedness. paragraphs.text: I think it is important to mention here that the diamond which is known as Kohinúr [Koh-i-Noor] was the locket [pendant] on Shrii Krśńaʼs jewelled necklace. After many battles and campaigns it came into the hands of Nadir Shah, and thereafter Punjabkesharii Ranjit Singh. After him, Jhindan acquired it, and finally it came into the hands of the East India Company. They had it cut and polished in Holland and then had it set in the British Royal Crown, although some people are of the opinion that it was not set in the crown but was preserved in a different location. Whatever the case may be, Krśńaʼs kaostúbhamańi and the kohinúr are one and the same.

paragraphs.text: Nurjahan was a Persian lady. This uncommonly beautiful woman was sold by her father in India. Her real name was Meher-Un-Nisa. During Akbarʼs time, Burdwan ( 2 ) was the capital of Bengal. It was during this time that she was married to Sher Afgan, the governor (or subedar) of Bengal. Selim, the son of Akbarʼs Rajput wife (later known as Jahangiir ( 3 ) after ascending the throne), put pressure on Sher Afgan to surrender Meher-Un-Nisa to him, but Sher Afgan did not agree. There followed a fierce battle in Burdwan between Sher Afgan and the Mughal army. ( 4 ) Sher Afgan was slain in the battle (his grave is still in Burdwan city) and Jahangiir forcibly abducted Meher-Un-Nisa. At first Meher-Un-Nisa refused to marry her husbandʼs killer, Jahangiir, but later, under pressure of circumstances, she agreed.

It was during this time that she was married to Sher Afgan, the governor (or subedar) of Bengal.
At first Meher-Un-Nisa refused to marry her husbandʼs killer, Jahangiir, but later, under pressure of circumstances, she agreed.

paragraphs.text: After her marriage to Jahangiir her new name became Nurjahan. Jahangiir was an unstable drunkard; India was actually ruled by Nurjahan. Both Rajiya Begum during Pathan rule and Nurjahan during Mughal rule became famous as especially skilled female administrators. But the name of Nurjahan is more famous for iitr. Nurjahan was also a highly skilled kavii [poet] ( 5 ) in the Farsi language.

paragraphs.text: Speaking about iitr reminds me of an experience from the old days. I was staying in an ordinary hotel in the city of Gaya doing research on the culture and civilization of Magadh. At the time I was working in the hilly wilds around Gaya searching for the deep, hidden similarities between the pre-Buddhist Magadh civilization and the ancient civilization of Ráŕh. I had found a striking similarity between the two and had never before felt such excitement and enthusiasm in my research. In terms of my river valley research I was concentrating then on the Naeranjana-Mohaniya-Phalgu River Basin.

At the time I was working in the hilly wilds around Gaya searching for the deep, hidden similarities between the pre-Buddhist Magadh civilization and the ancient civilization of Ráŕh.

paragraphs.text: The hotel was small but neat, clean and orderly, as if someoneʼs house had been turned into a hotel. I arrived there about six in the evening, took a good look at the bedroom and the bathroom, and then, after finishing some important work, I retired early, tired after the dayʼs labours. Sleep came on quickly. Ah yes, before sleeping I noticed a white stone iitr-pot in one corner of the dressing table, a Gayan artifact of ancient Mágadhii culture. I could tell that the iitr-pot had not been used in a long time because it did not smell at all of iitr.

paragraphs.text: Sometime later, Iʼm not sure exactly what time it was, I was awakened by a strange sensation just above the ankle. There was a dim light in the room – the rest of the lights I had turned off before going to bed. What did I see in that dim light when I looked down but what looked like a pair of hands catching me just above the ankles! I freed my legs with a jerk and called out in Magahi: “Who are you? Why have you come into my room like this? This is not good.”

What did I see in that dim light when I looked down but what looked like a pair of hands catching me just above the ankles!
Why have you come into my room like this?

paragraphs.text: The two hands drew back. Then I saw a shadowy figure slowly move back into the dark part of the room and lose itself behind the dressing table. I quickly got up, turned on the lights and thoroughly searched the bedroom and the bathroom as well as the closet but no one was there. The door was still locked from the inside as I had left it, which meant that nobody had come in from outside. Then what was it? Whose hands was it with their indistinct touch? And those hands had left the scent of jasmine essence!
summary: The two hands drew back.
The door was still locked from the inside as I had left it, which meant that nobody had come in from outside.

paragraphs.text: Keeping the light on I lay down and called out mentally: “Hey, bodiless one, have courage, come out once again. I never do anyone any harm, so there is no possibility of your being harmed by me. Come and tell me your untold story.” But nothing or no one came out.

” But nothing or no one came out.

paragraphs.text: Then suddenly I see… what is this? Astonishing! Smoke is rising out of that abandoned iitr-pot. But how? And that smoke was filled with the scent of jasmine. I was dumbfounded. Gradually the smoke began to twist into coils. They became denser and denser, but what was behind those coils of smoke could not be seen or understood.

And that smoke was filled with the scent of jasmine.

paragraphs.text: After a short time the smoke began to thin and what did I see behind the coils but a young man of good breeding, perhaps twenty-four or twenty-five years old. He looked at me and greeted me politely with folded hands, stood silently for a while, then softly made his way towards the door. He opened the locked door and quietly went outside. I found this all very mysterious.

He opened the locked door and quietly went outside.
I found this all very mysterious.

paragraphs.text: He went down the stairs from the first floor to the ground floor, but his footsteps were completely silent. He was walking, but no sound was coming. I also followed silently behind him, determined not to leave him until I found out who he was… for what reason he had entered my room at one in the morning… what it was he wanted to say.

paragraphs.text: The main entry door to the hotel was locked, but he opened it and went straight out into the street. I was following right behind him, but he never turned back to look. The city was dead quiet. Not even a dog was awake and about. He walked on and so did I. Not far from the hotel was the Phalgu River, and after a short time he reached the river and stopped. He stood there silently for a short time, then turned around to look at me and said in Magahi: “I have given you trouble… quite a lot of trouble… please donʼt mind.”

paragraphs.text: “What trouble have you given me?” I replied. “I followed you of my own accord. I wanted to see what your destination would be.”

paragraphs.text: He looked around once carefully in all directions and then began. “At the moment there is no one here besides the two of us; in these surroundings my words will make a stronger impression.

paragraphs.text: “I am a child of Magadh. History has never done full justice to this land of Magadh. Every dust particle of its villages and markets is mixed with the gold-dust of its heritage, but no one has properly recognized it or recorded it. The little that has been written about it has been written by foreign historians – some out of sport, some out of merriment. The shrivelled Phalgu that you see today was not always in this condition. The hills of southern Magadh were once covered with dense forests. Beyond the mountains, from the north to the south, the Mágadhii River valley was also covered with thick forests. Even a portion of the plains and the banks of the river were also forested. This heavily-forested Magadh used to enjoy an abundance of rainfall and thus the rivers were full of water twelve months out of the year. Because of the abundance of forests there was no problem of soil erosion, and because the forests contained the water there was very little severe flooding. Seeing the Magadh of today, it is difficult to imagine the lush green Magadh that once was.
summary: “I am a child of Magadh.
The hills of southern Magadh were once covered with dense forests.
Seeing the Magadh of today, it is difficult to imagine the lush green Magadh that once was.

paragraphs.text: “You are certainly aware of the fact that Magadh was once a vast empire. At the time of Ashoka and Samudragupta it was probably the largest empire in the world – but nothing lasts forever. Those glorious days came to an end and a cimmerian darkness descended over Magadh. The most difficult days in Magadhʼs history drew nigh during the reign of Skandagupta.”
summary: “You are certainly aware of the fact that Magadh was once a vast empire.
Those glorious days came to an end and a cimmerian darkness descended over Magadh.
The most difficult days in Magadhʼs history drew nigh during the reign of Skandagupta.

paragraphs.text: “Tell me a little more, in brief.”
summary: “Tell me a little more, in brief.

paragraphs.text: He went on. “Skandagupta was one in a string of unworthy sovereigns to occupy the throne of Magadh. At that time the empire had disintegrated and the kingdom was on the point of collapse, confined to its ancient borders. To the north was the Ganges and north of that Mithila, which was at one time part of the empire of Magadh and which Ráŕhʼs King Shashanka had wrested from the hands of Magadh. To the east were the Grdhrakút́a and Cakravarttii Mountains. In the eastern region of the Grdhrakút́a Mountains was Angadesh and the Magadh Empire. King Shashanka of Ráŕh also took possession of these areas. In the eastern regions of the Cakravarttii Mountains was the land of Ráŕh, which came under Shashankaʼs direct rule. The southeast cornerʼs border was Sametashikhar. Next came ancient Ráŕh, which the king of Ráŕh had conquered. The southern portion of the Ramgarh Mountains to the south, and the western portion of the Shon River to the west were first controlled by the king of Kashi, Citrasena. After his fall, this entire area was controlled by the royal house of Thaniishvar. Magadh did not have a direct struggle with Prabhakaravardhana but rather with Rajyavardhana and Harsavardhana.
summary: “Skandagupta was one in a string of unworthy sovereigns to occupy the throne of Magadh.
In the eastern regions of the Cakravarttii Mountains was the land of Ráŕh, which came under Shashankaʼs direct rule.
Magadh did not have a direct struggle with Prabhakaravardhana but rather with Rajyavardhana and Harsavardhana.

paragraphs.text: “Iʼve gone on quite a bit about the borders of Magadh at that time. I hope you didnʼt mind. Without it the picture would not be complete.”

paragraphs.text: “Magadh had lost all its previous power and glory,” he continued. “King Skandagupta was a weak-minded, vacillating drunkard. He did very little of what we normally consider great deeds; rather he led Magadh to the brink of destruction.
summary: “Magadh had lost all its previous power and glory,” he continued.
“King Skandagupta was a weak-minded, vacillating drunkard.
He did very little of what we normally consider great deeds; rather he led Magadh to the brink of destruction.

paragraphs.text: “Of course, nothing in this world is completely one-sided. No matter how much historians blame him, Skandagupta did some good also. This city of Gaya, which we are standing in the heart of, was designed by him. He founded Sanskrit schools and training centres in various parts of Magadh, such as Dvádashavardhaká (Barbigha), Brhadhiká (Barahiya), Madhukamadhá (Mokama), Urubilva (Arawal), Grdhrakút́a (Gidhaor), and so forth, which endured for quite some time. He was the first to introduce the use of the Mágadhii language of that time (Western Demi-Mágadhii) in government service alongside Sanskrit. Still, he watched the Magadh Empire crumble in front of his eyes. He died watching an entire empire fall apart due to his own incompetence.
summary: “Of course, nothing in this world is completely one-sided.

He founded Sanskrit schools and training centres in various parts of Magadh, such as Dvádashavardhaká (Barbigha), Brhadhiká (Barahiya), Madhukamadhá (Mokama), Urubilva (Arawal), Grdhrakút́a (Gidhaor), and so forth, which endured for quite some time.
He died watching an entire empire fall apart due to his own incompetence.

paragraphs.text: “At that time there was a fierce struggle going on for the capture of Magadh between King Rajyavardhana of the royal house of Thaniisvar and Ráŕhʼs King Shashanka. Thanisvaraʼs kings used to repeatedly move their capital from place to place, but Shashanka did not. Rather, he would enlarge his capital according to necessity and befitting the times. He founded Paiṋca Gaoŕa [the five ancient parts of Bengal] after capturing Anga and Mithila and then North Bengal (Barendra), Central Bengal (Samatat) and East Bengal (Vauṋga). That is, during his time Bengal was divided into five political divisions: 1) Ráŕh, 2) Mithila, 3) Samatat, 4) Barendra, and 5) Vauṋga-D́abák (East Bengal or Shriibhúmi or Cat́t́al was then included in Bengal) – but he kept his capital at Karnasuvarna. ( 6 )
summary: “At that time there was a fierce struggle going on for the capture of Magadh between King Rajyavardhana of the royal house of Thaniisvar and Ráŕhʼs King Shashanka.
Rather, he would enlarge his capital according to necessity and befitting the times.

paragraphs.text: “There were several reasons for the war between Rajyavardhana and Shashanka. Rajyavardhanaʼs aims were to plunder Magadhʼs wealth and to take possession of Angabhumi. Shashankaʼs main aims were to take possession of Angabhumi and to root out the Buddhist religion and culture from Magadh. Although Rajyavardhana put on a show of liberality he was really narrow-minded. In actual fact, he never treated the Shaivite religion as equal to the Buddhist religion. Shashanka was a staunch follower of Shaivism and completely against Buddhism. He openly declared that as long as one drop of blood remained in his body, he would not allow Buddhism the right to enter either Ráŕh or Paiṋca Gaoŕa ( 7 ) (Bengal).
summary: “There were several reasons for the war between Rajyavardhana and Shashanka.
Although Rajyavardhana put on a show of liberality he was really narrow-minded.
He openly declared that as long as one drop of blood remained in his body, he would not allow Buddhism the right to enter either Ráŕh or Paiṋca Gaoŕa ( 7 ) (Bengal).

paragraphs.text: “I am sure you are familiar with Ambabhumi, ( 8 ) which is situated in the western part of our Magadh. Ambabhumi was the ancient name of that fertile region (modern name Mokámá T́ál) composed of the western areas of what is now Monghyr District – Surajagara, Laksmiisarai, Baravigha, Barhiya, and so on; the eastern portion of Patna District, especially Mokama and surrounding areas; the eastern part of present-day Nalanda District; and the northeast areas of present-day Nawada District. There was no other region in all of India which was as fertile and as affluent at that time. Thus everyone had their greedy eyes set on Ambabhumi. Rajyavardhana and Shashanka were no exceptions.
summary: “I am sure you are familiar with Ambabhumi, ( 8 ) which is situated in the western part of our Magadh.
There was no other region in all of India which was as fertile and as affluent at that time.
Rajyavardhana and Shashanka were no exceptions.

paragraphs.text: “Their style of attack, however, differed. Rajyavardhana wanted to plunder wealth, so he would set fire to peopleʼs houses and ransack them. Shashankaʼs aim was to destroy Buddhist monasteries (what are now called gaŕa in modern Magahi) and Maháyána Buddhist images and idols. You are certainly aware of the fact that, according to social and religious regulations, idols can no longer be used for worship once there is any defect or deformation in them. So Shashanka had the different statues of Buddhist gods and goddesses deformed with a chisel. Today you will find that most of the ancient Buddhist religious statues still in existence have had their noses broken off.
