You are certainly aware of the fact that, according to social and religious regulations, idols can no longer be used for worship once there is any defect or deformation in them.
Today you will find that most of the ancient Buddhist religious statues still in existence have had their noses broken off.

paragraphs.text: “Foreign historians claim that they were damaged during the time of Baktiar Khiljii, or Kálápáháŕ. ( 9 ) Although there is a grain or two of truth in this, it is, for the most part, a false assertion. They were actively fostering conflict between the Hindus and Muslims of our country, because they followed the policy of ‘divide and rule’. Actually Shashanka was responsible. He was not interested in looting. In this way, with Rajyavardhana burning his way from the west and Shashanka applying pressure from the east, the two of them brought Magadh to its last gasp.
summary: “Foreign historians claim that they were damaged during the time of Baktiar Khiljii, or Kálápáháŕ.
Actually Shashanka was responsible.
In this way, with Rajyavardhana burning his way from the west and Shashanka applying pressure from the east, the two of them brought Magadh to its last gasp.

paragraphs.text: “Now the sacred banyan tree that you were sitting under yesterday was not the real Bodhi Tree where Siddhartha attained enlightenment. Ashokaʼs son, Mahendra, took a branch from the original tree and brought it to Sri Lanka. That branch grew into a second Bodhi Tree in Sri Lanka and a branch was taken from that second tree and brought here and planted. This Bodhi Tree was produced from that branch. Shashanka not only extirpated that ancient Bodhi Tree, he also dug a deep ditch around it afterwards and filled it with honey so that the ants would come and eat whatever remained of the roots while they devoured the honey; as a result that Bodhi Tree could not grow back again.
summary: “Now the sacred banyan tree that you were sitting under yesterday was not the real Bodhi Tree where Siddhartha attained enlightenment.
That branch grew into a second Bodhi Tree in Sri Lanka and a branch was taken from that second tree and brought here and planted.

Shashanka not only extirpated that ancient Bodhi Tree, he also dug a deep ditch around it afterwards and filled it with honey so that the ants would come and eat whatever remained of the roots while they devoured the honey; as a result that Bodhi Tree could not grow back again.

paragraphs.text: “This is the history of my Magadh of those times.”
summary: “This is the history of my Magadh of those times.

paragraphs.text: “You canʼt be very old,” I said. “One could say that you are still a lad, so how is it you know so much? There was no clear or formulated system of studying or teaching history in those days. The study and teaching of history in India was first provided for by Emperor Nasiruddiin during Pathan rule and by several foreign travelers during the Mughal era. Thus there were no history books in either Sanskrit or any of the Prákrta languages. The real beginning of the teaching and study of history came during the time of British rule. So the things you have been talking about have never been properly recorded.”
summary: “You canʼt be very old,” I said.
The study and teaching of history in India was first provided for by Emperor Nasiruddiin during Pathan rule and by several foreign travelers during the Mughal era.
So the things you have been talking about have never been properly recorded.

paragraphs.text: “I am not saying all this myself,” he replied. “I am thinking about you and whatever you are thinking about is coming out through my mouth.”
summary: “I am not saying all this myself,” he replied.
“I am thinking about you and whatever you are thinking about is coming out through my mouth.

paragraphs.text: “I appreciate your competence and erudition very much,” I said.
summary: “I appreciate your competence and erudition very much,” I said.

paragraphs.text: “As a result of the clash between Shashanka and Rajyavardhana,” he continued, “the amount of harm that Magadh suffered was doubled. It would be a mistake to say that neither one wanted to see the other; neither one of them could even stand hearing the otherʼs name. Shashanka, in an unexpected development, captured Kanyakubja, slew its king, Cakrayudha (in some peopleʼs opinion, Inrayudha), the husband of Rajyavardhanaʼs sister, Rajyashrii, and installed his own nephew from Ráŕh, Keshariivijaya, on the throne, giving him the name Indrayudha (some say Cakrayudha). Rajyashrii returned to her fatherʼs house and instigated her brothers, Rajyavardhana and Harśavardhana, to turn against Ráŕh. As a result, Magadh, which lay between those two lands, had to suffer many outrages. This is our Magadh.
summary: “As a result of the clash between Shashanka and Rajyavardhana,” he continued, “the amount of harm that Magadh suffered was doubled.

Shashanka, in an unexpected development, captured Kanyakubja, slew its king, Cakrayudha (in some peopleʼs opinion, Inrayudha), the husband of Rajyavardhanaʼs sister, Rajyashrii, and installed his own nephew from Ráŕh, Keshariivijaya, on the throne, giving him the name Indrayudha (some say Cakrayudha).
As a result, Magadh, which lay between those two lands, had to suffer many outrages.

paragraphs.text: “Mag means ‘he who moves about independently’, that is, one who does not follow the Vedic injunctions. Dha means ‘follower’. The land which follows the anti-Vedic, Buddhist doctrine is Magadh. The Sanskrit dha is transformed into ha in Prákrta. Thus magadha becomes magaha – the name of the language is Magahi. Following the Buddhist era, the language of all of eastern India was this Magahii Prákrta. Lord Buddha, The Enlightened, made his appearance in this land.
summary: “Mag means ‘he who moves about independently’, that is, one who does not follow the Vedic injunctions.
The Sanskrit dha is transformed into ha in Prákrta.
Lord Buddha, The Enlightened, made his appearance in this land.

paragraphs.text: “Our Magadh is situated in the northeast corner of the prehistoric Gondwanaland. Since Gondwanaland is the oldest land on earth, it is also the original home of human beings, the birthplace of human civilization. Ráŕh is in eastern Gondwanaland. In the prehistoric era, human beings came from Ráŕh to make their home in Magadh and they brought with them the current of their civilization and culture. Just as the geography of Magadh slopes downwards from north to south and the rivers flow from north to south, similarly the culture and civilization flowed from south to north. Thus the people of Ráŕh and Magadh are fundamentally one. Like the people of Ráŕh, the common people of Magadh are dark-skinned. Magadh borders Ráŕh along its southeast border. The skin and bodily structure of the people of Ráŕh and Magadh are identical. There is also a noticeable similarity between their languages.
summary: “Our Magadh is situated in the northeast corner of the prehistoric Gondwanaland.
Thus the people of Ráŕh and Magadh are fundamentally one.
There is also a noticeable similarity between their languages.

paragraphs.text: “Earlier I told you that in those days Magadh was full of forests and had abundant rainfall so there was no need of irrigation. The pre-Aryan people of Magadh used to believe that their land received rainfall due to the grace of the sun-god. Thus they used to worship the sun-god according to their ancient local customs, once during the autumn paddy harvest and again during the spring sun harvest (chaetii harvest). This sun-worship of pre-Aryan Magadh is known today as chat́ pújá. This worship was not performed according to Aryan rules. It was a completely local Magadh practice. The people of Magadh did not bow their heads and submissively accept any of the Aryan practices. For that reason the Aryans called the land Magadh. They were afraid of Magadh and used to pay it respect. Thus, to satisfy their grudge and vent their spite, they declared Magadh an unholy land. They said that if a man died there he would not go to heaven and they made efforts to forcibly impose their language, culture and civilization on Magadh. It is up to the historians and social scientists to consider just how successful they were in their efforts.
summary: “Earlier I told you that in those days Magadh was full of forests and had abundant rainfall so there was no need of irrigation.
The people of Magadh did not bow their heads and submissively accept any of the Aryan practices.
It is up to the historians and social scientists to consider just how successful they were in their efforts.

paragraphs.text: “Magadh did not accept the Aryan civilization. In ancient Magadh there was no custom of racial or caste divisions. The caste system in Magadh came much later due to the influence of the Aryans. Even after the advent of the caste system, the Kraoiṋcadviipii and Magadhʼs Shrotriya Brahmins did not like the severity of caste divisions. For this reason the Kraoiṋcadviipii and Magadhʼs Shrotriya Brahmins were not recognized by the Brahmins of northern India.”
summary: “Magadh did not accept the Aryan civilization.
The caste system in Magadh came much later due to the influence of the Aryans.
For this reason the Kraoiṋcadviipii and Magadhʼs Shrotriya Brahmins were not recognized by the Brahmins of northern India.

paragraphs.text: The boy looked at me and said with a choked voice, “You know, today Magadh is torn apart by caste differences. I want to hear from your lips if Magadh has a future or not.”
summary: The boy looked at me and said with a choked voice, “You know, today Magadh is torn apart by caste differences.
I want to hear from your lips if Magadh has a future or not.

paragraphs.text: “Why are you weeping?” I asked. “Why are you thinking in this way? I tell you, Magadh has a bright future. Magadh will once again break down the walls of narrow-mindedness and hold its head high in the world community. Magadhʼs past was bright and its future will be radiant.”
summary: “Why are you weeping?
I tell you, Magadh has a bright future.
Magadhʼs past was bright and its future will be radiant.

paragraphs.text: He was consoled and happy.
summary: He was consoled and happy.

paragraphs.text: “It was an unbelievable and unforgettable happening. Nearly two and a half thousand years ago two great spiritual leaders appeared on the earth at about the same time on the soil of Magadh to sow there the seeds of their spiritual teachings. One was Vardhaman Mahavir and the other was Gaotama Buddha. Gaotama Buddha was the son of the feudal king of the central terái, Shuddhodana (Malla dynasty, Shákya branch of the Kśatriyas), and his wife Mayadevii. He practised austerities for a long time in Magadh in the areas of the Barábar, Brahmayoni and Grdhrakút́ mountains. His guru in Sáḿkhya philosophy, Acarya Sanjaya (Nawada District), was also from Magadh. Although what is called avidyá in his philosophy is not the same as pradhána or prakrti in Sáḿkhya, there is some similarity between the Buddhaʼs concept of avidyá and the Sáḿkhya concept of pradhána.
summary: “It was an unbelievable and unforgettable happening.
Gaotama Buddha was the son of the feudal king of the central terái, Shuddhodana (Malla dynasty, Shákya branch of the Kśatriyas), and his wife Mayadevii.

Although what is called avidyá in his philosophy is not the same as pradhána or prakrti in Sáḿkhya, there is some similarity between the Buddhaʼs concept of avidyá and the Sáḿkhya concept of pradhána.

paragraphs.text: “The Buddha attained enlightenment in the village of Urubilva, located on the bank of the river Naeranjana (Urubilva is called Bodhgaya today). That Sujata who fed him kśiira [rice pudding] and saved his life at that moment when the period of his radiant austerities had brought him to the point of death, was Buddhaʼs cousin and the wife of a certain feudal king of Magadh. One should remember here that at that time the Naeraiṋjana River coming from the south joined the Mohaniká (Mohaniya) River near Urubilva and flowed together from there as the Phalgu River, later joining the Ganges near Modhukamadhá [Mokama]. About 2000 years ago the two rivers underwent some physical changes due to a huge earthquake and for that reason the Phalgu River of today is much smaller than it was.
summary: “The Buddha attained enlightenment in the village of Urubilva, located on the bank of the river Naeranjana (Urubilva is called Bodhgaya today).

One should remember here that at that time the Naeraiṋjana River coming from the south joined the Mohaniká (Mohaniya) River near Urubilva and flowed together from there as the Phalgu River, later joining the Ganges near Modhukamadhá [Mokama].
About 2000 years ago the two rivers underwent some physical changes due to a huge earthquake and for that reason the Phalgu River of today is much smaller than it was.

paragraphs.text: “At any rate, the prince of the Shakyas, Gaotama, attained enlightenment on Magadh soil. Many say that Buddha first introduced the Buddhist dharmacakra [wheel of dharma] and initiated his first disciple near Benares in the Isipattana Migadaba (Rśipattana deer grove, alias Sárauṋganáth or Saranath). Although this is partially correct, it is not the complete truth. It is certainly true that he introduced the dharmacakra in the Isipattana deer grove and that his five disciples, Kaondinya (Kaońdilya), Bappá (Vapra), Bhaddiiya (Bhadreya), Mahánáma, and Ashsháji (Ashvajit), were present there. But he gave his first initiations on Magadh soil – to Sáriputta, the son of Rúpasári, and Mahamoggallan Arhan, the son of Mahamoggalii.
summary: “At any rate, the prince of the Shakyas, Gaotama, attained enlightenment on Magadh soil.
Although this is partially correct, it is not the complete truth.
But he gave his first initiations on Magadh soil – to Sáriputta, the son of Rúpasári, and Mahamoggallan Arhan, the son of Mahamoggalii.

paragraphs.text: “In those days Magadhʼs matriarchal system still retained some influence alongside the patriarchal system. So Buddhaʼs first two disciples in Magadh were known by their mothersʼ names. The merchant that the city of Pataliputra was named after due to his philanthropy also carried his motherʼs name in accordance with the matriarchal system. The name of the merchantʼs mother was Pát́alii.
summary: “In those days Magadhʼs matriarchal system still retained some influence alongside the patriarchal system.
The merchant that the city of Pataliputra was named after due to his philanthropy also carried his motherʼs name in accordance with the matriarchal system.
The name of the merchantʼs mother was Pát́alii.

paragraphs.text: “Vardhaman Mahavir was born in Vaeshálii in a Vaeshya family. His fatherʼs name was Siddhartha and his motherʼs name was Trishala. Like the Buddha, however, he did not propagate his teachings first in his native land but came to Magadh to do so.
summary: “Vardhaman Mahavir was born in Vaeshálii in a Vaeshya family.
His fatherʼs name was Siddhartha and his motherʼs name was Trishala.
Like the Buddha, however, he did not propagate his teachings first in his native land but came to Magadh to do so.

paragraphs.text: “One does not have to go far to find the reason why both of them selected Magadh as the proper place for their work. Magadh was not bound hand and foot with the bonds of the Vedic religion. Their natural liberal mentality gushed forth in all aspects of their lives. Buddha was successful in spreading his teachings (dharmadeshaná) there because they were based more on logic than on superstition and belief. Of course, the spirit of revolt against conventionality was present in Vardhaman Mahavirʼs teachings also, but in the opinion of the Magahi people his doctrine of ahiḿsá [non-violence] did not accord well with reality so they were not able to accept it easily. Of course, some people did accept it, but others considered him an unrealistic theoretician and tried to bring him down to earth by using occult powers. Thus he felt the need to go elsewhere to propagate his new religion.
summary: “One does not have to go far to find the reason why both of them selected Magadh as the proper place for their work.
Buddha was successful in spreading his teachings (dharmadeshaná) there because they were based more on logic than on superstition and belief.
Thus he felt the need to go elsewhere to propagate his new religion.

paragraphs.text: “At that time the most famous city for progressive thinking, education and culture was Ástikanagar (Atthinagar), the capital of Ráŕh. Vardhaman Mahavir went there and stayed nearly eight years. There he managed to fit his doctrine of ahiḿsá into a somewhat realistic framework. Some prominent merchants of Ástikanagar accepted his doctrine and they renamed the city Vardhaman [Burdwan] after him. Thus it is said that the Jain religion was first established in Ráŕh.
summary: “At that time the most famous city for progressive thinking, education and culture was Ástikanagar (Atthinagar), the capital of Ráŕh.
There he managed to fit his doctrine of ahiḿsá into a somewhat realistic framework.
Thus it is said that the Jain religion was first established in Ráŕh.

paragraphs.text: “Thereafter he took the road back to Magadh from Burdwan and stopped for a short time in a small village named Svámiisthána (Svámiisthána → Sáiṋitthán → Sáiṋithiiṋá → Saṋithiyá) on the banks of the Mayurakshi River to preach his gospels. By then he was an elderly man, while Gaotama Buddha was still a young man. He breathed his last in Pavapurii on Magadh soil.
summary: “Thereafter he took the road back to Magadh from Burdwan and stopped for a short time in a small village named Svámiisthána (Svámiisthána → Sáiṋitthán → Sáiṋithiiṋá → Saṋithiyá) on the banks of the Mayurakshi River to preach his gospels.
By then he was an elderly man, while Gaotama Buddha was still a young man.
He breathed his last in Pavapurii on Magadh soil.

paragraphs.text: “There were many in North India who did not appreciate this free mentality of Magadh. They did not spare any efforts to belittle Magadh in the eyes of the people, but Magadh was not discouraged by this.
summary: “There were many in North India who did not appreciate this free mentality of Magadh.
They did not spare any efforts to belittle Magadh in the eyes of the people, but Magadh was not discouraged by this.

paragraphs.text: “The seven Prákrta languages that arose after the demise of Sanskrit were as follows:
summary: “The seven Prákrta languages that arose after the demise of Sanskrit were as follows:

paragraphs.text: 1. Maháráśt́rii Prákrta, which was the forerunner of Konkanii, Marathi, Vaedarbhii (Váŕárii), etc.
summary: Maháráśt́rii Prákrta, which was the forerunner of Konkanii, Marathi, Vaedarbhii (Váŕárii), etc.

paragraphs.text: 2. Málavii Prákrta, which was the forerunner of Gujarati, Saorastrii, Kacchii, Málavii, Mewari, Haraotii and Marwari.
summary: Málavii Prákrta, which was the forerunner of Gujarati, Saorastrii, Kacchii, Málavii, Mewari, Haraotii and Marwari.

paragraphs.text: 3. Saendhavii or Saobiirii Prákrta which gave rise to Sindhi and Mulatani.
summary: Saendhavii or Saobiirii Prákrta which gave rise to Sindhi and Mulatani.

paragraphs.text: 4. Páshcáttya Prákrta, which was the forerunner of Pashtu, Káshmiirii, Uzbeki, Tazaki, etc.
summary: Páshcáttya Prákrta, which was the forerunner of Pashtu, Káshmiirii, Uzbeki, Tazaki, etc.

paragraphs.text: 5. Paeshácii Prákrta, which was the forerunner of Dogri, Pahari, and Punjabi.
summary: Paeshácii Prákrta, which was the forerunner of Dogri, Pahari, and Punjabi.

paragraphs.text: 6. Shaorasenii Prákrta, which was the forerunner of Hindi, Abadhi, Bundeli, Bagheli, and Vraja.
summary: Shaorasenii Prákrta, which was the forerunner of Hindi, Abadhi, Bundeli, Bagheli, and Vraja.

paragraphs.text: 7. Mágadhii Prákrta, which was the forerunner of Magahi, Bengali, Oriya, Angika, Assamese, Nagpuri, Maethili, Chatrishgarhi and Bhojpuri.
summary: Mágadhii Prákrta, which was the forerunner of Magahi, Bengali, Oriya, Angika, Assamese, Nagpuri, Maethili, Chatrishgarhi and Bhojpuri.

paragraphs.text: “This Mágadhii Prákrta had two daughters – Eastern Demi-Mágadhii and Western Demi-Mágadhii. Western Demi-Mágadhii later gave birth to the Magahii language. At one time Mágadhii Prákrta was used not only in eastern India, but in central India as well among the educated community for the exchange of thoughts. Educated people used to show the same zeal for learning Mágadhii Prákrta as they showed for learning Sanskrit. The structure of the Mágadhii Prákrta language is both straighforward and easy. The grammar is also not complex. Both Mahavir and Buddha gave their teachings in the Mágadhii Prákrta of that time, which many people today call Pali. A great deal of literature was composed in the Pali language and its successor, Occidental Demi-Mágadhii. Magadh also had its own script. Inscriptions in that ancient Mágadhii script can still be found in certain places in Bodhgaya. It is the younger sister of the Shriiharśa script and closely related to modern Maethili (Tirhuti) script and Bengali script.”
summary: “This Mágadhii Prákrta had two daughters – Eastern Demi-Mágadhii and Western Demi-Mágadhii.
The grammar is also not complex.
It is the younger sister of the Shriiharśa script and closely related to modern Maethili (Tirhuti) script and Bengali script.

paragraphs.text: The young man looked at me and smiled. “You know what the sad thing is? Today many educated people in Magadh are ashamed of speaking their mother tongue. They think that it is perhaps a rustic language, unsuitable for respectable society. Yet this Mágadhii – Occidental Demi-Mágadhii – was once the language of the state administration. Who else can I tell this sad tale to?
summary: The young man looked at me and smiled.
They think that it is perhaps a rustic language, unsuitable for respectable society.
Who else can I tell this sad tale to?

paragraphs.text: “Just as Magadhʼs language has its own style of pronunciation and syntax, its popular culture also shines with originality. Today this popular culture is being swept away, but do you know what is even sadder? At one time Magadh had a sound economic infrastructure, but since the time of Skandagupta that infrastructure has crumbled. Today, wherever you look, you see a stark picture of poverty and distress. There is no plan for economic development. The young people of Magadh do not have any economic legs to stand on. Magadh has not been built up; rather, for 1500 years it has been hammered into the dust.”
summary: “Just as Magadhʼs language has its own style of pronunciation and syntax, its popular culture also shines with originality.
Today, wherever you look, you see a stark picture of poverty and distress.
Magadh has not been built up; rather, for 1500 years it has been hammered into the dust.

paragraphs.text: The young man looked at me again and said in a tearful voice: “You know, it maddens me to think about Magadh. Anyhow, as I was saying, the war was going on between Ráŕh and Thanishvara, and Magadh, lying between the two, was being destroyed. Shashanka was an intelligent and courageous man. He built a large army through whatever means he had at his disposal and took Rajyavardhana by surprise when his adversary was temporarily absent from his capital, taking possession of the city. After this he waged a fierce war against Rajyavardhana in which Rajyavardhana was defeated and slain. Some people claim that under the pretence of a truce, Shashanka extended an invitation to Rajyavardhana, and then either stabbed or poisoned him when he came. One can say what one wants in this matter, but there is no sound historical evidence that Shashanka killed Rajyavardhana unfairly.
summary: The young man looked at me again and said in a tearful voice: “You know, it maddens me to think about Magadh.
He built a large army through whatever means he had at his disposal and took Rajyavardhana by surprise when his adversary was temporarily absent from his capital, taking possession of the city.
One can say what one wants in this matter, but there is no sound historical evidence that Shashanka killed Rajyavardhana unfairly.

paragraphs.text: “After Shashanka returned to Ráŕh, Rajyavardhanaʼs brother, Harsavardhana, liberated his kingdom once again and continued the struggle with Shashanka. As long as Shashanka was alive, the war against Thanishvara continued without pause. And so there was no end to Magadhʼs distress.
summary: “After Shashanka returned to Ráŕh, Rajyavardhanaʼs brother, Harsavardhana, liberated his kingdom once again and continued the struggle with Shashanka.
As long as Shashanka was alive, the war against Thanishvara continued without pause.
And so there was no end to Magadhʼs distress.

paragraphs.text: “After Shashankaʼs death his widow, Jayashankari (in some peopleʼs opinion, Trigunashankari), ruled Ráŕh along with Paiṋca Gaoŕa or Bengal after installing his under-age son, Mrigankashekhara, as the crown prince. Harsavardhana did not let this opportunity go by and struck a powerful blow against Ráŕh. War ensued and after two sanguinary battles at Nalhati and Parkat́iipur (Pakur), Ráŕh fell under Harsavardhanaʼs control. The same Harsavardhana who has achieved everlasting fame in India, who, as legend has it, was known for his generosity and who, in some peopleʼs opinion, was the founder of the Kumbhamela and the Mághamelá, also killed Ráŕhʼs Queen Jayashankari and her under-age son, Mrigankashekhara, with his own hand, and utterly exploited Magadh, tossing it aside like a worn-out banana peel. According to the scriptures, the elderly, the women, the sick, the disabled, conscientious dissenters, under-age men and emissaries must not be killed. Harsavardhana blatantly violated this scriptural injunction. Both the people of Bengal and the people of Magadh condemned and censured him for this.
summary: “After Shashankaʼs death his widow, Jayashankari (in some peopleʼs opinion, Trigunashankari), ruled Ráŕh along with Paiṋca Gaoŕa or Bengal after installing his under-age son, Mrigankashekhara, as the crown prince.

The same Harsavardhana who has achieved everlasting fame in India, who, as legend has it, was known for his generosity and who, in some peopleʼs opinion, was the founder of the Kumbhamela and the Mághamelá, also killed Ráŕhʼs Queen Jayashankari and her under-age son, Mrigankashekhara, with his own hand, and utterly exploited Magadh, tossing it aside like a worn-out banana peel.
Both the people of Bengal and the people of Magadh condemned and censured him for this.

paragraphs.text: “As long as Shashanka was alive, he did not allow the Buddhist religion into Ráŕh. After the defeat of Bengal by Harsavardhana, Buddhism, despite not enjoying his open support, became predominant, due to the tremendous indirect support he gave it. In their hearts the people remained Shaivites but on the outside they became Buddhists. Later on, during the time of Shankaracharya, a small number of Ráŕhʼs Jains and large numbers of Buddhists throughout Bengal accepted the Puranic religion. This may have been because in Ráŕh there was some similarity between the traditions of the Puranic religion and the Digambar Jain doctrine of that time. So Harsavardhana dealt a strong blow to the religious thought of Ráŕh, as well as Bengal, and by exploiting Magadh brought it to its lowest point.”
summary: “As long as Shashanka was alive, he did not allow the Buddhist religion into Ráŕh.
Later on, during the time of Shankaracharya, a small number of Ráŕhʼs Jains and large numbers of Buddhists throughout Bengal accepted the Puranic religion.
So Harsavardhana dealt a strong blow to the religious thought of Ráŕh, as well as Bengal, and by exploiting Magadh brought it to its lowest point.

paragraphs.text: The boy looked at me again and said in a choked voice: “Now tell me, who can I express this to? Today Iʼve poured my heart out to you.”
summary: The boy looked at me again and said in a choked voice: “Now tell me, who can I express this to?
Today Iʼve poured my heart out to you.

paragraphs.text: “Go on, go on,” I said. “Donʼt hold anything back.”
summary: “Go on, go on,” I said.
“Donʼt hold anything back.

paragraphs.text: “Magadhʼs misery is not a recent thing. It dates back to the time of Harsavardhana. The people of Magadh have tried to pull themselves up from time to time, but after so many blows theyʼve had their back broken. Now they can no longer stand up straight at all.”
summary: “Magadhʼs misery is not a recent thing.
The people of Magadh have tried to pull themselves up from time to time, but after so many blows theyʼve had their back broken.
Now they can no longer stand up straight at all.

paragraphs.text: “I am really moved by your sincerity, overwhelmed. There should be more boys like you all over Magadh.”
summary: “I am really moved by your sincerity, overwhelmed.
There should be more boys like you all over Magadh.

paragraphs.text: He continued. “While returning back after defeating Bengal, Harsavardhana tried to pulverize Magadh into submission even more. He knew about Magadhʼs tradition and was afraid that Magadh might overthrow his throne. At that time Magadhʼs last general, Agnimitra, and his younger brother, Chandraketu, were directing its final efforts to resist Harsavardhana and a great war ensued. In the battle of Barabar Hill, near the city of Gaya, Magadhʼs army was utterly routed and destroyed. Even then Agnimitra did not accept defeat. paragraphs.text: It was the full moon night in the middle of Hemanta ( 1 ) and a cool breeze was blowing; I had no trouble seeing even without a torch. I was feeling quite happy after having verified several important facts. The issue under consideration was whether or not the Buddhist Mantrayána was dominant in Magadh during the middle of the Buddhist era or the Kálacakrayána. In the Buddhist Mantrayána they recognized the goddess (which also happened later in Tantra and the Puranic religion) and she was also honoured in the Buddhist Kálacakrayána, but the two were divided along doctrinal lines – one accepted Vajratárá and the other Niiltárá or Niil Sarasvatii. ( 2 ) With the passage of time Niil Sarasvatii took the form of Prajiṋápáramitá in Tibet and later Prajiṋápáramitá was accepted in India by the followers of Maháyána. At the outset, Prajiṋápáramitá and Niil Sarasvatii were considered to be one and the same, but later they became separate goddesses. In the beginning, their dhyána mantra was also the same, but it also became different afterwards.

paragraphs.text: The city of Howrah is high in some places, low in others, replete with factories and neighborhoods of gentle, civilized folk. Howrah has been an industrial town since its very inception. There was a time when there was a factory here at every turn. It is difficult to find another such industrial town anywhere in the world, although at present Ludhiana and Batala of the Punjab can boast of a similar glory. This is quite good, no doubt, but Howrah should not lose its distinction.

paragraphs.text: Both government and private agencies derive a very good income from this industrial town, although in general we can say that the city is neglected. Only a very small fraction of what is spent for the improvement of Kolkata is spent on Howrah. Moreover, the sacrifices that Howrah has made for the improvement of Kolkata are indisputable. Kolkata is like a golden lamp with a slender wick made of fine cotton and clarified butter for fuel, while Howrah is like the lamp-stand that bears it on its head. It seems to bear the black stain from the lampʼs burnt oil.

chapters.title: Makarda – A Brief History of the Culture of Ráŕh

paragraphs.text: I was traveling from Maju to Makarda. On the way I suddenly ran into Manimohan Manna. Many of you know our Manimohan. We say about people who are artful talkers that puffed rice bursts open from their mouths, but in the case of Manimohan I would say that puffed rice coated with raw sugar bursts open from his mouth. He is an expert talker but his every word is so sugarcoated that it seems to be puffed rice dipped in the famous palm raw sugar of Kolaghat.

paragraphs.text: Anyhow, I was travelling from Maju to Makarda. This part of Howrah District is very fertile. It has been densely populated since ancient times. When Howrah fell within the jurisdiction of Burdwan, it was the pride of Bengal. Afterwards, when it came within Hooghly District, it was regarded as one of the prosperous areas of Hooghly District. Later on, when Hooghly District was divided and Howrah District was formed, this area remained within Howrah District. Partially without industry, partially industrialized, it was the jewel of the region, shedding its lustre on the whole of Bengal through its scholarship, industriousness and erudition. There was a time when the vast Sarasvati River used to flow through this area. The Sarasvati River came out of the main branch of the Bhagirathi River at Triveni in Hooghly Districtʼs Mogra Police Station. It came out from the right side of the Bhagirathi. The Yamuna [Jamuna, not the river of Uttar Pradesh] River came from the exact opposite direction, that is, from the left side of the Bhagirathi through the Chakda and Haringhata Police Stations of what was then Nadia District, the adjoining region. This confluence of the Ganges, Yamuna and Sarasvati Rivers is renowned as the Triveńitiirtha [holy confluence of three rivers] or the Mukta [liberated] Triveńii.

paragraphs.text: From there the Sarasvati flowed through the fertile, verdant grasslands and grain fields of Hooghly District until it reached Howrah District. There it used to flow past the meadows of kenduá on its right side. What we call nowadays the kenduá meadows was a vast lake in prehistoric times. The lake gradually filled up and turned into the kenduá marshlands or Kendua meadows. Up until a hundred years ago the rice and paddy crops never failed in the kenduá marshlands. Rice and rice paddy used to be exported from the port of Amta by ship to foreign lands along the Damodar River. Those days are gone. Nowadays the Damodar is almost dried up. Its water is not even knee-deep now, so the plying of ships is out of the question.

paragraphs.text: Makarda was situated close to the Sarasvati River in those days. Although a large part of the external trade of Bengal at that time was carried out from the Port de Bauṋgálá (Cat́t́agram) and the Port de Grandi (Saptagram), Makarda also was a busy port. Merchants belonging to the Saha, Tambuli, Gandhabanika and Suvaranabanika communities were the principle contributors to the growth of its wealth. Brahmins and Kayasthas brought the glow of scholarship, and the skilful peasants of the Máhiśya and Sadgope communities produced golden harvests. The heroism of the Kaevartta fishing community became famous far and wide. They were respected in the society as “Bara” [a surname], the best, and were primarily responsible for the formation of the navy of independent Bengal. This area was also home at that time to a shipbuilding factory where indigenous methods were used. That industry perished during British rule. The expert carpenters and Kaevartta fishermen of this place built those ships. The merchants of this area also set out to sea after loading their goods on those ships.
summary: Makarda was situated close to the Sarasvati River in those days.
They were respected in the society as “Bara” [a surname], the best, and were primarily responsible for the formation of the navy of independent Bengal.
The merchants of this area also set out to sea after loading their goods on those ships.

paragraphs.text: Today things have changed. Makarda or Sarasvati has moved on, the Sarasvati has dried up, and the wealth of Makarda has been transferred to other places. There are three chief reasons for this. The first reason is the changing of course and subsequent drying-up of the Sarasvatii. The second reason is the decline of rural industries. The third reason is the loss of economic balance and equilibrium owing to defects in education and the social system.
summary: Today things have changed.
The first reason is the changing of course and subsequent drying-up of the Sarasvatii.
The third reason is the loss of economic balance and equilibrium owing to defects in education and the social system.

paragraphs.text: In general, in order to build a strong economy in a certain area thirty to forty percent of the population of that area – neither more nor less – should be dependent directly on agriculture. If it is less then agriculture is neglected; conversely, if it is more, then there will be a heavy strain on agriculture. That is exactly what has happened in the Maju-Makarda region. What to speak of Maju-Makarda, the same thing has happened throughout Ráŕh, throughout Bengal, throughout India, and even in China and the whole of Southeast Asia. To combat this problem a new social and economic evaluation is necessary.
summary: In general, in order to build a strong economy in a certain area thirty to forty percent of the population of that area – neither more nor less – should be dependent directly on agriculture.
That is exactly what has happened in the Maju-Makarda region.
To combat this problem a new social and economic evaluation is necessary.

paragraphs.text: Just as agriculture should be built up on an advanced scientific foundation, industry should also be organized in perfect adjustment with agriculture. The percentage of the population depending directly on agriculture should not exceed forty percent. Where rural industries have been destroyed, a major part of the population once engaged in that sector is now moving towards agriculture. Just as the percentage of people depending directly on agriculture should be thirty to forty percent for balanced economic development, about twenty percent of the people should depend on agro-industries, twenty percent on agrico-industries, ten percent on general trade and commerce, and ten percent on intellectual or white collar jobs.
summary: Just as agriculture should be built up on an advanced scientific foundation, industry should also be organized in perfect adjustment with agriculture.
Where rural industries have been destroyed, a major part of the population once engaged in that sector is now moving towards agriculture.

Just as the percentage of people depending directly on agriculture should be thirty to forty percent for balanced economic development, about twenty percent of the people should depend on agro-industries, twenty percent on agrico-industries, ten percent on general trade and commerce, and ten percent on intellectual or white collar jobs.

paragraphs.text: Because village industries have been ruined, those who depended on those industries have turned to agriculture. The percentage of merchants has not increased much; rather, the opportunities for further growth have decreased. However, the number of people looking for white-collar jobs has increased, resulting in soaring unemployment.
summary: Because village industries have been ruined, those who depended on those industries have turned to agriculture.
The percentage of merchants has not increased much; rather, the opportunities for further growth have decreased.
However, the number of people looking for white-collar jobs has increased, resulting in soaring unemployment.

paragraphs.text: The sons of farmers, after receiving a little education, are no longer willing to labour in the fields. They want to become babus [title of a Hindu gentleman]; they consider farm work to be menial labour. As a consequence there is a dearth of educated youths in agriculture on the one hand, and on the other an increasing number of people from other vocations turning towards agriculture. In the rural areas the percentage of the population depending primarily on agriculture has gone up to seventy or eighty percent. What an unbearable situation! So just as social and economic life in other parts of Bengal have been turned upside down, Maju-Makarda is no exception. The Maju-Makarda region was Howrah Districtʼs greatest potential for economic development, but that hope has been shattered. Today the city of Howrah is neglected, so it is not capable of supplying vital energy to rural Bengal.
summary: The sons of farmers, after receiving a little education, are no longer willing to labour in the fields.
What an unbearable situation!

paragraphs.text: Non-agricultural industry (such as steel plants, brass industry, metal industry, oil refineries, salt industry and non-plant-based pharmaceuticals) refers to those industries that are neither direct agrico-industries (such as production of pick-axes, spades and tractors) nor industries that are directly dependent on agriculture, that is, agro-industries (such as jute mills, cloth factories, flour mills, paper mills and plant-based medicines). The percentage of people engaged in non-agricultural industry should be formed by reducing the percentage of people depending directly on agriculture, reducing the percentage of people depending on agrico-industries and reducing the percentage of people engaged in agro-industries. The percentage of people engaged in non-agricultural industries should be kept within twenty to thirty percent of the total population. If the percentage is less than twenty percent, the country is said to be industrially undeveloped and the per capita income of the people cannot be very high. The standard of living also cannot be very high because the purchasing capacity of the people remains very limited. Due to the reduced capacity for purchasing consumer goods, the import index remains lower than the export index, meaning the area has to remain the satellite of a developed country. As a consequence, the balance of power in the world is jeopardized and the possibility of war is always around the corner.
summary: Non-agricultural industry (such as steel plants, brass industry, metal industry, oil refineries, salt industry and non-plant-based pharmaceuticals) refers to those industries that are neither direct agrico-industries (such as production of pick-axes, spades and tractors) nor industries that are directly dependent on agriculture, that is, agro-industries (such as jute mills, cloth factories, flour mills, paper mills and plant-based medicines).
If the percentage is less than twenty percent, the country is said to be industrially undeveloped and the per capita income of the people cannot be very high.
As a consequence, the balance of power in the world is jeopardized and the possibility of war is always around the corner.

paragraphs.text: If the percentage of people engaged in non-agricultural industry is kept between twenty and thirty percent of the population, then it creates a state of balance, a balanced socio-economic system. If the percentage goes beyond thirty percent it becomes an industrially developed area. The more the percentage rises beyond thirty percent, the more the area goes from industrially developed to industrially over-developed. In order to procure agricultural produce the industrially over-developed countries try to convert agriculturally predominant regions into their satellites. They feel the need to keep these industrially undeveloped countries under their control in order to serve as a market for their finished goods. If they do not obtain markets for their industrially produced consumer goods, they will have to suffer from economic recessions and growing unemployment.
summary: If the percentage of people engaged in non-agricultural industry is kept between twenty and thirty percent of the population, then it creates a state of balance, a balanced socio-economic system.
In order to procure agricultural produce the industrially over-developed countries try to convert agriculturally predominant regions into their satellites.
If they do not obtain markets for their industrially produced consumer goods, they will have to suffer from economic recessions and growing unemployment.

paragraphs.text: In this regard, there is no difference between communist and non-communist countries. All of them are equally aggressive in their approach. They are desperately searching for the wish-fulfilling cow, which they want to keep tied to their door, feeding it the minimum amount of fodder. Is it any wonder there are so many wars and conflicts in the world, so much war psychosis and sabre-rattling? Efforts must be made so that each and every country of the world can enjoy a balanced state in both agriculture and industry; otherwise, the socio-economic balance of the world is bound to be destroyed.

paragraphs.text: The negative consequences of over-industrialization result in deterioration of personal, social and political health; due to the gradual psychic degeneration of both individuals and the collective, a kind of psychic epidemic may become rampant any moment which can endanger or jeopardize every expression of life. It may not happen today, but it will surely happen in the near future.
summary: The negative consequences of over-industrialization result in deterioration of personal, social and political health; due to the gradual psychic degeneration of both individuals and the collective, a kind of psychic epidemic may become rampant any moment which can endanger or jeopardize every expression of life.
It may not happen today, but it will surely happen in the near future.

paragraphs.text: Where the industrial system (whether it is agro-industry, agrico-industry or non-agricultural industry) depends on outside labourers, the situation becomes precarious. The speed of psychic degeneration accelerates. Such a region will suffer from a chronic scarcity of food. The possibility of expanding the markets for their consumer goods will gradually become curtailed. As an example, we can look at Howrah, Hooghly, 24 Parganas and Burdwan. Since the labourers there are outsiders, the local people will never see good days. However developed or over-developed these areas might become, they will have to endure the ill effects of over-industrialization without being able to enjoy any of the benefits of industrialization. This sort of scenario can be seen daily in Howrah District. Moreover there are still many such areas in India where ninety percent of the population consists of farmers. There is no industry whatsoever in those areas. They are completely surplus labour areas. A balanced socio-economic structure will have neither surplus labour nor deficit labour. It cannot be permitted.
summary: Where the industrial system (whether it is agro-industry, agrico-industry or non-agricultural industry) depends on outside labourers, the situation becomes precarious.
However developed or over-developed these areas might become, they will have to endure the ill effects of over-industrialization without being able to enjoy any of the benefits of industrialization.
It cannot be permitted.

paragraphs.text: The agricultural system should be built up similar to the industrial system; that is, the prices of agricultural produce should be determined by considering basic factors such as agricultural income, expenses and necessities. In other words, the farmers of Burdwan and Birbhum should not be forced to sell their rice at throwaway prices. Similarly, the farmers of Hooghly District should not be compelled to sell their potatoes at cheap prices, and the farmers of Nadia District should not be forced to sell their jute at low prices in order to pay off their debts.

paragraphs.text: Yes, Makarda is still some distance away. I remember now that old history of Makarda. Rich in scholarship and wealth, Makarda was once a center of Maháyána Buddhism. Just as Tamralipta (Tamluk) was a center of Maháyána Buddhism and an external port, so also was Makarda. Tamlukʼs Vargabhiimá is a goddess of the Buddhist period. Even though Makardaʼs Mákaŕcańd́ii (Márkańd́eyii Cámuńd́ii or Márkańd́eyii Vajratárá – both are canonized in Buddhist Tantric treatises) cannot exactly be said to be a Buddhist goddess; she is nevertheless a popular goddess from the Buddhist period.

paragraphs.text: When the Bengalees abandoned Buddhism they kept Mákaŕdácańd́ii but gave her a different name. However, the fact that Mákaŕdácańd́ii is a popular goddess from the Buddhist period is suggested by its dhyána mantra [incantation for ideation] and by its similarity to the idol. It also clearly indicates that Makarda is not from the present period.

paragraphs.text: According to some, nine islands rose in ancient times, one by one, from the depths of the Bay of Bengal. The people of Ráŕh, axes and shovels in hand, sailed there in boats, cleared the forests thereon, and set up habitation. A conglomeration of nine islands – it was named Navadviipa (nava means “nine” and dviipa means “island”). Included in these are Navadviipa, Agradviipa (Áyadá – present Hooghly District) and Madhyadviipa or Májhdiyá (Krishnaganj Police Station of Nadia District).

paragraphs.text: Some say that Raghunath Bhattacharya (Raghunath Shiromańi or Káná Raghunath), a talented son of Bengal, returned home after acquiring all the wisdom of Pakshadhar Mishra [a scholar and logician] of Mithila. The people of Bengal were delighted beyond measure at this. The pandits of Mithila would not allow anybody to copy their manuscripts on Navya Nyáya [new school of philosophy and logic], lest the pride of Mithila – the seat of Nyáya – be lost. Hearsay has it that Raghunath would copy one page of the manuscript every day and keep it hidden in the hollow of a tree. Thus he could bring along a copy of the entire manuscript when he returned. According to another opinion, Raghunath learnt the complete works by heart before he came back.

paragraphs.text: Nevertheless, thanks to Raghunath Bhattacharya, Bengal occupied the top position in matters related to Navya Nyáya. A book [on logic] was written by Vishwambhar Mishra (Mahaprabhu Chaitanyadev) also, who was the son of Jagannath Mishra. It is said that Mahaprabhuʼs treatise was even better [than one written by Raghunath]. It is said that Raghunath, on hearing this document read out to him, shed tears of sorrow. To console his friend, Mahaprabhu tore up his own manuscript and immersed it in the waters of the Ganges in Swarupganj. Thereafter he remarked, “Friend, I have sacrificed my document to the waters of the Ganges. Only your document will now survive. Stop crying.”

paragraphs.text: In any case, on Raghunathʼs return to his native land as a reputed pandit in Nyáya, the people of Bengal welcomed him by lighting nine large lamps on the bank of the Ganges. Raghunath was a product of Purvasthali in Burdwan District. In those days, Burdwan was spread across both shores of the Ganges. Even though the eastern bank was Samatat-Bagri, it was better known as Vauṋga-Ráŕh. Those nine lamps in Raghunathʼs honour were lit on the eastern bank. So thenceforth that eastern bank, instead of being called Vauṋga-Ráŕh, was called “Navadiipa” [“Nine Lamps”]. And in the course of time there evolved the present name “Nadiiyá” [spelled in English contexts “Nadia”]. As far as I can see, the name Navadviipa, signifying a group of nine islands, is more logical. But yes, whatever I have said about Raghunath is true.
summary: In any case, on Raghunathʼs return to his native land as a reputed pandit in Nyáya, the people of Bengal welcomed him by lighting nine large lamps on the bank of the Ganges.

paragraphs.text: It was in Navadviipa, on the moist soil of this same Nadia, that Mahaprabhu Chaitanyadev, whose real name is Vishwambhar Mishra, was born in the charming atmosphere of the full-moon day in the month of Phálgun. Although presently Navadviipa is politically a part of Nadia District, geographically it belongs to Burdwan District in Ráŕh. However, this was not the case when Mahaprabhu was born. The city of Navadviipa was located on the eastern bank of the river Bhagirathi – in the direction where Swarupganj is today. As the Bhagirathi has changed its course and now flows along the east of Navadviipa, the city has shifted to the west of river and has become a part of Ráŕh. Both Shriipát́h Máyápur and Navadviipa were situated on the same side of the Bhagirathi. Máyápur [Mayapur] was part of the city of Navadviipa [, but remained on the east side of the river and hence became separated]. So those who say that Mahaprabhu was born in Mayapur are correct. Also, those who say that he was born in Navadviipa are not incorrect. ( 4 ) Jagannatha Mishra, Mahaprabhuʼs father, was a Brahman from a western Vedic family of the Dháká-Daksiń village in Habigunj of the erstwhile Sylhet District. His predecessor, Arjun Mishra, had come from Mithila to Bengal at the invitation of King Shyamal Barman.
summary: It was in Navadviipa, on the moist soil of this same Nadia, that Mahaprabhu Chaitanyadev, whose real name is Vishwambhar Mishra, was born in the charming atmosphere of the full-moon day in the month of Phálgun.
Both Shriipát́h Máyápur and Navadviipa were situated on the same side of the Bhagirathi.
His predecessor, Arjun Mishra, had come from Mithila to Bengal at the invitation of King Shyamal Barman.

paragraphs.text: Jagannath Mishra had two reasons for coming to Navadviipa. One of them was the fact that his wife Shachidevi was the daughter of Nilamvar Chakravorty, a resident of Navadviipa. It was Shachideviʼs desire that her husband become a permanent resident of Navadviipa. The second reason was Jagannath Mishraʼs fondness for bathing in the Ganges. He had moved to Navadviipa with the hope that he would be able to take his bath in the Ganges till the day he breathed his last. During his stay at Dháká-Dakśiń, all of his daughters died of smallpox. He came to Navadviipa childless. Vishwarup Mishra, his first son, born when he was quite elderly, mastered vast knowledge at a young age and left home in search of spiritual treasures. His second son, who was also his last child, was Vishwambhar Mishra – the one who adopted the sannyásin name of Shriikrśńacaetanya Bháratii, in short, Mahaprabhu Chaitanyadev. His wisdom bloomed in his early youth. Like Raghunath Shiromańi, he also had in-depth knowledge of logic and philosophy. When Raghunath returned to Navadviipa as an expert in logic and philosophy, Mahaprabhu Chaitanyadev was about the same age. Subsequently, Mahaprabhu Chaitanyadev went on to study extensively subjects other than Nyáya philosophy and even propounded his own acintyabhedábheda tattva [theory of inconceivable difference in non-difference]. At the early age of eighteen, he gained reputation as a catuśpát́hii ( 5 ) pandit in Navadviipa in particular and across all of Bengal in general.

paragraphs.text: In a place called Poŕámá Talá in Navadviipa, he debated and defeated Mahápańd́ita Keshavakáshmiiri, a Sárvabhaoma pandit ( 6 ) of India of those days. It must be remembered in this context that Navadviipa or Nadia was a seat of the Shákta doctrine before the appearance of Mahaprabhu. The founding goddess of the city of Navadviipa, Poŕámá, is a Tantric goddess. After the fall of Keshavakáshmirii, Vasudeva Bandyopadhyaya was acknowledged as the Sárvabhaoma pandit of India on the strength of his vast knowledge. He became known as Vasudev Sárvabhaoma.

paragraphs.text: Mahaprabhu visited Utkala [Odisha] several times at the invitation of Prataparudradev, the king. The major part of his later life was spent in Cuttack. During his journeys to Niilácala, Mahaprabhu Chaitanyadeva stayed in Vasudev Sárvabhaomaʼs residence on several occasions. Despite the fact that Vasudev Sárvabhaoma was a very learned pandit and much older than Mahaprabhu, he regarded the latter with deep respect and honour. Neither Keshavakashmiiri nor Mahaprabhu ever entered into a debate contest with Vasudev Sárvabhaoma, nor were they inclined to be in such a position.

paragraphs.text: Though a recipient of worldwide fame, Vishwambhar Mishra, the darling of Navadviipa, was so moved by the miseries of living beings that he rushed to Kantakpura, or Kátoyá [Katwa], with the longing to sacrifice all earthly things and embrace the life of a hermit. This same Kantakpura or Katwa was a leading centre of wisdom of Ráŕh. It was here that Vishwambhar Mishra was initiated into sannyása [renunciation] by Keshav Bharati and adopted the name Shrikrishnachaitanya. During this period, Navadviipa was flooded with the lights of wisdom spread by Raghunath Shiromańi and with love for all creatures as preached by Mahaprabhu Chaitanyadev. This constituted a new recipe for life that inspired all of India. Neither Mahaprabhu nor Raghunath Shiromańi is alive, but their repository of knowledge is inextricably mixed with the life stream of Bengal. paragraphs.text: The luminaries who contributed to enhance the pride of Nadia are not just a handful. Phulia (Phulliká), located to the southeast of Nadia, was yet another centre where pandits and wise men lived. It is to this Phulia that Banamali Ojha, an inhabitant of Dhamarai (Dharmarájiká) of Dhaka-Vikramapur, came looking for an environment of learning. He was an extremely dhármika-minded person. His wife, Malini Devi, had the same love for dharma. Krittivas Mukhopadhyaya was their son. He had a vast knowledge of Sanskrit. His reputation did not remain restricted to Bengal, but spread across the whole of India. Hussain Shah, the ruler of Gaoŕa, had an intense desire to read the Rámáyańa in Bengali. However, the translation of Sanskrit into Bengali was not a matter that could be successfully tackled with a limited amount of knowledge. Hence he convened a gathering of the pandits of Gaoŕa. In this gathering, all the pandits without question acknowledged the fact that the wisest pandit was Krittivas of Phulia.

paragraphs.text: Kalikinkarʼs father, Mukundalal Kahali, was an eminent homoeopath. Kalikinkarʼs mother was a great devotee of Krśńa, and on looking at Kalikinkar, one would think that he was a devotee of the goddess Kálii. It was impossible to elicit from him the name of Krśńa or any word related to Krśńa, even by mistake, and in these matters his presence of mind was very sharp. Once, I thought that whatever Kalikinkar might do, he would not be able to distort a historical truth or a universal truth. With an intention to trap him, I told him, “Well, Kalikinkar, my knowledge of geography is very poor. Can you tell me under which police station your Majdia comes?”

paragraphs.text: I thought, let me catch Kalikinkar in another way. I said, “Kalikinkar, you must have heard that Hooghly is a district with a rich cultural heritage. It is well-nigh impossible to find the likes of it in terms of temple sculptures and fine aesthetic taste. Bankura-Manbhum (Purulia-Dhanbad-Singhbhum of the present time) has the greatest number of ancient temples. Mallabhum (the Vishnupur Subdivision of Bankura District) has the greatest number of temples. But it is difficult to find a match for the temples of Hooghly District in matters of delicate artistry and fine sensibility. Let alone the temple of Anantavásudeva, Hangseshwari of Banshbere and the Gupta Vrindaban temple of Guptipara, both the oldest church and the oldest mosque of Bengal are also situated in Hooghly District. The Imambara of Hooghly has a cultural heritage and the fame of Phurphurasharif has spread far and wide.

paragraphs.text: “Is that all, Kalikinkar? I said, “You intimately know the Ráŕh region.

paragraphs.text: “Dańd́a Bhukti has not received as much recognition in history as Varddhamána [Burdwan] Bhukti has, for various reasons. For some unknown reason, historians did not pay any great attention to Dańd́a Bhukti. If somebody wants to write the history of Dańd́a Bhukti they will see that there is so much material that if properly organized, one can write several Mahábháratas. As many famous people were born in this region, similarly there are also innumerable towns and villages of great cultural heritage here. Towards the end of the Pathan period Dańd́a Bhukti was renamed Hijli, and towards the end of the Moghul period its name was changed to Madinápur. When the British got the civil rights of Vardhaman, 24 Parganas and Chattagram, along with Madinápur, they renamed it Midnapore. In the course of time its Bengali name became Medinipur. The district, which is very large, has also made such a significant contribution to the art of town planning and civilization, not only to the entire Ráŕh region but also to the entire civilized world, that it is a veritable seat of human civilization. The sea that skirts it and the range of hills that borders the district, sloping from northwest to the southeast, led to a magnificent opulence of all kinds of earthly treasures. Starting with Kalidas, the great poet, many great people were born in this district. In the Buddhist period, Dantapurivihár of this district, the present name of which is Dáṋton, was built upon the place where a receptacle containing the relics of Buddhaʼs teeth – lay buried. It is here that Sarashanka, the most beautiful water tank, not only of the Ráŕh region but also of the entire Bengal, is situated.

footnotes.text: In undivided Bengal, Nadia had five subdivisional towns: Krishnanagar, the district headquarters, Ranaghat, Meherpur, Chuadanga and Kusthia. At the time of partition, Nadia District was divided into two: Krishnanagar Sadar and Ranaghat subdivisional towns were included in India, and the subdivisional town of Kusthia became part of Pakistan. Of the four police station areas of Meherpur subdivisional town, Karimpur and Tehatta became Indian territory, and Meherpur and Gangni became part of Pakistan. Of the five police station areas of Chuadanga, Krishnaganj became part of India and the other four police stations, that is, Chuadanga, Alamdanga, Damurhuda and Jibannagar, became part of Pakistan. In the beginning, the part of Nadia District included in Pakistan retained the name Nadia, and the district headquarters was in Kusthia. The part of Nadia retained in India was named Nabadwip District, and the district headquarters continued to be in Krishnanagar. After some time, the name of Pak-Nadia district was changed to Kusthia District. Then the name of the Indian district of Nadia was again changed from Nabadwip District back to Nadia District. From the Mughal period, the district headquarters of Nadia District was Goari-Krshnanagar. However, the capital of the maharaja of Nadia was in Gangni in the beginning (during the time of Ram Samaddar and Kali Samaddar), later it was in Matiari and then in Rewi. The name of the village of Rewi was later changed to Krishnanagar. The two villages, Goari and Ghurni, adjacent to Krishnanagar, were already there. It was Allal Dastur Pir who did the town planning for Krishnanagar.
The land formed by nine islands that surfaced from the ocean in very ancient times was named “Navadviipa” (“nine islands”), Navadviipa → Naodiia → Nadiiyá [Nadia] → Nade.

Most of our original bananas came into existence as a result of experimentation with different kinds of seedy bananas. Compared to our familiar bananas like cáṋpá, martamán, ciiniicáṋpá, kánáibáshii, málbhog, dudhiyá, the káṋt́álii kalá [káṋt́álii banana] is somewhat of recent origin. It originated from the seedy banana some 2000 years ago, during the Buddhist period in Bengal. In size, it is slightly bigger than the cáṋpá banana. Unlike cáṋpá kalá it has costae [ridges] on the skin. The cáṋpá kalá tastes a little sour, particularly after sunset, but that is not the case with káṋt́álii kalá. If properly cultivated, cáṋpá kalá yields twice a year, while káṋt́álii kalá yields twice in a year and a half. If uncared for, cáṋpá kalá remains cáṋpá kalá; only its size is reduced. But the káṋt́álii kalá, if not properly taken care of, becomes a seedy banana again. This means that its relation with the seedy banana has not yet been severed.

paragraphs.text: Midnight was upon me. It was as if the Mahákaola [the great spiritual master] was saying: “The mahánishá [great darkness] of your life has come. Throw off the earthly bondages and come out. Maybe it is not the new moon night (amánishá) but the full-moon night (púrńimá). The darkest, subtlest particles of the new moon night can be transformed into particles of moonlight. Cannot the new moon night of oneʼs life takes the form of the full moon? That terrible shadow of time that has trampled the human soul for so long, sometimes frowning outwardly, sometimes being wasted by the deep sense of ignorance, making the human being stumble on their path – is it eternal?” Truly, the Mahákaola was calling me.

paragraphs.text: I went out alone and found myself in the middle of the forest. To the south was the Damodar River and to the east was the Devidaha [big lake]. At that time this part of Burdwan District was vast marshland. Whatever it may be – pond, lake, marsh – the Devidaha does not have any comparison. The prehistoric Gáuṋguŕ [Gangur] or Behula River was a lost tributary of the Damodar River. The Behula of legend took the dead body of the imaginary Lakhindar on her lap, climbed on a raft and floated down the Gangur towards heaven. The Behula River has turned into the Devidaha of today.

paragraphs.text: I walked slowly and came to the edge of the Devidaha. The Devidaha that we are talking about was partially destroyed in the Damodar flood of 1913. It was swallowed anew by the Damodar during the time of the Second World War. The time that I am talking about was shortly before the Second World War.
summary: I walked slowly and came to the edge of the Devidaha.
It was swallowed anew by the Damodar during the time of the Second World War.

paragraphs.text: The Devidaha was created during the time when Shashanka was the king of Ráŕh. The Devidaha was not simply a large pond. Like the Damodar, Banka, Khari, Badai and other rivers, the vast waters of the Devidaha as well as the Gangur used to keep Burdwan District green with grain. Sugar cane was first cultivated in Ráŕh on both banks of the Devidaha while cotton was cultivated on its west bank. Historically, it can be seen that Burdwan District was the pioneer in sugar cane and cotton cultivation, the leading producer. The sugar cane there was sweeter than any place else. Unfortunately the farmers in Burdwan today are not so eager to cultivate sugar cane because sugar cane ties up the land for nearly the entire year, while if other crops can be grown on that same land then three harvests can be taken home [annually].
summary: The Devidaha was created during the time when Shashanka was the king of Ráŕh.
Sugar cane was first cultivated in Ráŕh on both banks of the Devidaha while cotton was cultivated on its west bank.

Unfortunately the farmers in Burdwan today are not so eager to cultivate sugar cane because sugar cane ties up the land for nearly the entire year, while if other crops can be grown on that same land then three harvests can be taken home [annually].

paragraphs.text: For the very same reason, the cultivation of both the mághii [winter] and caetii [spring] types of pigeon-peas (aŕahar dál) is fast diminishing in Burdwan. They are scarcely to be seen nowadays. Even though the Balagarh area of neighbouring Hooghly District was at one time considered the best for pigeon-pea cultivation, it bears mentioning that there also its cultivation has diminished greatly. Nowadays Purulia and Nadia Districts are preserving the standard of pigeon-pea production in Bengal. If some of the land in Purulia were not used for pigeon-peas, then it would remain barren for most of the year; thus, there is no recourse but to grow pigeon-peas there. And in Nadia the greater part of the soil is doṋyásh [mixed sandy and clayey soil]. Since there is very little clayey soil, many crops cannot be grown there. Still, in the Chakdah, Haringhata and Kalyani areas of Nadia the cultivation of both sugar cane and pigeon-peas (kandula – Kandulaḿ baladaḿ jiṋeyaḿ cośńaḿ tu hitakárakaḿ) is diminishing and kitchen vegetables are being grown in their place. Today Nadia District has turned into the worldʼs best district for growing vegetables. Of course, the traditional areas for growing potatoes have been Hooghly, Burdwan, Nalanda [Bihar] and Farukhbad [U.P.] Districts. The seeds that we import while sitting in Kolkata, such as the recently brought biliti tomato seeds from America, the difficult-to-get red radish seeds from Japan, the extremely long kuli eggplant seeds from China – some perhaps come from abroad but the better part of them are brought from Nadia Districtʼs Nagar-Ukhra, bought at bulk rate and stuffed into jute sacks.

And in Nadia the greater part of the soil is doṋyásh [mixed sandy and clayey soil].

The seeds that we import while sitting in Kolkata, such as the recently brought biliti tomato seeds from America, the difficult-to-get red radish seeds from Japan, the extremely long kuli eggplant seeds from China – some perhaps come from abroad but the better part of them are brought from Nadia Districtʼs Nagar-Ukhra, bought at bulk rate and stuffed into jute sacks.

paragraphs.text: The variety of cotton plant which was known as deva-kápás in Burdwan has the longest fibres and is suitable for making the finest thread. The climate of Burdwan is somewhat drier than that of the rest of Bengal, thus those areas which are wetter than Burdwan used to buy cotton thread from Burdwan for weaving fine cloth. Cotton does not grow well in wetter climates; the cotton is subject to insect attack. However, these wetter climates are more suitable for weaving fine cloth. Thus Burdwan was not as famous for the weaving of cloth as it was for the production of cotton. This is not Burdwanʼs fault; its weather is to be blamed. This situation continued unchecked up until the time of Akbar.
summary: The variety of cotton plant which was known as deva-kápás in Burdwan has the longest fibres and is suitable for making the finest thread.
However, these wetter climates are more suitable for weaving fine cloth.
This situation continued unchecked up until the time of Akbar.

paragraphs.text: I went and sat under a huge silk-cotton tree on the western bank of the Devidaha. Behind me stretched a vast, dense jungle. This jungle stretched up to my village in one direction, and to the Damodar River in the other. It does not do justice to simply call it a jungle – it was a dense jungle. There were large snakes in the jungle, not large but medium-sized tigers, wild boars, and the niilgái and krśńasár varieties of antelope. The roaring of tigers could be heard at night from the courtyard of my house.
summary: I went and sat under a huge silk-cotton tree on the western bank of the Devidaha.
It does not do justice to simply call it a jungle – it was a dense jungle.
The roaring of tigers could be heard at night from the courtyard of my house.

paragraphs.text: I was sitting on the western bank of the Devidaha, a short way from the village of Pátun, the village of Maharshi Patanjali, the propounder of Seshvara Sáḿkhya philosophy. Patanjali had not been satisfied with the Sáḿkhya philosophy of Kapil. Kapil did not say anything clearly one way or the existence of Parama Puruśa though he accepted His existence. Patanjali openly acknowledged His existence.
summary: I was sitting on the western bank of the Devidaha, a short way from the village of Pátun, the village of Maharshi Patanjali, the propounder of Seshvara Sáḿkhya philosophy.
Kapil did not say anything clearly one way or the existence of Parama Puruśa though he accepted His existence.

paragraphs.text: I sat and thought for a while about Patanjali. On the other side of the Devidaha I saw six or seven wild boars drinking water. A short distance from me was a large crocodile, half in and half out of the water; he seemed to be staring in a certain direction.

On the other side of the Devidaha I saw six or seven wild boars drinking water.
A short distance from me was a large crocodile, half in and half out of the water; he seemed to be staring in a certain direction.

paragraphs.text: I was alone and solitary. I didnʼt see any other living creatures in the vicinity, nor did I hear any tiger roars. A short distance away ran the ruined remains of the Badshahi Road, the same road that Pathan Badshah Shershah constructed at the beginning of the Mughal era, with only a few skeletal traces left to identify it. Burdwan was then the capital of the province of Bengal. Badshahi Road used to connect Burdwan to Delhi in one direction, and in the other direction it connected to the principal port of the time, Saptagrám or Sátgáoṋ, to which the Portuguese gave the name Port-de-Grandee – it extended south along the Bhagirathi till Shyampur, and on the other bank it used to go via Jessore to Dhaka Districtʼs Suvarnagram (Sońárgáoṋ). At that time Hooghly was part of Burdwan District.
summary: I was alone and solitary.
Burdwan was then the capital of the province of Bengal.
At that time Hooghly was part of Burdwan District.

paragraphs.text: How busy Badshahi Road used to be! Gazing in the direction of the road, I thought back to how many horse-carts used to travel along it at one time, how many marriage processions, how many richly ornamented, newly-married brides, how many funeral bearers – the finality of the human beingʼs existence is reduced to ashes and those ashes were left to float in the waters of the Bhagirathi. Today the Badshahi Road is abandoned; some can recognize it if they see it, and some cannot.

points.body: The Aryans were not the original inhabitants of the present India. When the Aryans entered India through the Northwest Frontier Province, they contemptuously called the indigenous population whom they defeated in battle, “Anáryas” [“Non-Aryans”]. The appellation “Anáryas” did not apply to any group in particular, but rather to all the then inhabitants of India in general: the Mongolians, the Austrics and the Dravidians (a mixture of Austric and Negro). My discourse today will give a brief overview of the transformation that occurred in the civilizations of these peoples after the arrival of the Aryans, and of the effect that the Aryan migration had on the Aryans themselves. I will try to concentrate particularly upon the influence of Tantra on the Aryans.

points.body: The original home of the Aryans was in the northern part of Central Asia. By descent they were a fair, tall and healthy race. They were people of nomadic nature whose main means of subsistence was hunting. When, however, it became impossible for them to procure enough food by hunting, they started rearing cattle. But the merciless nature of Central Asia made their lives unbearable: snowstorms diminished the numbers both of their people and of their animals, and there was a chronic shortage of animal fodder. Just to survive, they had to spend almost all their time collecting food. Not only did this acute food shortage force them to make unending efforts as a group to collect food and rear cattle, it also led to perpetual inter-group skirmishes and even slaughter.

points.body: The constant fighting during this period, this kśatriya-dominated era, led to the eventual emergence of a class of intellectuals who greatly assisted the kśatriya-dominated society. They provided the kśatriya leaders with new inventions and discoveries, and satisfied their mental hunger by sharing their knowledge and wisdom. In the language of the day, these intellectuals were called rśis. The group leaders bowed their heads in reverence before these mighty intellectuals and followed the precepts framed by them. The society used to call their ideology Árśa Dharma [Religion of the Sages].

points.body: All their gods and goddesses were laokik figures [creations of the people]. They arose out of the peoples' worldly needs. Hence the storm, the thunder, the lightning, the rain, the sun, and the moon were all their gods. In that era of undeveloped science what they feared most was the darkness of night, so they not only regarded the night and the evening as their gods, they actually revered them as well. In their fear, they would try to escape from the darkness by making fire with flint. They would never dare to displease the night and the evening, so whenever they made a fire they would first make obeisance to the evening with the fire before doing anything else. At night's end, when the eastern horizon glowed red, the Aryans would sing the song of the dawn in unison. Aruńa, the mythological charioteer of the sun's seven-horsed chariot (the seven horses corresponding to the seven distinct colours of the sun's rays), was also their god, as, indeed, was the sun itself.

points.body: As the southern part of Kashmiira was littered with pebbles resembling the jambu fruit [Eugenia jambolana Lam], the Aryans named it “Jambu Dviipa” (modern Jammu). Subsequently, Jambu Dviipa came to mean the whole of India. Possibly in the sandy beds of the many rivers that transect Jambu Dviipa they discovered gold for the first time, and so gold came to be known as jámbunada. When still later they settled throughout the entire land of India, they realized that it was ideal not only for habitation, but also for self-development. Thus they named it “Bháratavarśa”. Bhara means “that which feeds”; ta means “that which gives”, or “that which helps in the process of expansion”; and varśa means “a vast stretch of land”. Thus, bháratavarśa means “a vast expanse of land which helps in the all-round development of its inhabitants”.

points.body: The inconvenience that the non-Indian Aryans had faced for want of script no doubt disappeared after the Indianized Aryans learned it, but owing to their old superstitions, most of the Aryans were reluctant to put the Vedas in black and white. They refused to believe that the reason that the Vedas were not written at the time of their composition was simply the lack of script. They adhered to their illogical reasoning even after the scripts came into being: they thought that the rśis had not written out the Vedas, one, because it was improper, and two, because the Vedas were named shruti. However, much later, in Kashmiira, ( 1 ) the Vedas were written down in the Sáradá script in use there at the time. There was really no alternative to writing them down, because there was almost nobody left who knew all the Vedas by heart, and the number of people who knew even parts of them was very small. When the Kashmiira scholars finally did write down the Vedas, it was discovered that many parts of them were missing for good.
