points.body: Let us discuss the science of colour. In Saḿskrta language there are two similar words: varńa and rága. Though the meanings are approximately the same, they are not completely synonymous. Varńa means colour (what is termed in Bengali as rauṋg). But this word varńa does not indicate the colour which will colour other objects as well; an object has its own colour but its colour may not necessarily dye other objects. But the word rága means that particular colour which can dye other objects also. So the inner spirit of the science of colour in Vaeshnavii Tantra is this – that each and every expression of this universe has its own rhythm, its own vibration, its own sound, and its own colour, and thus it has its own form as well. And as it has its own sound, it has a particular sweetness of its own. Suppose there is a person who is dumb but very good; and there is another person who is equally good, but speaks well also. Obviously you will prefer the second man, because he possesses the power of expression. Dumb people can give expression to their inner thoughts only with their gestures and postures, whereas those who can speak can express themselves with gesture, posture, and also language. A dumb person can only look at you and express through gesture to come to him, but a person who can speak can say, “Come little child, come to me.” This vocal expression of the second person conveys more sweetness.

points.body: When Tantra was first invented, there was only one science of Tantra; but later various cults emerged according to their respective philosophical viewpoints. Each had a different name although their inner spirit was the same: for instance, Baoddha Tantra, Jaina Tantra, and in later times Shaeva Tantra, Shákta Tantra, Saora Tantra, Gáńapatya Tantra, Vaeśńviiya Tantra, etc. The inner idea of the Vaeśńaviiya Tantra is that there is form and colour (both rága and varńa) in the rhythmic expressions of Parama Puruśa, and those cosmic rhythms also have a sweet sonic vibration. This sonic vibration is instrumental in giving expression to various other forms in this universe as well. The resonance of the collective vibrations of the universe is called the flute sound of Krśńa, another name for oṋḿkára, the cosmic sound which reaches the ears of spiritual aspirants in various ways. When human beings attain spiritual progress step by step, they will also hear this sound with their own ears.

points.body: The scriptures on devotion emphatically insist that only He knows the answer, no one else. It is a fact that human beings with their limited intellect can never understand the secrets of why and how Parama Puruśa has been creating this universe; their wisdom can never fathom this mystery. That is why the scriptures say, “Be a good person, but do not be foolish. Be intelligent and clever.” Now what is the clever approach? Just as on the one hand you are moving towards Parama Puruśa to attain Him by concentrating your mind through mudrá, práńáyáma and kiirtana, at the same time you should constantly remember why He is creating all these things, and what is your relation with Him. You should think, “My little intellect cannot fathom all this – rather let me do one thing, let me establish a relation of sweet love with Him. However, [during the later of these periods] Bengali became prevalent for matters related to the general public. From the Pathan period onwards, the language of the court became Persian; but Bengali remained the peopleʼs language. During British rule, English became the language of the court, yet Bengali continued to be used as language for matters relating to the common people, and this is still the practice today. Since the proceedings of the court continued to be conducted for a long time in Sanskrit, many legal terms are still in Sanskrit. Neglecting those words and attempting to create new terminologies are simply a waste of time and energy.

points.body: To the south of Samantabhum and Shikharbhum, three kingdoms existed side by side. One was Mallabhum. (The Vishnupur Subdivision of present Bankura District; the kings bore the surname “Malla”, which is why the kingdom was called “Mallabhum”.) Exactly to its west was Senbhum, consisting of Bankura Subdivisional headquarters and parts of Purulia and Midnapur Districts. The kings were Vaidyas with “Sen” as their surname. That is why the name of the kingdom was “Senbhum”. Its ancient capital was Senpahari. Later, King Banku Roy set up a new capital at the confluence of the Darakeshwar and Gandheshwari Rivers, and the new capital was called Bankura after the king, Banku Roy.

points.body: To the west of Senbhum was Manbhum or Paiṋcakot́, [also known as] Páchet́i Kingdom or Páiṋcet Kingdom. Later, the kingdom was named Manbhum after King Mansinghadev, and its capital was Manbazar. To the north of the kingdom was the river Damodar, to the south Barahabhum, to the east the Sushunia Hills, and to the west Jharkhand or Chut́iá-Nagpur. The western boundary of Manbhum was near Angara where the hills ended and the plains of Ranchi began.

points.body: To the south of Mallabhum, Senbhum and Manbhum was Shabarbhum (Midnapur). Shabars, that is, Kheriá Muńd́á kings, ruled the kingdom. To the west of Shabarbhum was Dhabalbhum, which consisted of Jhargram Subdivision of the present Midnapur District, part of the present Bankura District, and Dhabalbhum Subdivision (Tatanagar) of the present Jharkhand State. The surname of the kings was “Dhabaldev”. For this reason, the kingdom was named “Dhabalbhum”.

points.body: Adjacent to the north and northwestern extremities of Dhabalbhum was Barahabhum (Barabhum). Its capital was Barahabazar (Barabazar). Two Muńd́á brothers, Adibaraha and Keshbaraha, founded the kingdom. Barahabhum Kingdom consisted of the southern part of the present-day Purulia District, Chandil of Singbhum District and Patamda, and the Ichagar and Nimdih Police Stations of Singhbhum District. The kingdom is surrounded by the Dalma Hills range. Very ancient relics of the Bengali language and script have been found and are still being found, largely in Barahabhum. On the western side of Dhabalbhum was Singbhum. The kings of that kingdom belonged to the Kole sub-tribe. Singbhum was bifurcated some time before the Pathan era. The western part retained the name of Singbhum, and the eastern part was named Porahat. (The Keraikela kingdom, situated southeast of Ranchi District, was included.) Later, the Porahat kingdom split in two parts – the western part was called Kharsoan and the eastern part Seraikela. To the south of the Dhabalbhum and Porahat kingdoms was Bhanjabhum (the current name is Mayurbhanja). Since the kings of that kingdom used the surname Bhanjadeo, it was named “Bhanjabhúm”. They used the peacock symbol in their thrones and crowns and in the ornaments of their queens, so the kingdom later came to be called “Mayurbhanj”. ( 2 )

This portion was once called the kingdom of Bhurisreśt́ha [Bhurishreshtha]. Today we colloquially call it Bhurshut. The capital, Gar Mandaran, was located where the Amodar River, which originates from Sumudrabandh [Lake], converges with the Damodar.

points.body: From very ancient days to the time of the Sen dynasty, the kings of Ráŕh were practically independent. Of course, they used to pay a nominal tribute (nazráńá) to the king of Gaoŕa (Bengal) or, if not paying so, would accept in writing the sovereignty of the king. I came across the ruins of an ancient Jain Shiva temple at Mardu village in the Silli Police Station on the banks of the Suvarnarekha River, in the ancient kingdom of Manbhum or Panchakot. I also found near the house of a Muńd́á villager, a stone statue of Dákśáyańii. Dákśáyańii was the state goddess of Bengal during the Sur dynasty, which means that Manbhum Kingdom acknowledged the sovereignty of the Sur kings of Gaoŕa. During the Pathan rule, most of the kingdoms of Ráŕh were independent principalities. Only under the Mughals did these principalities accept the suzerainty of the nawab of Bengal. They paid only a nominal tribute to him. In Bhurshut, the Mughal rulers had tremendous influence. Burdwan, in Bhurshut, was the capital of Bengal a number of times. [Some say] the word “Burdwan” came from [the Persian] bár-e-diiván. The British spelled it “Burdwan”. Previously the name of this administrative division was Sharifabad.

points.body: In those days, the bhúmyadhikáriis or bhaomiks (bhaomik → bhouaṋa → bhuṋiá) [landlords] of Bengal struggled hard to maintain their independence. King Pratapaditya of Jessore, King Kandarpanarayana of Chandradvip, King Lakshmanmanikya of Bhulua, and also Isha Khan, Kedar Roy and Sitaram Roy were amongst them. It is difficult to say what the outcome would have been had all these kings cooperated with each other. However, as each of them fought alone, they were defeated.

points.body: The king of Jaipur, Raja Man Singh, entered into an agreement with Akbar, the emperor in Delhi, and became commander-in-chief of the Mughal army. There were twelve [kings] who were particularly prominent. Raja Man Singh took upon himself the onerous responsibility of subduing these twelve. He defeated Pratapaditya of Jessore and carried off the statue of Yashoreshvarii, the guardian deity of Jessore. He installed her in the Ambar Fort of Jaipur, bringing the Bengalee priest of the temple along with her. It was Raja Man Singh who built the Ramnakali, or Dhakeshvari, temple in Dacca.

points.body: When King Jagatnarayan of Bhurshut saw other rulers of Bengal in rebellion against Mughal rule, he too became encouraged to revolt. The nawab of Bengal used to stay sometimes in Burdwan and sometimes in Dhaka. One commander [under the nawab] was posted in Dhaka, one in Gaoŕa [Samatat], one in Burdwan and another in Azimabad (the present Patna city). Emperor Akbar separated Suba Bihar from Suba Bengal, so Azimabad was no longer part of Bengal. A new nawab was posted in Azimabad. Many soldiers were transferred to this newly-established capital from the Burdwan Commissionary [in Bhurshut].

points.body: King Jagatnarayan decided to declare independence, taking advantage of the circumstances. This decision was welcomed by his ministers, as well as his own queen, Bhavasundari. Everyone agreed that when Bhurishrestha was superior to many other principalities and had a glorious heritage of its own – in art and architecture, in wisdom, in literature and in all spheres of life – then surely it should declare its independence to uphold its dignity. Bhurishrestha was the best not only in name, it had then reached the pinnacle of glory in agriculture and industry, trade and commerce, education and knowledge, etc. Why should such a kingdom remain under the bondage of the far-off Delhi emperor? Why should it not launch a struggle to assert its own sovereignty and dignity?

The Ugra Kśatriyas, Sadgopes, Máhiśyas and Bágdis of Bengal volunteered for the army. They shouted the slogan, “Outsiders stay out! Bhurishreshtha has never submitted and never will.”

points.body: Akbar sensed danger. Bhurshut was the most fertile and prosperous territory within his empire. Bhurshut produced the largest crops of sugar cane, the most raw sugar, the largest crops of cotton, the most cloth, the largest crops of rice paddy, the largest mining output and the most silk, all of which the merchants used to export abroad, making huge profits. Akbar would collect a huge fortune for the royal treasury by levying taxes on those merchants. As such, the important Bhurshut could not be allowed to secede from the empire.

points.body: The emperor sent his commander-in-chief, Man Singh, to suppress the rebellion. Even at that time the journey to Burdwan from Delhi or Agra was not difficult. During the middle part of the Mughal era there had suddenly emerged a mighty Pathan emperor, Shershah Suri. He was an intelligent ruler and a prominent mass leader. He introduced radical agrarian reforms by popularizing the system of leasing land. He built a long, broad highway from Suvarna Gram in Dacca via Kalighat, Sutanuti and Govindapur, and from there through Howrah and Burdwan to Delhi and up to Attak, Punjab. In those days people used to call this royal highway variously such names as the Benares Road, the Kashi Road, or the Kingʼs Road. The British called it the Grand Trunk Road [in short G.T. Road]. Man Singh with his large army marched to Burdwan along this highway.

points.body: It is Burdwan which emerged and developed in prehistoric times. The Rgveda does not mention it. Astiknagar, referred to in the Yajurveda, is the ancient name of this Burdwan. Astiknagar and Kanchannagar – both these names were prevalent side by side. Astiknagar and Kanchannagar now lie buried under the earth. One can still hear groans from the graves of this city. It is this very Burdwan where King Chandraketu ruled during the Mahábhárata era. Bithur (Briśt́ipur) or Prayag (Allahabad), the oldest town in North India, had not yet been built. Of course, Mathura existed, but it emerged in the post-Vedic era. It is the same Burdwan that was resplendent with pride and glory during the rule of Ashoka and Chandragupta. And it is in this very Burdwan, then the capital of Gaoŕa, where the great king Vikramaditya used to hear [stories] from the lips of Betal [a legendary figure].

points.body: During the Buddhist era, when Sanskrit was transmuted into Mágadhii Prákrta, the name of Astiknagar became Atthinagar. When the Buddhist era began, Vardhaman Mahavir visited Astiknagar. He was the son of the famous tradesman, Siddhartha, of Vaishali town in the land of Videha. His motherʼs name was Trishala. For several years in Magadh, Vardhaman Mahavir preached his ideals, his religious doctrines, his precept that “non-violence is the supreme dharma,” and his doctrine of nirgrantha [nudism]. The people of Magadh could not accept his excessive non-violence or his doctrine of nirgrantha.

points.body: In those days, the residents of Magadh used to follow the path of argument [and debate.] The reasons for which Magadh could not accept the Vedas were the same as for its rejection of Vardhaman Mahavirʼs nirgrantha doctrine (the Digambar doctrine) and its obsession with non-violence. Vardhaman Mahavir came to Atthinagar, and preached his religious ideas there for seven long years. For the same purpose, he went from Atthinagar to even as far as Swamisthan. Swamisthan later became a sacred religious place for the Jains. The present name of Swamisthan is Sáiṋthiyá (Sainthia). The well-to-do vaeshyas [merchants] of Atthinagar, who were extremely fascinated by him, changed the name of their town to Vardhaman (Burdwan). At that time, for a brief period Pandua was the capital of Ráŕh, and later on Mahanad [of Hooghly District].

points.body: Since then, the name “Vardhaman” has remained. During Akbarʼs time, the name “Vardhaman” became “Bar-e-diwan” (from which has come the English name “Burdwan”), which is a slightly distorted form of “Vardhaman”.

points.body: Man Singh pitched his tents at Shákt́igar ( 4 ) [Shaktigarh]. The news of the arrival of the Mughal army reached Mandaran. Mandaran is not very far from Shaktigarh. If one proceeds a little farther east along the bank of the Damodar, one soon reaches Mandaran. It was just at the confluence of the Damodar and the Amodar. King Jagatnarayanʼs courage was deflated when he heard the news of Raja Man Singhʼs arrival. His bravery waned; he stopped bragging and boasting about his military strength. He called his ministers and said, “I am just a small castor-oil plant. How can I dare to fight against the huge banyan tree? I want you to send a messenger with a white flag to Man Singh at Shaktigarh. I want to unconditionally surrender. The sun of Bhurishresthaʼs days of glory are over. It will never again see the glorious dawn.”

points.body: Queen Bhavasundari received the news through the prime minister. She immediately rushed to Jagatnarayan. She said, “It is not a question of your personal honour, neither is it a question of the honour of the kingdom. It is a question of the dignity of the whole country of Bengal. Moreover, it is not merely a matter of prestige; it is for the survival of the entire Bengalee race. I beg you to summon all your courage and rise to the occasion. We are all with you. Whether you win or lose, the honour of Bengal will be enhanced.”

points.body: King Jagatnarayan took no heed of his queenʼs advice. Rather he remonstrated, saying, “You are just a woman who should keep to [your] inner apartments. How little you know and understand about warfare – donʼt meddle in these delicate issues. Itʼs better to go back to the royal apartments and attend to the petty household duties.” Bhavasundari turned away with a heavy heart. A violent storm was raging in her mind. She could not bear to sit silent, so she called the council of ministers to the royal apartments.

The honour and prestige of all Bengal depends on you and me. Under these circumstances, are you willing to go to Man Singh at Shákt́igaŕ carrying a white flag in hand?”

points.body: The emperorʼs forces had already reached Shákt́igaŕ, a village just beside the Grand Trunk Road. I have said before that the Grand Trunk Road was a cobblestone road. There were no metalled roads in those days to be found either in India or anywhere else in the world. Some time after the death of Akbar, Emperor Jahangir surfaced the road with stones and gravel. That gravel was collected from the quarries of Birbhum. However, when the battle was fought with the forces of Mansingh, there was no imperial highway cobbled with gravel.

points.body: Speaking of Jahangir brings to mind a few more stories. Jahangir was a man of extremes, both in merits and demerits. He had many positive qualities, along with a cornucopia of defects. This son of Akbarʼs Rajput wife, as a prince, was known as Selim. An alcoholic with an impetuous nature, Selim cared little for any rules. Several times Emperor Akbar received complaints that Prince Selim was not offering prayers [namáz in Islamic parlance] and not observing rozá [holy fasting from sunrise to sundown during the month of Ramadan] and was an extreme alcoholic. Emperor Akbar usually did not interfere in anyoneʼs religious affairs. Thus Selimʼs waywardness was on the rise.

points.title: At that time Burdwan was the capital of Bengal, and Sher Afghan was the governor

Although Sher Afghanʼs name included “Afghan”, the family had come from Persia.

points.body: At that time Burdwan was the capital of Bengal, and Sher Afghan was the governor. His wife, Meher-Un-Nisa, was a Persian lady. This exquisitely beautiful woman fell into many hands before coming to India and was at last married to Sher Afghan. Although Sher Afghanʼs name included “Afghan”, the family had come from Persia. Hence though they spoke Bengali in public, they spoke Persian at home. Urdu had not yet become the state language of India; it became the state language starting from the time of Shahjahan.

points.title: Prince Selim had his eyes on Meher-Un-Nisa
points.prompt: Recall and explain from memory: Prince Selim had his eyes on Meher-Un-Nisa
summary: Prince Selim had his eyes on Meher-Un-Nisa.
In those days, Báṋká was a lively river.
The recently discovered Bardhamaneshvar Shiva is a very ancient Jain Shiva.
points.body: Prince Selim had his eyes on Meher-Un-Nisa. He tried several times to snatch her by force from Sher Afghan. Emperor Akbar expressed his extreme displeasure and severely rebuked Selim for this. After Akbarʼs death, there was no one to keep Selim in check. He took the name of Emperor Jahangir and occupied the throne of Delhi. After becoming the emperor, his first act was to lead an army to Burdwan. With his army, he reached Burdwan by the royal highway. He asked Sher Afghan to hand over Meher-Un-Nisa. Sher Afghan refused and a fierce battle followed. It was fought in the northeastern part of the then Burdwan. From Baje Pratappur to Kanai Natshal – this extensive area turned into a battle field. Plenty of blood was shed in this fierce battle. Thousands of innocent soldiers, who had nothing whatsoever to do with either Selimʼs appetites or Sher Afghanʼs honour, died. In those days, Báṋká was a lively river. In addition, it was the rainy season. It is said that thousands of bodies of slaughtered soldiers, without being buried, were set afloat in the river Báṋká. Sher Afghan died where the present Burdwan railway station stands. Since thousands of people died at that spot, the residents of Burdwan deserted the place. No one would go anywhere near it after dark. The place came alive only after the railway station came into existence. After the construction of the Curzon gate, the town gradually extended towards the east. One after another, several small and large mountains run parallel to each other. The summit of the second mountain was the highest place among them. I used to arrive there in the middle of the afternoon and stay there until about eight at night. Then I would climb through the gáb (a large variety of kendu or mangosteen) forest that lay in the valley between two mountains. In this valley there was also a small lake. First I would cross the mountain, passing by the right side of the lake, and then I would take a shortcut back home.

Behind me, that is, to the east, there was a high plateau that was completely covered with woods. Most of the trees were sal [Shorea robusta], piyál (piyáshál) [Mimosa odoratassima], and palásh [Butea monosperma]. In front of me, that is, to the west, on the slope of the mountain, was a dense gáb forest. After that, in the valley in front, was an old tamarind tree. Other than this, there was very little vegetation. The mountain in front was completely barren.

points.body: “There was one more thing worth mentioning about these last days of Mughal political dominance. The Bengalee people were unable to consider the family of the nawab of Murshidabad as their own. No matter how much fuss and bother the writers and historians of today make over Siraj, the family of Murshidabadʼs nawab was very distant from the common people of Bengal. It was not only that they were Urdu-speaking immigrant Shias; ( 7 ) though they had settled in Bengal and were Bengalees in the eyes of the law, they did not think of themselves as Bengalees. They called the Bengalees ”rustics“ or ”Muslim rustics” (cáśá Musalmán). ( 8 ) Of course, they learned to speak Bengali, more or less, so that they could communicate with these Muslim rustics, but at home they spoke Urdu or a corrupted form of Urdu that was mixed with Bengali, and put on airs that they were not out-of-fashion Bengalees. This mental attitude kept them quite removed from the common people.

points.body: “Neither Viirendravijaya nor Viireshavijaya could support Mir Jafar. Mir Jafar was an undisciplined, power-hungry, spineless drunkard. His main preoccupation was to keep his nawabship intact by whatever means possible. For some time after his death the throne of Bengal was thrown into confusion. Thereafter Mir Qasim became the nawab. His conduct was spirited, his behaviour showed individuality, and he was a man of strong character. Viireshavijaya came into contact with him and Mir Qasim, touched by his sincerity, befriended him. ”In those days the throne was the nawabʼs in name only. The power was in the hands of the East India Company; the administration was in the hands of the nawab but the economic power was not. Moreover, if one was to repel the East India Company, it would not be possible to accumulate power by sitting in Murshidabad because Murshidabad was right next to the East India Companyʼs chief outpost. Viireshavijaya advised Mir Qasim to shift his capital from Murshidabad to Monghyr. He did not advise him to move his capital to Azimabad (Patna) because Azimabad was, to some extent, a centre for the East India Company.

points.body: “There were one or two other reasons for making Monghyr the capital of Bengal. During the time of the Mahábhárata, when Angadesh was first accepted as an independent kingdom, Duryodhana made Karna the king of Angadesh, and rather than consider him a vassal, he allowed him to wear the crown of a sovereign king. Since ancient times the Anga region was not considered part of northern India. Neither Anga, Vauṋga nor Kalinga were considered part of northern India. Starting from this time, Anga was declared an appendix, or auṋga, of northern India and hence its name became ”Auṋgadesha”. Vauṋga remained outside of northern India. Kalinga gained acceptance as a part of southern India. Thus even today, Oriya Brahmins are sometimes known as Dakśińátya Vedic Brahmins in Bengal. At the time of Karna the capital of Angadesh was Champakanagar. ( 9 ) Karna also founded an auxiliary capital in Mudgagiri (mudgagiri → muuṋgagiri → muuṋgir → muuṋger), on the western border of the kingdom of Anga. Hence Monghyr has a tradition as a capital. ( 10 )

points.title: “When Gujaratʼs Rastrakuts [a royal dynasty] defeated eastern India, then Angadesh came…

points.body: “When Gujaratʼs Rastrakuts [a royal dynasty] defeated eastern India, then Angadesh came under their jurisdiction. The Khirkhiriya Hills that we are sitting on were the eastern boundary of the Rastrakut kingdom. Thus they established a capital in their border city of Muṋgagiri. So we see that Monghyr became a capital more than once. At that time the road system of Bengal, as well as India, was not at all developed. The long highway Shershah built that extended from Suvarnagram in Dhaka District to the city of At́ak [Attak] in western Punjab via Teota (Manikganj Subdivision) and Howrah-Burdwan, and passing by Kolkata, did not afford much convenience to Murshidabad, Monghyr or Patna, but Monghyrʼs water-route transport system was good. The waterway worked well all the way from Dhaka to Benares-Allahabad passing via Narayanganj, Teota, Rampur, Boyaliya (Rajsahi), Lalagola Ghat, Godagarii Ghat, Chapaghati, Rajmahal (at one time Rajmahal was the capital of Bengal), Bhagalpur, Monghyr and Azimabad. Benares and Allahabad used to be aided by the Shershah-built Badshahii Road. Thus, since Monghyr was marked as an important centre of water transport, the capital could be established there without any communication problems as such.

points.body: “Mir Qasim accepted Viireshavijayaʼs reasoning and moved the capital to Monghyr. On Viireshavijayaʼs advice, the nawab set about preparing the capital in Monghyr with great speed and began constructing his armoury. A great fortress was built in Monghyr as well as a munitions factory, heavy-weapons arsenal, huge parade grounds (Karheya Maidan or Kora Maidan), and a new cultural centre, Kasimbazar. The East India Company recognized the danger. Seizing on various small pretexts they declared war against Mir Qasim. They had economic power and were prepared for war – the nawab had nothing. He had just begun organizing. On the other side, the East India Company had concentrated their power at Fort William in Kolkata and in Alinagar (present-day Alipur, now a part of Kolkata).

points.body: “The first battle was a trifling affair; it took place in Katwa and the nawab was defeated. The second battle took place in Gheriya and there also the nawab was defeated. The third took place in Udhuya or in the Udhuyanala. The East India Company advanced along the Ganges in the direction of Monghyr. A great battle took place in the Dakra Canal. With his finger, my visitor pointed out to me the Dakra Canal which originated on the western border of the Khirkhiriya Hills and joined the Ganges a little to the west of Monghyr. In reality, the Dakra was not a canal but a river. In the East India Company records it is mistakenly called a canal. At the time of the monsoon deluge, the water of the Ganges goes upstream through the Dakra River and floods a wide area in Monghyr District. At the time my visitor pointed out the Dakra Canal there was heavy flooding.

points.body: “When the nawab was defeated in the battle of Dakra Canal he started heading by water for Azimabad. The map and plans of the next battle site remained in the hands of Viireshavijaya. ( 11 ) The southern border was the source of the Chandan River, a little to the north of Deoghar. On the western border was Ramdiri and Shamhodira (Samidhá) near Beguserai, and the eastern border was the Rajmahal Hills near Sahebganj where they approach the Ganges. The Rajmahal Hill Range occupies a large area in eastern Angadesh. Their eastern branch stops abruptly near Sahebganj and the Ganges; its western branch ends near Monghyr by the side of the Ganges. The western branchʼs Sanskrit name is the Kśirakśiriká Hills. In Auṋgiká [Angika] they are called Khirkhiriya Hills and in English the Kharagpur Hills. The Kharagpur Hills are a branch of the Rajmahal Hills.

The Chekáchekii dialect is spoken in the far eastern region where the Rajmahal Hills approach the Ganges near Sahebganj, and in the western border area where the Khirkhiriya Hills stop near the Ganges. Miirzachauki, near Sahebganj, was at the border of the provinces of Bengal and Bihar during the time of Akbar. Miirzachauki was a busy checkpost. It occupied a narrow strip of land between the Ganges and the mountains and thus was an ideal spot for a checkpost. The Muṋgeriyá dialect is prevalent west of the Khirkhiriya Hills in the Dakra River Basin.

points.body: “Besides these, there are also two mixed sub-dialects of Angika: The first is the Shriipuriyá sub-dialect, which is used in the region lying between Purnea and Kisanganj. Purneaʼs language is Angika, and Bengali is the language of Kisanganj. The Shriipuriyá language that is spoken in the interlying areas is a mixture of Angika and Rauṋapurii Bengali (Suryapurii). The second sub-dialect is the Northern Khot́t́á dialect, which is used in the region between Katihar and Maldah. The language of Katihar is Angika, and in Maldah, Bengali. In certain places between the two one can find this Northern Khot́t́á sub-dialect. It is a mixture of Angika and Shershahabad Bengali. In Muṋgeriyá Angika one can find some influence of Magahi. Similarly, in the Magahi of the Kiul River Basin there is some influence of Angika.”

points.body: “I am that Viireshavijaya Vasumálika,” he replied. Saying this, he threw himself into the water. The rapids flung his body around violently and carried him off towards a deep cavern. After that his body sank and disappeared from sight. A sudden strong gust of wind blew at my back from the direction of the forest. Then the gust of wind started blowing towards the mountain in front of me. All around me I could hear the sound soṋ, soṋ, soṋ [sound of the wind]. If someone else had been there they would not have heard anything else, but in the middle of this soṋ-soṋ sound I could hear Viireshavijayaʼs last words “má-má-má go” [mother, mother, oh my dear mother]. With steadfast eyes I looked at the rapids. Unknowingly, my eyes lit upon a few drops of water. In all directions one could hear the hills reverberating with the sound – má-má-má go.

points.body: I think it is important to mention here that the diamond which is known as Kohinúr [Koh-i-Noor] was the locket [pendant] on Shrii Krśńaʼs jewelled necklace. After many battles and campaigns it came into the hands of Nadir Shah, and thereafter Punjabkesharii Ranjit Singh. After him, Jhindan acquired it, and finally it came into the hands of the East India Company. They had it cut and polished in Holland and then had it set in the British Royal Crown, although some people are of the opinion that it was not set in the crown but was preserved in a different location. Whatever the case may be, Krśńaʼs kaostúbhamańi and the kohinúr are one and the same.

points.body: Nurjahan was a Persian lady. This uncommonly beautiful woman was sold by her father in India. Her real name was Meher-Un-Nisa. During Akbarʼs time, Burdwan ( 2 ) was the capital of Bengal. It was during this time that she was married to Sher Afgan, the governor (or subedar) of Bengal. Selim, the son of Akbarʼs Rajput wife (later known as Jahangiir ( 3 ) after ascending the throne), put pressure on Sher Afgan to surrender Meher-Un-Nisa to him, but Sher Afgan did not agree. There followed a fierce battle in Burdwan between Sher Afgan and the Mughal army. ( 4 ) Sher Afgan was slain in the battle (his grave is still in Burdwan city) and Jahangiir forcibly abducted Meher-Un-Nisa. At first Meher-Un-Nisa refused to marry her husbandʼs killer, Jahangiir, but later, under pressure of circumstances, she agreed.

summary: “I am a child of Magadh.

points.body: “I am a child of Magadh. History has never done full justice to this land of Magadh. Every dust particle of its villages and markets is mixed with the gold-dust of its heritage, but no one has properly recognized it or recorded it. The little that has been written about it has been written by foreign historians – some out of sport, some out of merriment. The shrivelled Phalgu that you see today was not always in this condition. The hills of southern Magadh were once covered with dense forests. Beyond the mountains, from the north to the south, the Mágadhii River valley was also covered with thick forests. Even a portion of the plains and the banks of the river were also forested. This heavily-forested Magadh used to enjoy an abundance of rainfall and thus the rivers were full of water twelve months out of the year. Because of the abundance of forests there was no problem of soil erosion, and because the forests contained the water there was very little severe flooding. Seeing the Magadh of today, it is difficult to imagine the lush green Magadh that once was.

points.body: “You are certainly aware of the fact that Magadh was once a vast empire. At the time of Ashoka and Samudragupta it was probably the largest empire in the world – but nothing lasts forever. Those glorious days came to an end and a cimmerian darkness descended over Magadh. The most difficult days in Magadhʼs history drew nigh during the reign of Skandagupta.”

points.body: He went on. “Skandagupta was one in a string of unworthy sovereigns to occupy the throne of Magadh. At that time the empire had disintegrated and the kingdom was on the point of collapse, confined to its ancient borders. To the north was the Ganges and north of that Mithila, which was at one time part of the empire of Magadh and which Ráŕhʼs King Shashanka had wrested from the hands of Magadh. To the east were the Grdhrakút́a and Cakravarttii Mountains. In the eastern region of the Grdhrakút́a Mountains was Angadesh and the Magadh Empire. King Shashanka of Ráŕh also took possession of these areas. In the eastern regions of the Cakravarttii Mountains was the land of Ráŕh, which came under Shashankaʼs direct rule. The southeast cornerʼs border was Sametashikhar. Next came ancient Ráŕh, which the king of Ráŕh had conquered. The southern portion of the Ramgarh Mountains to the south, and the western portion of the Shon River to the west were first controlled by the king of Kashi, Citrasena. After his fall, this entire area was controlled by the royal house of Thaniishvar. Magadh did not have a direct struggle with Prabhakaravardhana but rather with Rajyavardhana and Harsavardhana.

He founded Sanskrit schools and training centres in various parts of Magadh, such as Dvádashavardhaká (Barbigha), Brhadhiká (Barahiya), Madhukamadhá (Mokama), Urubilva (Arawal), Grdhrakút́a (Gidhaor), and so forth, which endured for quite some time.

points.body: “Of course, nothing in this world is completely one-sided. No matter how much historians blame him, Skandagupta did some good also. This city of Gaya, which we are standing in the heart of, was designed by him. He founded Sanskrit schools and training centres in various parts of Magadh, such as Dvádashavardhaká (Barbigha), Brhadhiká (Barahiya), Madhukamadhá (Mokama), Urubilva (Arawal), Grdhrakút́a (Gidhaor), and so forth, which endured for quite some time. He was the first to introduce the use of the Mágadhii language of that time (Western Demi-Mágadhii) in government service alongside Sanskrit. Still, he watched the Magadh Empire crumble in front of his eyes. He died watching an entire empire fall apart due to his own incompetence.

That is, during his time Bengal was divided into five political divisions: 1) Ráŕh, 2) Mithila, 3) Samatat, 4) Barendra, and 5) Vauṋga-D́abák (East Bengal or Shriibhúmi or Cat́t́al was then included in Bengal) – but he kept his capital at Karnasuvarna.
points.body: “At that time there was a fierce struggle going on for the capture of Magadh between King Rajyavardhana of the royal house of Thaniisvar and Ráŕhʼs King Shashanka. Thanisvaraʼs kings used to repeatedly move their capital from place to place, but Shashanka did not. Rather, he would enlarge his capital according to necessity and befitting the times. He founded Paiṋca Gaoŕa [the five ancient parts of Bengal] after capturing Anga and Mithila and then North Bengal (Barendra), Central Bengal (Samatat) and East Bengal (Vauṋga). That is, during his time Bengal was divided into five political divisions: 1) Ráŕh, 2) Mithila, 3) Samatat, 4) Barendra, and 5) Vauṋga-D́abák (East Bengal or Shriibhúmi or Cat́t́al was then included in Bengal) – but he kept his capital at Karnasuvarna. ( 6 )

points.title: “There were several reasons for the war between Rajyavardhana and Shashanka
points.prompt: Recall and explain from memory: “There were several reasons for the war between Rajyavardhana and Shashanka
summary: “There were several reasons for the war between Rajyavardhana and Shashanka.
Although Rajyavardhana put on a show of liberality he was really narrow-minded.
He openly declared that as long as one drop of blood remained in his body, he would not allow Buddhism the right to enter either Ráŕh or Paiṋca Gaoŕa ( 7 ) (Bengal).
points.body: “There were several reasons for the war between Rajyavardhana and Shashanka. Rajyavardhanaʼs aims were to plunder Magadhʼs wealth and to take possession of Angabhumi. Shashankaʼs main aims were to take possession of Angabhumi and to root out the Buddhist religion and culture from Magadh. Although Rajyavardhana put on a show of liberality he was really narrow-minded. In actual fact, he never treated the Shaivite religion as equal to the Buddhist religion. Shashanka was a staunch follower of Shaivism and completely against Buddhism. He openly declared that as long as one drop of blood remained in his body, he would not allow Buddhism the right to enter either Ráŕh or Paiṋca Gaoŕa ( 7 ) (Bengal).

points.body: “I am sure you are familiar with Ambabhumi, ( 8 ) which is situated in the western part of our Magadh. Ambabhumi was the ancient name of that fertile region (modern name Mokámá T́ál) composed of the western areas of what is now Monghyr District – Surajagara, Laksmiisarai, Baravigha, Barhiya, and so on; the eastern portion of Patna District, especially Mokama and surrounding areas; the eastern part of present-day Nalanda District; and the northeast areas of present-day Nawada District. There was no other region in all of India which was as fertile and as affluent at that time. Thus everyone had their greedy eyes set on Ambabhumi. Rajyavardhana and Shashanka were no exceptions.

You are certainly aware of the fact that, according to social and religious regulations, idols can no longer be used for worship once there is any defect or deformation in them.

points.body: “Their style of attack, however, differed. Rajyavardhana wanted to plunder wealth, so he would set fire to peopleʼs houses and ransack them. Shashankaʼs aim was to destroy Buddhist monasteries (what are now called gaŕa in modern Magahi) and Maháyána Buddhist images and idols. You are certainly aware of the fact that, according to social and religious regulations, idols can no longer be used for worship once there is any defect or deformation in them. So Shashanka had the different statues of Buddhist gods and goddesses deformed with a chisel. Today you will find that most of the ancient Buddhist religious statues still in existence have had their noses broken off.

Just as the geography of Magadh slopes downwards from north to south and the rivers flow from north to south, similarly the culture and civilization flowed from south to north. points.body: “Earlier I told you that in those days Magadh was full of forests and had abundant rainfall so there was no need of irrigation. The pre-Aryan people of Magadh used to believe that their land received rainfall due to the grace of the sun-god. Thus they used to worship the sun-god according to their ancient local customs, once during the autumn paddy harvest and again during the spring sun harvest (chaetii harvest). This sun-worship of pre-Aryan Magadh is known today as chat́ pújá. This worship was not performed according to Aryan rules. It was a completely local Magadh practice. The people of Magadh did not bow their heads and submissively accept any of the Aryan practices. For that reason the Aryans called the land Magadh. They were afraid of Magadh and used to pay it respect. Thus, to satisfy their grudge and vent their spite, they declared Magadh an unholy land. They said that if a man died there he would not go to heaven and they made efforts to forcibly impose their language, culture and civilization on Magadh. It is up to the historians and social scientists to consider just how successful they were in their efforts.

Of course, the spirit of revolt against conventionality was present in Vardhaman Mahavirʼs teachings also, but in the opinion of the Magahi people his doctrine of ahiḿsá [non-violence] did not accord well with reality so they were not able to accept it easily. Such was the case in this situation. Two youths of that time, Manotos Basu from Malakha Nagar in Dhaka District, and Shubhendu Narayana Guha from Banaripara in Bakharganj District, plunged bravely into terrorism under the inspiration of the itinerant poet, Mukunda Das. The police chief of East Bengal and Assam Province, Mr. Tegartt, scoured the region in a furious effort to capture them. Thereafter they quit East Bengal and Assam and came to Bengal where they continued to conduct their terrorist activities from Nawada in Gaya District. Nowadays I have realized that liberty means not only escaping the clutches of an external enemy; liberty means gaining oneʼs freedom from all kinds of bondages – economic, dialectical, intellectual, educational, linguistic and cultural. Geo-sentiment and racial sentiment alone are not all there is to freedom. External forces ruled this country because they were able to extract its essence, its vital juices. When they saw that they had to expend a lot of money to maintain the sugar cane production, when they saw that it was no longer profitable after having sucked the industry dry, then they left. They did not go due to any other pressure; economic difficulties forced them to leave. It is important to remember, both then and now, that it cannot be called freedom when black exploiters take the place of white exploiters. Even though the foreign powers have left, their exploitative machinery is still in place. That machinery will have to go. points.body: Anyhow, I was travelling from Maju to Makarda. This part of Howrah District is very fertile. It has been densely populated since ancient times. When Howrah fell within the jurisdiction of Burdwan, it was the pride of Bengal. Afterwards, when it came within Hooghly District, it was regarded as one of the prosperous areas of Hooghly District. Later on, when Hooghly District was divided and Howrah District was formed, this area remained within Howrah District. Partially without industry, partially industrialized, it was the jewel of the region, shedding its lustre on the whole of Bengal through its scholarship, industriousness and erudition. There was a time when the vast Sarasvati River used to flow through this area. The Sarasvati River came out of the main branch of the Bhagirathi River at Triveni in Hooghly Districtʼs Mogra Police Station. It came out from the right side of the Bhagirathi. The Yamuna [Jamuna, not the river of Uttar Pradesh] River came from the exact opposite direction, that is, from the left side of the Bhagirathi through the Chakda and Haringhata Police Stations of what was then Nadia District, the adjoining region. This confluence of the Ganges, Yamuna and Sarasvati Rivers is renowned as the Triveńitiirtha [holy confluence of three rivers] or the Mukta [liberated] Triveńii.

points.body: From there the Sarasvati flowed through the fertile, verdant grasslands and grain fields of Hooghly District until it reached Howrah District. There it used to flow past the meadows of kenduá on its right side. What we call nowadays the kenduá meadows was a vast lake in prehistoric times. The lake gradually filled up and turned into the kenduá marshlands or Kendua meadows. Up until a hundred years ago the rice and paddy crops never failed in the kenduá marshlands. Rice and rice paddy used to be exported from the port of Amta by ship to foreign lands along the Damodar River. Those days are gone. Nowadays the Damodar is almost dried up. Its water is not even knee-deep now, so the plying of ships is out of the question.

points.body: Makarda was situated close to the Sarasvati River in those days. Although a large part of the external trade of Bengal at that time was carried out from the Port de Bauṋgálá (Cat́t́agram) and the Port de Grandi (Saptagram), Makarda also was a busy port. Merchants belonging to the Saha, Tambuli, Gandhabanika and Suvaranabanika communities were the principle contributors to the growth of its wealth. Brahmins and Kayasthas brought the glow of scholarship, and the skilful peasants of the Máhiśya and Sadgope communities produced golden harvests. The heroism of the Kaevartta fishing community became famous far and wide. They were respected in the society as “Bara” [a surname], the best, and were primarily responsible for the formation of the navy of independent Bengal. This area was also home at that time to a shipbuilding factory where indigenous methods were used. That industry perished during British rule. The expert carpenters and Kaevartta fishermen of this place built those ships. The merchants of this area also set out to sea after loading their goods on those ships.

The pandits of Mithila would not allow anybody to copy their manuscripts on Navya Nyáya [new school of philosophy and logic], lest the pride of Mithila – the seat of Nyáya – be lost. points.body: In any case, on Raghunathʼs return to his native land as a reputed pandit in Nyáya, the people of Bengal welcomed him by lighting nine large lamps on the bank of the Ganges. Raghunath was a product of Purvasthali in Burdwan District. In those days, Burdwan was spread across both shores of the Ganges. Even though the eastern bank was Samatat-Bagri, it was better known as Vauṋga-Ráŕh. Those nine lamps in Raghunathʼs honour were lit on the eastern bank. So thenceforth that eastern bank, instead of being called Vauṋga-Ráŕh, was called “Navadiipa” [“Nine Lamps”]. And in the course of time there evolved the present name “Nadiiyá” [spelled in English contexts “Nadia”]. As far as I can see, the name Navadviipa, signifying a group of nine islands, is more logical. But yes, whatever I have said about Raghunath is true.

Like the Damodar, Banka, Khari, Badai and other rivers, the vast waters of the Devidaha as well as the Gangur used to keep Burdwan District green with grain. Historically, it can be seen that Burdwan District was the pioneer in sugar cane and cotton cultivation, the leading producer. The sugar cane there was sweeter than any place else. points.body: For the very same reason, the cultivation of both the mághii [winter] and caetii [spring] types of pigeon-peas (aŕahar dál) is fast diminishing in Burdwan. They are scarcely to be seen nowadays. Even though the Balagarh area of neighbouring Hooghly District was at one time considered the best for pigeon-pea cultivation, it bears mentioning that there also its cultivation has diminished greatly. Nowadays Purulia and Nadia Districts are preserving the standard of pigeon-pea production in Bengal. If some of the land in Purulia were not used for pigeon-peas, then it would remain barren for most of the year; thus, there is no recourse but to grow pigeon-peas there. And in Nadia the greater part of the soil is doṋyásh [mixed sandy and clayey soil]. Since there is very little clayey soil, many crops cannot be grown there. Still, in the Chakdah, Haringhata and Kalyani areas of Nadia the cultivation of both sugar cane and pigeon-peas (kandula – Kandulaḿ baladaḿ jiṋeyaḿ cośńaḿ tu hitakárakaḿ) is diminishing and kitchen vegetables are being grown in their place. Today Nadia District has turned into the worldʼs best district for growing vegetables. Of course, the traditional areas for growing potatoes have been Hooghly, Burdwan, Nalanda [Bihar] and Farukhbad [U.P.] Districts. The seeds that we import while sitting in Kolkata, such as the recently brought biliti tomato seeds from America, the difficult-to-get red radish seeds from Japan, the extremely long kuli eggplant seeds from China – some perhaps come from abroad but the better part of them are brought from Nadia Districtʼs Nagar-Ukhra, bought at bulk rate and stuffed into jute sacks.

The climate of Burdwan is somewhat drier than that of the rest of Bengal, thus those areas which are wetter than Burdwan used to buy cotton thread from Burdwan for weaving fine cloth. Cotton does not grow well in wetter climates; the cotton is subject to insect attack. However, these wetter climates are more suitable for weaving fine cloth. A short distance away ran the ruined remains of the Badshahi Road, the same road that Pathan Badshah Shershah constructed at the beginning of the Mughal era, with only a few skeletal traces left to identify it. Burdwan was then the capital of the province of Bengal. Badshahi Road used to connect Burdwan to Delhi in one direction, and in the other direction it connected to the principal port of the time, Saptagrám or Sátgáoṋ, to which the Portuguese gave the name Port-de-Grandee – it extended south along the Bhagirathi till Shyampur, and on the other bank it used to go via Jessore to Dhaka Districtʼs Suvarnagram (Sońárgáoṋ). Today the Badshahi Road is abandoned; some can recognize it if they see it, and some cannot.

summary: The classical language of India.
Although not a spoken language today except in very limited circumstances, it is still important for its vast literature, especially spiritual literature.
Sanskrit pronunciation was perfected by non-Aryan Tantrics in such a way that each of the fifty letters of the Sanskrit alphabet constitutes one acoustic root of Tantra.
points.body: SANSKRIT: SAḾSKRTA. The classical language of India. It first emerged during the Post-Shiva period, and as a spoken language it began to be supplanted by Prákrta prior to the Krśńa period. Although not a spoken language today except in very limited circumstances, it is still important for its vast literature, especially spiritual literature. Sanskrit and English are the languages of the world that have the richest vocabularies. Sanskrit pronunciation was perfected by non-Aryan Tantrics in such a way that each of the fifty letters of the Sanskrit alphabet constitutes one acoustic root of Tantra.

SAḾSKRTA. The classical language of India. It first emerged during the Post-Shiva period, and as a spoken language it began to be supplanted by Prákrta prior to the Krśńa period. Although not a spoken language today except in very limited circumstances, it is still important for its vast literature, especially spiritual literature. Sanskrit and English are the languages of the world that have the richest vocabularies. Sanskrit pronunciation was perfected by non-Aryan Tantrics in such a way that each of the fifty letters of the Sanskrit alphabet constitutes one acoustic root of Tantra.
